spot_at_127827.title: Deokgasan Mountain
spot_at_127827.overview: Deokgasan Mountain is a beautiful peak located in Kim Sat-gat-myeon, Yeongwol-gun, Gangwon-do. Standing at an elevation of 832 meters, it is famous for its magnificent joints, valleys, and waterfalls spanning dozens of meters. From the summit of Deokgasan, hikers can view Yeongwol's major prominent mountains at a glance, making it a favorite hiking course among mountaineers. One of the most popular spots on Deokgasan is the Eolkuri Valley and Waterfall. Eolkuri Valley is a clear and refreshing stream flowing along the Okdongcheon Stream, perfect for water play in the summer. There are several waterfalls of varying heights, of which Eolkuri Waterfall is the tallest at approximately 20 meters. With its high vantage point, the powerfully cascading water and the deep pool below are breathtaking. Gossi-gul Cave, situated on the southern foothills of Deokgasan, got its name from the legend that people with the surname Go lived there during the Goryeo Dynasty. Approximately 300 meters long, the cave houses various types of limestone formations and cave dwelling organisms. At the cave entrance, the Gossi-gul Cave Cultural Center offers detailed insights into the cave's history and ecology. Near the summit of Deokgasan stands a stone pagoda structure presumed to be built during the Joseon Dynasty, featuring decorative patterns and carvings on each of its five tiers. Combining living nature and history, Deokgasan is frequently visited by hikers and tourists alike.

spot_at_127826.title: Gukjisan Mountain
spot_at_127826.overview: Gukjisan Mountain is an elevation 626m peak located south of the Seogang River, marking the tail end of the Yeongwol-jimaek mountain ridge. Connected to Wangbaksan, Gachangsan, Samtaesan, and Taehwasan, it sits about 5 km south of Cheongnyeongpo, the place of exile for King Danjong, the 6th monarch of the Joseon Dynasty. Visitors can view the monument of King Danjong and Chilyongdong-gol Valley together. Its gentle and soft mountain terrain makes it ideal for family hikes. Rather than the summit, it is recommended to enjoy the view from Mangbawi Rock just before reaching the peak. To the north, Bongraesan and Gyejoksan embrace Yeongwol-eup, with the ridges of Wantraeksan and Gogosan peaks stretching between them. To the southeast, Taehwasan stands like a folding screen, while far to the right, the main ridge of Sobaeksan Mountain connecting to Sinseonbong, Gukmangbong, and Sobaeksan can also be admired. There are two hiking trails: one starting from Hanjaesan Mountain and another from Sinseonbong. The trail from Hanjaesan is about 4.5 km long, takes roughly 3 hours, and follows Gukjigol-gil Road. The trail from Sinseonbong is about 3 km long, takes roughly 2 hours, and passes through Geomgaksan Mountain. From the summit of Gukjisan, hikers can appreciate the winding Seogang River and surrounding peaks. Nearby attractions include Cheongnyeongpo Exile Camp, Seonam Village's Korean Peninsula Topography, and Jangneung (the tomb of King Danjong surrounded by lush pine forests), making it wonderful to combine nature and cultural heritage visits in Yeongwol.

spot_at_127303.title: Moguasan Mountain
spot_at_127303.overview: Moguasan Mountain stands at an elevation of 1,066 meters, adjacent between Nokjeon-ri in Jungdong-myeon and Naeri-ri in Hadong-myeon. Moguasan is called by different names depending on the viewing angle. In Nokjeon-ri, Sansol-myeon, it is called Moguasan because many cattle were grazed here, whereas in Naeri-ri, Kim Sat-gat-myeon, it is called Sangyeobong Peak because the rock peak resembles a traditional funeral bier (sangyeo). In the local dialect of Yeongwol-gun, Sangyeobong is also referred to as Saengaebong Peak. Okdongcheon Stream flows to the north and Naericheon Stream flows to the south, merging west of Moguasan. Being deeply remote, it served as a hideout for partisans after liberation, and ruins of houses and hideouts where armed guerrillas from Uljin-Samcheok infiltrated and massacred civilians in the 1960s still remain along the hiking trail. From the summit, visitors can view breathtaking panoramas of Taehwasan, Taebaeksan, and the scenic beauty of Nokjeon-ri and Naeri Valleys. It is also popular among rock-climbing enthusiasts due to various rock-climbing courses of different difficulties. Large-scale campsites operate in Naeri Valley at the southern foot, allowing campers to enjoy the beautiful natural scenery of Moguasan. There are two hiking routes for Moguasan: one in Nokjeon-ri, Sansol-myeon, and the other in Naeri-ri, Kim Sat-gat-myeon. The Nokjeon-ri route starts from Eonghyeon-dong, Nokjeon-ri, Sansol-myeon—where National Route 31 connecting Yeongwol and Taebaek passes—and ascends to the main ridge via Moguasa Temple. Descending via the right path from the summit, hikers head down to Jeolgol via the fork. Currently, the Nokjeon-ri route is the most common. The Naeri-ri route in Kim Sat-gat-myeon starts from Soyachi and ascends to the summit.

spot_at_1395991.title: Ulsan Theme Botanic Gardens
spot_at_1395991.overview: Ulsan Theme Botanic Gardens is a forest recreation and cultural space in the southern region of the East Sea, serving as a venue for nature study and academic research featuring various trees and native plants. Key facilities include Rosemary Road, a fruit tree garden, crape myrtle garden, conifer garden, maple garden, petroglyph waterfall garden, Rose of Sharon garden, greenhouse, experiential learning center, and aquatic botanical garden, alongside amenities like a rest area, sky observatory, gallery, and café. Additional attractions include a reptile experience center, rest areas, sculpture park, summer event space, sledding slope, and a playground. It also runs nature ecology programs, career experience programs, environmental education programs, and forest interpretation programs for everyone from kindergarteners to elementary, middle, and high school students, as well as the general public. Horseback riding and feeding experiences are also available. Distinguishing itself from amusement-focused botanical gardens, it aims to be an integrated and systematic botanical garden that preserves the natural environment to the utmost while considering plant characteristics, visitor convenience, and land use. Through the propagation and management of disappearing native plants, it promotes the permanent preservation and restoration of rare and endangered species through ex-situ conservation.

spot_at_1624499.title: Sungansungmot Ecological Park
spot_at_1624499.overview: Located in Jung-gu, Ulsan, Sungmot Ecological Park is a relaxing resting space for local residents where they can enjoy peaceful views of lotuses and water lilies. Well-maintained walking trails, benches, fountains, and pedestrian decks make it an even more pleasant place to visit. Sungmot Pond is associated with the legends of 'Dongbangsak, who lived for 30 kalpas,' and 'Grandma Mago,' who reportedly caught him. Although it was once a tiny pond comparable to a small wooden bowl, it has now been expanded with support from the city, giving it the true stature of a proper pond.

spot_at_1824216.title: Seonam Lake Park
spot_at_1824216.overview: For 40 years, barbed wire fences were installed across the entire 1.2㎢ watershed area for water quality preservation and safety following the installation of industrial water supply facilities, turning it into an alienated and underdeveloped area avoided by people compared to other regions. The barbed wire fences dividing nature and humans have been removed, and walking trails and facilities with various themes have been created utilizing the beautiful natural scenery around the reservoir. Visitors can take a relaxing stroll around the lake while breathing in phytoncides.

spot_fo_3024302.title: Sanneomeo Namchon
spot_fo_3024302.overview: Sanneomeo Namchon specializes in dried Alaska pollock (kodari) braised with radish greens (siraegi), featuring a special sauce crafted by the owner—whose hometown is Gangwon-do—and premium siraegi supplied exclusively through contract farming with Gangwon farms. Starting with its main branch near Jujeon Mongdol Beach and Jujeon Port in Dong-gu, Ulsan, the restaurant now also operates a 2nd branch (Ilsan Branch) near Ilsan Beach. Recognized as a gourmet spot by Ulsan locals, it has been acclaimed for nearly 10 years as a specialist in braised siraegi kodari. It has appeared on MBC and KBS television broadcasts and was selected as one of Ulsan's representative restaurants by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport in 2019. Additionally, the owner runs a café on the 3rd floor of the same building; visitors presenting their restaurant receipt receive discounts on all menu beverages and ice cream, and the café can be rented for group reservations. Savor the braised siraegi kodari on the 2nd floor, then relax with a dessert drink on the 3rd floor.

spot_at_126260.title: Jikso Falls (Jeonbuk West Coast National Geopark)
spot_at_126260.overview: Jikso Falls is a representative attraction in Naebyeonsan, Buan. Standing about 30 meters tall, water plunges directly into a round basin below, earning it the name 'Jikso' (meaning 'directing straight'). As the 2nd valley of Bongraegugok, it features a bottomless dragon pool (yongso) beneath the falls. Legend has it that a dragon once lived here, and local magistrates used to hold rain rituals in times of severe drought. Designated as a West Coast National Geopark site, visitors can learn about the formation process of Byeonsan tuff and columnar joints surrounding the falls. These columns, mostly pentagons and hexagons under 1m wide, form a vertical colonnade stretching dozens of meters high. Formed through rapid cooling and contraction of volcanic tephra, Jikso's hidden beauty has earned it the nickname 'Little Geumgang of the Inland'. With a gentle slope accessible to all ages, it is a popular 2.3km trail in Byeonsan-gwan peninsula National Park taking about 50 minutes. Beautiful flowers, including cherry blossoms in late April, and nearby spots like Silsangsa Temple make it a year-round favorite.

spot_at_1611910.title: Janggunmok Tourist Resort
spot_at_1611910.overview: Located in Naeryong Village, Ochi-ri, 7km from Donggye-myeon, Janggunmok Resort preserves the pristine natural scenery of the upper reaches of the Seomjingang River. Flowing down from Demisaem Spring in Jinan, the river reveals rocks that look like kneaded dough, creating unique shapes and stunning scenery that drew visitors over time. The local freshwater snails (daseulgi) are small, plump, and dark brown, producing a deeply refreshing, clear bluish broth. The Seomjingang River flowing through Sunchang-gun—from Janggunmok in Naeryong Village to Hyangga Village in Daega-ri, Pungsan-myeon—is also called Jeokseonggang River.

spot_at_231953.title: Iksan Ipjeom-ri Tombs
spot_at_231953.overview: The Iksan Ipjeom-ri Tombs are a Baekje-era tomb cluster located in Ipjeom-ri, Ungpo-myeon, Iksan-si, Jeollabuk-do. In the spring of 1986, a local resident accidentally discovered a tomb and found artifacts such as a gilt-bronze cap. An emergency investigation in the fall of 1986 excavated 8 tombs, and further investigations by Wonkwang University's Mahan Baekje Cultural Research Institute in 1998 identified 13 more tombs as part of a restoration project. Out of 21 tombs in total, 19 were Baekje tombs, comprising 11 stone-lined pit tombs, 1 stone-lined tomb with an open entrance, and 7 stone-chamber tombs with corridor entrances. Believed to date back to the 5th century, these tombs offer valuable insight into how Baekje central ruling-class burial systems penetrated and took root in a region previously dominated by indigenous local ruling-class customs.

spot_fo_2870741.overview: Located in Deokjin-gu, Jeonju-si, Jeongin Garden is a renowned duck cuisine restaurant that operated near the Jeonju Museum for decades before relocating to a newly built facility in Palbok-dong. Continuing a 27-year tradition of duck culinary excellence in Jeonju, it offers healthy food highlighted by its popular, crowd-pleasing duck jumulog served with an abundance of fresh ssam (wrap) vegetables. spot_at_129282.title: Geum-myeon Cotton Park
spot_at_129282.addr: 1860 Goksun-ro, Geum-myeon, Gokseong-gun, Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated City
spot_at_129282.overview: In autumn, Cotton Park blooms with cotton and buckwheat flowers, offering plenty of shade to escape the summer heat. Located on the riverbank of Geum-myeoncheon Stream flowing between the Honam Expressway and National Route 27, the park features stepping stones and wooden deck bridges that submerge slightly when water levels rise, allowing easy access. Inside the deck path, visitors can relax in a pavilion and read informative signs about cotton production. The park features a small playground, a pond, and a plant tunnel cutting across the cotton field. For an extended experience, Geum-myeon Cotton Village is located 530m straight across the stream. Dorimsa Valley is also a 15-minute drive (about 13km) away.

spot_at_250346.title: Deogyangseowon Confucian Academy (Gokseong)
spot_at_250346.addr: 42 Deogyangseowon-gil, Oegok-myeon, Gokseong-gun, Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated City
spot_at_250346.overview: Deogyangseowon is a Confucian academy dedicated to General Sin Sung-gyeom, the founder of the Pyeongsan Sin clan and a key contributor to the founding of Goryeo. General Sin aided Wang Geon in overthrowing Gungye and establishing Goryeo, earning top merits as a founding contributor. Originally built in the 22nd year of King Seonjo's reign (1589) to enshrine his spirit tablet, the academy was entirely burned down during the Japanese Invasions of Korea (Imjin War). The shrine was restored in the 36th year of King Seonjo (1603) and completely rebuilt to its pre-1655 scale by the 6th year of King Hyeonjong (1665). It received the royal signboard 'Deogyang' in 1695, contributing to ancestral veneration and local education until it was dismantled in 1871 under Daewongun's decree. It was later restored in 1934 by local Confucian scholars and stands to this day. The complex includes a lecture hall, Yeonseojae (east study), Deogyangsa (shrine), Sindeokjae (west study), Jeonsacheong (ritual storage), and outer and inner gates. Notable heritage items include the Deogyangseowon Gonsasajeokbi Monument and 19 hanging boards inside the lecture hall and Yeonseojae. It is designated as part of the 'Gokseong Sin Sung-gyeom Historic Site' (Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated City Monument) alongside Yongsanjae, Gyemaseok, and Yeongjeokbigak. Located at the end of Deogyangseowon-gil, it is a 7-minute drive (4 km) from Gokseong Bus Terminal.

paragraphs: Deogyangseowon is a Confucian academy dedicated to General Sin Sung-gyeom, the founder of the Pyeongsan Sin clan and a key contributor to the founding of Goryeo. Originally built in the 22nd year of King Seonjo's reign (1589) to enshrine his spirit tablet, the academy was entirely burned down during the Japanese Invasions of Korea (Imjin War). The shrine was restored in the 36th year of King Seonjo (1603) and completely rebuilt to its pre-1655 scale by the 6th year of King Hyeonjong (1665). It received the royal signboard 'Deogyang' in 1695, contributing to ancestral veneration and local education until it was dismantled in 1871 under Daewongun's decree. It was later restored in 1934 by local Confucian scholars and stands to this day. The complex includes a lecture hall, Yeonseojae (east study), Deogyangsa (shrine), Sindeokjae (west study), Jeonsacheong (ritual storage), and outer and inner gates. Notable heritage items include the Deogyangseowon Gonsasajeokbi Monument and 19 hanging boards inside the lecture hall and Yeonseojae. It is designated as part of the 'Gokseong Sin Sung-gyeom Historic Site' (Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated City Monument) alongside Yongsanjae, Gyemaseok, and Yeongjeokbigak. Located at the end of Deogyangseowon-gil, it is a 7-minute drive (4 km) from Gokseong Bus Terminal.

spot_at_128082.title: Gwaneunsa Temple (Gokseong)
spot_at_128082.addr: 453 Seongdeokgwaneun-gil, Osan-myeon, Gokseong-gun, Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated City
spot_at_128082.overview: Gwaneunsa Temple in Gokseong can be reached by following the valley further up from Sanse-maeul Village. According to legend, the temple was founded in the 3rd year of King Bunseo of Baekje (300 AD), when Bodhisattva Seongdeok brought and enshrined a gilt-bronze Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva statue from Beolgyo in Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated City. During the Korean War, guerillas used Gwaneunsa as a base for a prolonged period, leading troops to set fire to the temple to flush them out. As a result, the Wontongjeon Hall—a designated national treasure dating back to the Goryeo Dynasty—burned down, and the enshrined National Treasure Gilt-Bronze Seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva was damaged by fire, leaving only the head intact. Gwaneunsa is associated with the touching folktale of Won Hong-jang, known for her profound filial piety and devotion. This story is widely known to be related to the classic novel 'Simcheongjeon'. The Gwaneunsasajeokgi (Chronicles of Gwaneunsa Temple), believed to be the origin of the ancient novel Simcheongjeon, is currently preserved at Songgwangsa Temple in Suncheon.

spot_fo_2871838.title: Illo Jangteo Baekban
spot_fo_2871838.addr: 17-12 Sijang-gil, Muan-gun, Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated City (Illo Jangteo Baekban)
spot_fo_2871838.overview: Illo Jangteo Baekban is a hearty homestyle restaurant that fully embodies the flavors and warm hospitality of Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated City. Illo, known as the birthplace of Korea's first traditional market during the Joseon Dynasty, features several baekban (rice and side dishes) eateries. Among them, Illo Jangteo Baekban stands out for offering a table overflowing with delicious side dishes at an affordable price. Serving a single baekban set menu, their rice cooked with green peas is delightfully chewy and flavorful. True to Jeolla-do cuisine, various pickled vegetables (jangajji), scallion kimchi, and traditional kimchi offer the authentic taste of Korean home cooking. This popular dining spot has also been featured on TV broadcasts.

spot_fo_2871886.title: Yulpo Botjae Garden
spot_fo_2871886.addr: 2299 Nambu Gwanwang-ro, Boseong-gun, Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated City
spot_fo_2871886.overview: Yulpo Botjae Garden is a renowned restaurant near Yulpo Beach. The name 'Botjae' carries the meaning of putting down a heavy baggage bundle and taking a short rest. Their green tea cockle bibimbap has been featured on the TV show 'Live Broadcast Today'. The signature menu is gangdoenjang ssambap (wrapped rice with thick soybean paste), featuring homemade gangdoenjang crafted from 14 different ingredients. The standard ssambap course includes green tea marsh snail gangdoenjang ssambap, stir-fried spicy pork, seasoned raw cockles, and cheonggukjang (rich fermented soybean paste stew). Cheonggukjang, gangdoenjang, and salted hairtail viscera (galchisokjeot) are also available for purchase separately, and extra rice can be ordered if needed. With 110 seats available, it is well-suited for group gatherings. They also operate a minbak (guesthouse); guests who dine or stay can purchase discount vouchers for Boseong's famous seawater baths. Conveniently located near the Boseong Green Tea Fields and Yulpo Beach, it is an ideal spot to explore.

spot_at_2758472.title: Wonsusan Wetland Ecological Park
spot_at_2758472.overview: Located in Sejong-ri, Yeongi-myeon, Sejong Special Self-Governing City, Wonsusan Wetland Ecological Park is an ecological experience space where visitors can fully enjoy nature in the city center. Designed to preserve the natural environment of Mount Wonsusan, this space allows visitors to observe a wetland ecosystem inhabited by various organisms and plants. Connected to the Wonsusan Dulle-gil (perimeter trail), visitors can enjoy walking and ecological experiences simultaneously amidst nature. It also serves as a venue for environmental education through communion with nature. The wetland park is especially popular among children and family visitors as a place to realize the value of nature. The perimeter trail features a gentle slope, making it safe for children and the elderly, and is equipped with wooden boardwalks and resting areas for a comfortable relaxation.

spot_at_2761431.addr: Yeongdae-ri, Geumnam-myeon, Sejong Special Self-Governing City
spot_at_2761431.overview: Baramjae Rest Area is located in Yeongdae-ri, Geumnam-myeon, Sejong City, and can be encountered while walking along Courses 1 and 2 of the Bihaksan-Geumbyeongsan Nurigil Trail. The Nurigil is a trekking course suitable for the whole family, featuring lush forests that allow visitors to enjoy a cool and comfortable hike beneath tree shades even in summer. It is also famous as a pit stop where bicycle riders drop by to take a break. The rest area is well-equipped with a photo zone, pavilions, resting benches, exercise equipment, and walking paths. Nearby attractions include the Geumgang Waterside Park Campground and South Sejong IC.

spot_at_2761645.title: Wonsusan MTB Park
spot_at_2761645.overview: Wonsusan MTB Park is located in Sejong-ri, Yeongi-myeon, Sejong City, offering refreshing views of Mount Wonsusan from the park. The park is equipped with an administration office, a bicycle repair shop, rest areas, hiking trails, MTB courses, and a BMX stadium. The BMX stadium was established by the Korea Cycling Federation, funded by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the National Sports Promotion Foundation, with the site provided by Sejong City to nurture youth athletes. The MTB courses for cycling include Wonsusan Course A (a basic beginner course with gentle and low slopes), Wonsusan Downhill Course A (a downhill course utilizing natural terrain), and Wonsusan Course B (featuring steep gradients and rugged terrain). In addition, hiking trails for walkers are well-marked with guide signs for easy navigation.

spot_fo_2871496.title: Songha Min-eo-gui (Grilled Croaker)
spot_fo_2871496.addr: 72 Unjusan-ro, Jochiwon-eup, Sejong Special Self-Governing City
spot_fo_2871496.overview: Located in Jochiwon, Sejong City, Songha Min-eo-gui is a Korean restaurant specializing in mi-eo (brown croaker) dishes. Built in traditional Korean hanok style, the exterior exudes classical elegance, while the interior is decorated with a warm and serene atmosphere. The signature menu here is a set menu featuring grilled croaker and bulgogi hot pot, available in various sizes from 2 to 5 people, making it a great choice for groups. The croaker is neatly cleaned and prepared for easy eating, offering a light, tender flavor completely free of any fishy odor, leaving diners highly satisfied. It is also a popular summer stamina-boosting food. Thanks to its quiet and comfortable atmosphere, it is an ideal venue for family gatherings or small get-togethers with friends.

With a clean and calm exterior and interior, it features a window with a panoramic mountain view, allowing visitors to enjoy brunch while looking out at the forest and trees. The signature menu is the Sous-Vide Whole Chicken Salad, which features a whole sous-vide chicken roasted in a traditional kiln with spicy barbecue seasoning, topped with a balsamic-based salad. Other options include hollow-bread salad, burrata cheese salad, flat iron cube steak, margherita pizza, and gorgonzola pizza. Coffee, ades, and beverages made with homemade fruit preserves are also available to complement the meal. Nearby attractions include the Geumgang Arboretum and Sejong Children's Astronomical Observatory, making it a great place to visit together.

spot_fo_2871723.title: Daenamu Hansoban
spot_fo_2871723.overview: Daenamu Hansoban is a Korean table d'hôte (hanjeongsik) specialty restaurant located in Bongan-ri, Janggun-myeon, Sejong-si. Its signature dish is gochujang bulgogi (spicy pork stir-fried with red chili paste), popular for its deep and harmonious seasoning. In addition, various dishes such as braised cod (kodari-jjim), grilled tteokgalbi, barley gulbi (dried yellow croaker), and mushroom bulgogi are available, each characterized by healthy flavors that highlight the natural taste of the ingredients. Set menus combining popular dishes like gochujang bulgogi with barley gulbi, or grilled tteokgalbi with barley gulbi, are also offered so guests can enjoy multiple dishes in one sitting. The spacious and comfortable interior features group seating, making it suitable for group gatherings and family events such as formal wedding-negotiation meetings. After the meal, visitors can spend time exploring nearby attractions like the National Sejong Arboretum and Sejong Lake Park.

spot_at_3447787.title: Seongheungsan Love Tree (Buyeo Garimseong Zelkova Tree)
spot_at_3447787.overview: Climbing the stairs next to the rock cliff reveals a huge tree standing tall on a stone foundation. This zelkova tree is over 400 years old and has grown into a heart shape, earning it the nickname 'Seongheungsan Love Tree'. With its half-heart-shaped branches and long history of over 400 years, the Love Tree was registered as a Natural Monument in 2021, drawing countless tourists every year. Serving as a scenic backdrop, the tree has gained popularity as a filming location for various TV dramas such as <Seodongyo>, <Painter of the Wind>, and <Hotel Del Luna>. Various events, such as the Sunrise Festival and memorial rites for the nameless soldiers of Baekje, are held in the open area where the Love Tree stands.

spot_at_125990.title: Seosan Haemi Eupseong Walled Town
spot_at_125990.overview: Constructed in 1491 during the reign of King Seongjong of the Joseon Dynasty, Seosan Haemi Eupseong is a representative flatland walled town featuring well-preserved stone walls approximately 1.8 km in circumference, along with the East, South, and West gates. Following restoration projects, it is now established as a historical park where visitors can walk along the fortress walls and examine Joseon-era architecture and defense systems. The expansive interior and serene scenery make it a popular destination for enjoying both history and a peaceful walk. This site is also where countless Catholics suffered torture and martyrdom during the Catholic persecutions in the late Joseon Dynasty, leaving behind historical remains imbued with painful history, such as prison sites, scholar trees, and execution stones. These historical traces left across the fortress walls evoke the sorrow of modern Korean history and the meaning of faith, making it a deeply meaningful space for historical education and cultural exploration.

spot_at_3036485.title: Wolyeongsan Suspension Bridge
spot_at_3036485.overview: Wolyeongsan Suspension Bridge is a towerless bridge designed with a height of 45m, a length of 275m, and a width of 1.5m, connecting Wolyeongsan and Buungsan Mountains. It is also known as the Wolyeongsan Hendeuldaри (Rocking Bridge). Flowing beneath the suspension bridge are the upstream waters of the Geumgang River, allowing visitors to take in a panoramic view of the beautiful waterfront scenery where mountains and river harmonize. Designed without main towers, the bridge offers an intense swaying sensation, providing an exhilarating thrill. After enjoying the thrill, visitors can experience nature by walking along a 1-km deck trail connected to the Wongol Artificial Waterfall. In addition, the nearby Ginseng Eojuk Village offers a chance to taste eojuk (spicy fish porridge with noodles and rice), a representative local delicacy of Geumsan. The Wolyeongsan Suspension Bridge is accessible via Provincial Road No. 68 from the Geumsan, Okcheon, and Yeongdong directions, and is also close to Geumsan IC on the Daejeon-Tongyeong Expressway.

spot_at_125841.title: Muchangpo Beach
spot_at_125841.overview: Opened in 1928, Muchangpo Beach is the oldest bathing resort on the west coast. Featuring a 1.5-km sandy beach, a water depth of 1-2 meters, a 50-meter width, a water temperature of 22°C, and a 4-degree slope, it is surrounded by lush pine forests, allowing visitors to enjoy both sea bathing and forest bathing. Enhanced by the picturesque natural scenery of bizarre rocks and pine trees, Muchangpo Beach attracts numerous tourists every year for sea fishing and abundant groundwater. In particular, 2 to 3 times around the full moon and new moon of the lunar calendar each month, a 1.5-km sea path opens from the beach to Seokdaedo Island, known as the 'Miracle of Moses'. This mysterious parting of the sea occurs during low tide when the seabed is exposed, and once the path opens, it is a delight to catch crabs and clams along the way. Climbing the Muchangpo Observatory, located on a hill 50 meters from the entrance of Muchangpo, offers a panoramic view of the magnificent sea parting spectacle. Inspired by this parting phenomenon, the Muchangpo Mystic Sea Road Festival is held annually to coincide with the opening of the sea path during the lunar full and new moons, featuring celebrity congratulatory performances, torchlight fishing experiences, a torchlight parade along the mystical sea road, bare-handed fish catching, and various hands-on activities such as doksal fishing, clam gathering, and razor clam catching.

spot_at_2746222.title: Maetdolpo Port
spot_at_2746222.overview: Maetdolpo Port is a cozy little harbor where fishing boats are moored. It is called Maetdolpo because when the tide comes in, the bow turns to the right, and when the tide goes out, it turns to the left, resembling a traditional stone mill (maetdol). This place is frequently visited by fishing enthusiasts. You can often see people sitting on folding chairs set up on one side of the pier, enjoying fishing while admiring the sea in front of Maetdolpo. Many visitors also stop by nearby restaurants to taste fresh seafood. Not far from the port are Sapgyocheo Battleship Park and Dangjin Marine Camping Park, making it great for a combined tour.

spot_at_250259.title: Buyeo Naseong Fortress [UNESCO World Heritage]
spot_at_250259.overview: Buyeo Naseong is an outer wall fortress built to protect Sabi, the capital of Baekje, and to distinguish the inside and outside of the capital city. It is estimated to have been constructed around 538 when the capital was relocated from Ungjin to Sabi, utilizing natural terrain to defend the capital. It was built by connecting hills and low flatlands, with construction methods varying according to the terrain. On the hills, the outer part of the rammed-earth wall was finished with stones, while in the low-lying flatlands, the foundation was reinforced by laying branches and leaves or driving wooden stakes. Along with neighboring mountain fortresses, it formed the defense system of the capital Sabi. Nearby attractions include the Buyeo Royal Tombs, Neungangol Ancient Tombs in Buyeo, and the National Buyeo Museum.

spot_at_3033248.title: Gwanggyosan Mountain Hyeongjebong Peak
spot_at_3033248.overview: Hyeongjebong Peak is a 448-meter-high peak located in the southern part of Gwanggyosan Mountain, stretching across Suwon, Yongin, and Uiwang. With a round-trip hiking course of about 2 to 4 hours, it is close to the city center and not too difficult even for beginners, making it a constantly bustling destination. Gwanggyosan Mountain, ranked as the 2nd of the 8 Scenic Views of Yongin, boasts lush forests that allow for shaded hiking and forest bathing even in summer, as well as beautiful snowscapes. In particular, the hiking trail leading up to Hyeongjebong features Cheonnyeonsu Mineral Spring, famous for its great-tasting water. Hyeongjebong can be climbed from both Yongin and Suwon. The representative Yongin course starts from Teacher Jo Gwang-jo's Tomb (Sanghyeon-dong) → Maebong Mineral Spring → Beodeulchi Pass → Cheonnyeonsu Spring → Hyeongjebong, totaling 5.3 km and taking about 2 to 2.5 hours—the longest among the routes. With an average slope of 17 degrees, it is generally manageable; however, the Beodeulchi Pass to Cheonnyeonsu Spring section has a milder 7-degree slope, which might feel slightly tame for thrill-seeking hikers. The Suwon course typically runs from Kyongji University / Gwanggyo Park → Firefly Restroom → Cheonnyeonsu Spring → Baegnyeonsu Summit → Hyeongjebong, covering 3.4 km in about 1 to 1.5 hours, making it relatively short. Also suitable for children in upper elementary grades and above, it features a large parking lot and restrooms, making it the most popular starting point. Regardless of whether you start from Yongin or Suwon, the trails merge at Cheonnyeonsu Spring before heading to Baegnyeonsu and the Hyeongjebong summit, where a breathtaking panoramic view awaits. For those with extra energy, you can continue past Hyeongjebong (448m) and Birobong (490m) all the way to Sirubong (585m), the highest peak of Gwanggyosan. Most hikers prefer starting from the Suwon side because the large Gwanggyo Public Parking Lot (located in Gwanggyo Reservoir and Park) and Kyonggi University Suwon Campus parking lot connect directly to the trailhead. Note that the Firefly Restroom at the entrance of the hiking trail is the last restroom available, so be sure to use it before starting your hike.

spot_at_2633936.title: Oido Prehistoric Village
spot_at_2633936.overview: Oido Site is a representative shell midden (shell mound) on the central west coast of South Korea, providing invaluable material for studying the coastal lifestyle and culture of prehistoric Korea. Designated as National Historic Site No. 441 in 2002, the Oido Prehistoric Village was established to preserve and utilize this national heritage, officially opening on April 10, 2018. The park features a Prehistoric Experience Village showcasing various ancient lifestyles, a camping village where visitors can experience dugout huts, excavation sites, and hunting grounds. Additionally, it offers diverse attractions including the Shell Midden Exhibition Hall highlighting the significance of the Neolithic Oido shell mounds, an observatory to enjoy Oido's stunning sunsets, and the scenic Silver Grass Walking Path.

spot_at_2662927.title: Mulwang Lake
spot_at_2662927.overview: Mulwang Lake, the largest lake in Siheung-si, is also known as Heungbu Reservoir. When the reservoir was created in 1945, the administrative districts were Siheung-gun and Bucheon-gun, combining 'Heung' from Siheung and 'Bu' from Bucheon. It is the largest freshwater lake and a premier resting spot in Siheung. Located close to the Seoul metropolitan area including Anyang and Ansan, it is surrounded by Gwanmusan (also known as Seonginbong), Mahasan, and Unhungsan mountains. A bicycle path between Podong Abandoned Salt Farm and Mulwang Lake was established in 2003, and its proximity to the Suin Industrial Road ensures convenient transportation and abundant amenities. Renamed from Mulwang Reservoir to Mulwang Lake in 2023, the rainbow that stretches across the lake after rain is said to be as beautiful as a fairy tale landscape. With its stunning nighttime lake views enhanced by colorful lighting, Mulwang Lake is a place visitors want to return to, offering the fun of discovering hidden local eateries and diverse cafes tucked away in every corner, complemented by seasonal flowers and trees.

spot_at_2732218.title: Yongin Mir Stadium (Yongin Citizens Sports Park)
spot_at_2732218.overview: Equipped with natural turf, a playing field, and a urethane track, this stadium is the first of its kind of a similar scale in Korea to use a pure Korean name. It is a compound word of 'Mir', the pure Korean word for dragon, and 'Stadium'. It consists of the main stadium, Yongin Children's Forest of Imagination, ticket booth deck plaza, and a health walking path. On the 2nd floor of the main stadium, there is an 800m walking path covered with natural turf where visitors can take a stroll regardless of heatwaves or rain.

spot_fo_2867494.title: Changnaeri Mukjib
spot_fo_2867494.overview: Changnaeri Mukjib is a mukbab (rice in acorn jelly soup) restaurant located in Changnae-ri, Osong-myeon, Pyeongtaek-si, Gyeonggi-do. Operating with just a banner instead of a signboard, it has gained word-of-mouth fame enough to be featured on TV programs. Because it uses a regular residential house, the interior features both Western-style tables and traditional sitting tables in the master room with mother-of-pearl wardrobes and the wide wooden porch (daecheongmaru), giving it a cozy, familiar feel like visiting a country home. The signature menu is mukbab, but they also serve potato pancakes, seasoned acorn jelly salad, handmade dumpling soup, and goat soup. Mukbab can be ordered cold or warm, and is served with a mix of acorn jelly (dotorimuk) and mung bean jelly (changpomuk). It comes with a bowl of rice so you can mix it in or eat it separately according to your preference. The jelly salad features thick strips of acorn jelly tossed with various vegetables, and the potato pancakes are thick yet crispy. They also sell homemade dongdongju (traditional rice wine).

spot_fo_2867277.title: Patseonsaeng
spot_fo_2867277.overview: Patseonsaeng is a red bean porridge specialty restaurant located in Bisan-dong, Anyang. All ingredients are domestically sourced, and piles of pumpkins and red beans greet visitors upon entering. Patseonsaeng is popular among many visitors for offering red bean porridge made with local ingredients at a very affordable price. The red bean porridge is not overly sweet and has just the right seasoning. With generous portions, it makes a hearty and satisfying meal. The pumpkin porridge is savory without being too sweet. All porridges are served with a tangy side of dongchimi (water kimchi). Another popular menu item is patbingsu (shaved ice with red beans), available year-round. The individual red beans retain their texture for a great chew. The red beans aren't overly sweet; instead, condensed milk provides the sweetness, topped with soybean powder for a harmonious flavor. All menu items are available for takeout. Their sikhye (sweet rice punch) is also very popular and can be ordered to go. There are many pleasant parks nearby to explore, such as Hakun Park, Pyeonghwa Park, and Dalan Park within 1 km, and Pyeongchon Central Park within 2 km.

spot_at_2372036.title: Jungwondang (Cheongmyeongju Brewery)
spot_at_2372036.overview: Cheongmyeongju is a traditional liquor designated as a Chungbuk Intangible Cultural Heritage, currently preserved through its 4th generation by the Gimhae Gim clan lineage in Chungju, Chungcheongbuk-do. According to 'Oju Yeonmun Jangjeon San-go' by the Joseon Dynasty silhak (practical learning) scholar Lee Gyu-gyung, Cheongmyeongju can only be made with the people and water of Chungju, and even if other regions try to copy it, it cannot be replicated—testament to its deep tradition and pride. It is a traditional premium liquor fermented and aged at low temperatures for about 100 days using native whole wheat and glutinous rice, and the brewery also offers educational and hands-on experience programs.

spot_at_2434888.title: Mokgyenaru Ferry
spot_at_2434888.overview: Chungju, the birthplace of Jungwon culture, was a vital strategic hub connecting the east, west, south, and north of Korea for both water and land transportation, with Mokgyenaru Ferry serving as the center of water transport. Mokgyenaru is a complex cultural space established to inherit and develop the cultural spirit of Mokgye's past, consisting of a river boat experience hall, traditional tavern (jumak), merchant street (jeojatgeori), and water activity facilities. The River Boat Experience Hall is designed with the motif of the boats that once filled Mokgyenaru, allowing visitors to actually see and feel the historical river boats, and offers experiences such as making wishing paper boats. In addition, Jeojatgeori, a traditional play yard, recreates the atmosphere of the old Mokgyenaru marketplace with various traditional experiences and food, offering enriching educational tourism for children and family visitors.

spot_at_2613451.title: Chungju Gangbyeong-gil (Riverside Trail)
spot_at_2613451.overview: Chungju Gangbyeong-gil is a scenic walking trail created along the riverside below Chungju Dam. It is part of the 'Chungju Landscape Trails,' which spans a total of 91 km across 9 courses and was the only storytelling-themed trail selected nationwide by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism. The 'Gangbyeong-gil' course runs from Chungwon-gyo Bridge to the Freshwater Fish Exhibition Hall, offering breathtaking views of Lake Chungju. Spanning 1 km, the trail takes about an hour to complete. In spring, the path bursts into full bloom with cherry blossoms, making the stunning scenery of Lake Chungju even more magical.

spot_fo_2608178.overview: Located in Eumseong, Yeongbingwan is a third-generation Chinese restaurant specializing in authentic Chinese cuisine backed by years of expertise. spot_at_319485.title: Seonseoksa Temple (Gyeongbuk)
spot_at_319485.overview: Seonseoksa Temple, a branch temple of Donghwasa Temple (the head temple of the 9th Diocese of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism), is located on the mid-slope of Seojinsan Mountain and is the largest temple in Seongju-gun. Like many temples in the Gyeongbuk region, it was completely burned down during the Japanese invasions of Korea (Imjin War), leaving no precise records of its founding date or founder. However, it is said to have been founded in 692 (the 1st year of King Hyoso) by Master Uisang under the name Shinkwangsa Temple. At the time of its founding, it was located further west. Towards the end of the Goryeo Dynasty, Master Naong attempted to move it to the current site, where a large rock was discovered during excavation, leading to the name Seonseoksa. After being burnt down during the Imjin War in 1592, it was reconstructed in 1684 by monks Haemuk and Naheon, moved back to its old western site in 1725, and finally relocated to its present location by monk Seoyun in 1804. Structures such as Daeungjeon Hall, Myeongbujeon Hall, and others were built, though the royal autograph pavilion (Eopilgak) was later lost to a fire. Recently, an outdoor Maitreya Buddha was enshrined beneath the bamboo grove behind Daeungjeon Hall. Notably, it was designated as a temple to safeguard the royal placenta chambers (Taesil) during the Joseon Dynasty. About 200 meters away from the temple is Taebong, where the placenta chambers of King Sejong's princes are located. As a guardian temple for the placenta chambers, it received royal calligraphy from King Yeongjo and witnessed historical shifts caused by royal power struggles. Embracing the twists and turns of history, Seonseoksa is now reborn as a spiritual sanctuary for the people of Seongju, living alongside the local community through events like the annual spring temple music concert, cultural programs, spiritual training, and educational spaces.

spot_at_3444338.title: Wanjeong Gotek (Traditional House)
spot_at_3444338.overview: This historic house is the head family residence (Jongtaek) of Wanseokjeong Lee Eon-yeong (1568–1639). It is nestled against the foot of a hill behind Homshil Myeonggok Village, a clan village of the Byeokjin Lee clan, and is arranged facing east inside a nearly square earthen wall. The head house was built by Lee Eon-yeong's 7th-generation descendant, Lee Jon-yeong (1787–1849). Lee Eon-yeong passed the civil service examination with top honors in the 36th year of King Seonjo's reign (1603) and entered official service. In 1613 (the 5th year of King Gwanghaegun's reign), when Jeong On protested the wrongful death of Grand Prince Yeongchang and was branded a traitor, Lee defended him and subsequently stepped down from office. Reinstated during the Injo Restoration, he served as a royal secretary (Seungji) and as the magistrate of Cheongju, Seonsan, and Miryang, and authored the collection of writings 'Wanjeongjip.' The estate consists of six buildings, including the Sarangchae (men's quarters), Anchae (women's quarters), Daemunganche (gate quarters), shrine, and inner/outer gates. The Sarangchae, originally a 6-room thatched-roof house, was dismantled and rebuilt in its current form in 1947 by head descendant Lee Yeong-gi, who also attached a 3-room gate quarters to it. The Anchae measures 5 rooms wide and 5.5 rooms deep, featuring a 3-room wooden-floored hall (Daecheong) in the center with perpendicular wings extending forward and backward at a slightly lower level, creating an H-shaped layout. The shrine was rebuilt in 1984 due to the aging of the original structure, and the former shrine building was converted into the current inner gate.

Reinstated during the Injo Restoration, he served as a royal secretary (Seungji) and as the magistrate of Cheongju, Seonsan, and Miryang, and authored the collection of writings 'Wanjeongjip.' The estate consists of six buildings, including the Sarangchae, Anchae, Daemunganche, shrine, and inner/outer gates. The Sarangchae, originally a 6-room thatched-roof house, was dismantled and rebuilt in its current form in 1947 by head descendant Lee Yeong-gi, who also attached a 3-room gate quarters to it. The Anchae measures 5 rooms wide and 5.5 rooms deep, featuring a 3-room wooden-floored hall in the center with perpendicular wings extending forward and backward at a slightly lower level, forming an H-shaped layout.

spot_at_3444683.title: Birthplace of Simsan Kim Chang-suk
spot_at_3444683.overview: This traditional house is the birthplace of Simsan Kim Chang-suk (1879–1962), who dedicated his entire life to the independence movement and the promotion of education. All original ancestral buildings that had been passed down through generations were destroyed by fire, and the current Anchae (women's quarters) was reconstructed in the 5th year of Gwangmu (1901). Located about 100 meters to the right of Cheongcheon Seodang (Confucian Academy), the birthplace features an Anchae, a Sarangchae built in 1991, and a printing block storage (Pankakgo) arranged in a 'ㄷ' (digit-shaped) layout within a rectangular earthen-stone wall. Kim Chang-suk’s pen names were Simsah and Byeokong, and his clan origin was Uiseong. As a descendant of Donggang Kim U-ong—a renowned scholar and meritorious official during the reign of King Seonjo of Joseon—he devoted himself to the Patriotic Enlightenment Movement even before Korea's Japanese annexation, and afterward played a significant role in the independence movement as a Confucian scholar. He was imprisoned and subjected to severe torture by the Japanese colonial authorities. After liberation, he led the movement against the trusteeship, organized the Confucian association Yudo-hoe, and founded Sungkyunkwan University, serving as its first president. Kim Chang-suk was a national leader who made immense contributions throughout his life to the independence movement, the creation of national culture, and public education. In recognition of these achievements, he was posthumously awarded the Republic of Korea Medal of the Order of Merit for National Foundation in 1962.

spot_at_127717.title: Seongju Hangee Village
spot_at_127717.overview: Seongju Hangee Village is a quintessential clan village where the Seongsan Lee clan has lived for generations. Lee U, who served as the Moksa (Magistrate) of Jinju during the reign of King Sejong of Joseon, first migrated here to establish the village. Today, descendants of Wolbong Lee Jeong-hyeon form a concentrated clan community, preserving the traditional Korean hanok village. To the north, Yeongchwi-san Mountain (331.7m) stretches out like the Blue Dragon on the left and the White Tiger on the right, while Baekcheon Stream flows to the southwest, forming one of the most propitious geomantic sites in the Yeongnam region. It is also renowned for producing many prominent scholars since ancient times, including the late-Joseon Neo-Confucianist Lee Jin-sang and Eungwa Lee Won-jo. Hangee Village features unique stone-and-earth walls that offer a distinctive visual attraction. These walls are largely divided into outer and inner boundaries. The outer walls vary in height; those bordering the mountain slopes and the side walls facing east are relatively high due to the sloping terrain, while the walls dividing the front and back yards of houses are lower. The inner walls are lower than the eaves of the residential buildings, visually blocking or connecting the spaces on either side. Overall, the earth-and-stone walls, which are characteristic of the village, harmonize beautifully with the traditional hanok homes, naturally guiding visitors' movements and blending seamlessly into the picturesque scenery.

spot_at_127813.title: Seopjikoji
spot_at_127813.overview: As the name 'Koji' (a Jeju dialect meaning a cape) suggests, Seopjikoji is a protruding terrain shaped like the tip of a nose. Geographically, it juts out onto the coast of Sinyang-ri, Seongsan-eup, Seogwipo-si. It may not be very easy for outsiders to find, but generally, you can enter the village from the Sinyang-ri coastal national highway, follow the signposts, and take the concrete-paved road to the end of the cape. Alternatively, if coming from Seogwipo, pass through Pyoseon downtown, drive about 7 km until you see a coastal road sign on the right, turn right here, drive straight along the sea with the panoramic view of Seopjikoji in front of you, soon see the sandy beach of Sinyang Beach, turn right in front of the village, and follow the concrete road similarly. The canola flowers here, matching the bright sunlight and blue sea color, display a more vivid and delicate hue than anywhere else. On the wide and flat Koji hill, Hyeopjayeondae, a stone beacon mound used to light beacon fires in the past, is erected. It is a square shape about 4m high and 9m on each side, relatively well-preserved in its original form. The peak rising northeast from the beacon mound is the so-called Bulgeun Oreum,

spot_at_2798882.title: Udo Cheonjin Port Waiting Room
spot_at_2798882.overview: Udo, located at the eastern end of Jeju Island, got its name because it looks like a water buffalo sticking its head out (Uduhyeong). It is an island in Jeju Island that is about 1/100th the size of Seoul and has a population of about 1,800. There are two ports in Udo: Cheonjin Port and Haumokdong Port. Cheonjin Port is the gateway port of Udo and the most well-known place to tourists. Attached directly to the Udo Canola Flower Village Information Center, the Udo Cheonjin Port Waiting Room is small in scale, featuring a ticket office, waiting seats, and a convenience store where you can buy simple snacks and souvenirs. Near the waiting room, electric car rental shops are lined up for the convenience of Udo tourism. When entering Udo, you can bring cars and scooters. For cars, after purchasing a shipping certificate, they must be loaded by a license holder following the crew's instructions up to 10 minutes before departure time.

spot_at_126452.title: Manjanggul Cave (Jeju National Geopark)
spot_at_126452.overview: Located in Gimnyeong-ri, Gujwa-eup, Jeju-si, Manjanggul Cave is a lava tube belonging to the Geomunoreum Lava Tube System (Hwang Sang-gu et al., 2005), which is part of the Jeju World Natural Heritage, with a total length of about 7,400 m, a maximum height of about 25 m, and a maximum width of about 18 m. In particular, the main passage is a globally large-scale cave with a width of 18 m and a height of 23 m. Although there are many lava tubes distributed around the world, lava tubes formed hundreds of thousands of years ago like Manjanggul with well-preserved internal shapes and topography are rare, making their academic and conservation value extremely high. Manjanggul has three entrances formed by the collapse of the ceiling in the middle part of the cave. Currently, the entrance accessible to the general public is the 2nd entrance, and only a 1 km section can be explored. Inside Manjanggul, various lava tube formations such as lava stalactites, lava stalagmites, lava flowstone, lava lines, lava shelves, and lava rafts are developed. In particular, the approximately 7.6-meter-high lava column seen at the end of the open section is known to be the largest scale in the world. (Source: Jeju World Geopark)

spot_at_126447.title: Sinyang Seopji Beach
spot_at_126447.overview: Along with Seongsan Ilchulbong Peak, Seopjikoji is a representative tourist destination in the eastern part of Jeju Island. 'Koji' is a Jeju dialect for a cape, meaning a landform protruding into the sea. Known as the windy hill of Jeju Island and used as a shooting location for many movies, dramas, and commercials, it continuously attracts domestic and foreign tourists. Before climbing toward Seopjikoji, you can find Sinyang Seopji Beach on the right, also called Sinyang Beach. Sinyang Seopji Beach is nestled inside the cape tip of Seopjikoji, retaining its untouched natural beauty. Shaped like a round crescent moon, this semi-circular beach has calm and cozy waves, making it safe for children to swim, and the sandy beach is covered with fine and soft light brown sand instead of stones and pebbles. Away from the village, it is a recommended resort for those who want to enjoy a leisurely and quiet atmosphere. On the opposite side of the beach, you can also appreciate the beautiful scenery where the sea, Seongsan Ilchulbong Peak, and canola flowers harmonize. In addition, it is a place where the international windsurfing competition was held, loved by windsurfing enthusiasts, and nearby tourist attractions include Seopjikoji, Aqua Planet, Seongsan Ilchulbong Peak, and Onpyeong-ri Honinji.

spot_at_126448.title: Iho Tewoo Beach
spot_at_126448.overview: Iho Tewoo Beach (Iho Beach) is a great photo spot in Jeju Island known for its pony lighthouses, where the sharply contrasting colors of the red and white ponies present an exotic scenery. In addition, being closest to downtown Jeju, transportation is convenient and convenience facilities are well-equipped. The slope of the sandy beach is gentle, attracting many vacationers, and a pine forest is formed, making it perfect for camping. During the ebb tide when the sea level is at its lowest, you can see the endless wide sandy beach along the appearance of Wondam. Wondam is one of Jeju's traditional fishing methods using the difference between high and low tides to catch fish, and Iho Tewoo Beach (Iho Beach) features Iho Mosalwon, where that space has been restored.

spot_at_126145.title: Gyeongchungsa Shrine (Historical Site of General Jeong Gi-ryong)
spot_at_126145.overview: This is the shrine dedicated to General Jeong Gi-ryong (Chungui-gong), who served as a meritorious subject and Grand Internal Han-gwan during the Joseon Dynasty. Born in 1562 (the 17th year of King Myeongjong's reign) with the pen name Maeheon, he passed the military service examination and earned renown during the Imjin War by rescuing General Jo Gyeong, the Defense Commander of Gyeongsang Right Province, from enemy capture. He achieved over 80 victories in various battles and later rose to high military offices including Commander of the Three Naval Provinces. Local scholars and descendants built this shrine in 1932 to honor his loyalty and righteousness, and ancestral rites are held here. Since 1989, as part of the shrine's sanctification project, a youth training village has also been established in Hadong-gun.

spot_at_126015.title: Hallyeosudo National Marine Park (Hadong)
spot_at_126015.overview: Hallyeosudo centers on the natural coastal landscapes of the southern archipelago, stretching from Geoje-si, Gyeongsangnam-do to Yeosu-si, Jeollanam-do. The terrain is characterized by low mountains averaging around 500 meters behind the coast. Along this waterway, countless islands and coastal areas offer camellia flowers in spring and blue seas in summer, creating a harmonious natural setting. Every bend in the waterway holds historical sites related to the military exploits of Admiral Yi Sun-sin, leading to its designation as a national park on December 31, 1968. Hallyeohaesang encompasses the natural scenery of the southern archipelago, connecting Geoje Island's Haegeumgang and Hansando districts through Sacheon and Noryang to Namhae Island's Geumsan district and Yeosu's Odongdo district. (Source: Hadong County Culture and Tourism Website)

spot_at_128503.title: Esin Village
spot_at_128503.overview: Esin Village is a cozy settlement nestled in the upper reaches of the Hwagae-dong valley, which the great Unified Silla scholar Choe Chi-won once praised in poetry as a utopia inside a gourd bottle. The village name originates from 'Esinsa', a temple that existed until the early Joseon Dynasty, and the village grew as it became known during the Joseon era as a secluded haven of pristine nature in Jirisan. Preserving beautiful scenery across all four seasons, including Jirisan Mountain and Esin Valley, the village produces high-quality specialties such as wild mountain greens, medicinal herbs, pine mushrooms, and gorosoe (maple) sap. It offers various historical and cultural resources, including the Seosan Daesa Old Path where visitors can walk along cool streams and wildflower paths while following the footsteps of Great Master Seosan, the Jirisan History Museum showcasing the history of partisans, and Wontongam Hermitage where Seosan Daesa entered the Buddhist priesthood.

spot_fo_2843594.title: Tajja Duck House Main Branch
spot_fo_2843594.overview: Tajja Duck House Main Branch is located along the roadside leading into Hajeong-ri on National Route 3 from Jinju toward Sancheong. Signature menu items include seasoned duck bulgogi, eotang-guksu (spicy fish soup noodles), and perilla seed sujebi (hand-pulled dough soup), bustling with diners looking for healthy meals during lunch hours on both weekdays and weekends. Although the main dining hall is not huge, there is a second floor, making it pleasant and spacious. As Sancheong is a major producer of garlic and onions, the pickled onions served here are exceptional. The ssam (wrap) vegetables are grown using organic fertilizer made from snow crab and king crab shells, ensuring absolute freshness. Suwol Waterfall in Seonyudong Valley, located in Sinan-myeon, Sancheong, is a nearby tourist attraction worth visiting together.

spot_fo_2843670.title: Anui Galbitang
spot_fo_2843670.overview: Located right next to Jinjuseong Fortress in Bonseong-dong, Jinju-si, Anui Galbitang is a prominent local restaurant with a 30-year tradition run by two generations. Representative menu items include beef short rib soup (galbitang) and braised short ribs (galbijjim). The galbitang boasts a rich yet clean broth, while the galbijjim features tender ribs tossed in an appealingly spicy sauce. The second floor offers banquet seating for large groups. For parking, tour buses can use the Jinjuseong Gongbukmun Gate parking lot, while passenger cars can use the street parking in front of the Samsung Service Center located right in front of the restaurant or near the nearby Youth Center; a 1-hour free parking ticket is provided. With Jinjuseong Fortress only a 2-minute walk away, it offers a convenient combination of dining and sightseeing.

spot_fo_2843923.overview: Featuring a spacious parking lot right in front, Daegajib is located in Seosang-myeon, Hamyang. It is well-known as a specialty restaurant for king-size beef short rib soup (wang-galbitang). The soup bowl is packed with a large beef rib bone, glass noodles, and green onions, and the staff neatly slices the meat off the bone for easy eating. Broth refills are available upon request, and mixing in the seasoning paste provided at the table makes it even more flavorful. Spicy braised pork short ribs are another popular menu item here, served with crisp bean sprouts piled on top for a unique texture and taste. You can also mix fried rice into the remaining sauce after finishing the meat. In addition, premium Korean beef (hanwoo) for grilling is prepared at the entrance, allowing you to choose your cut visually before bringing it to your table to grill. After your meal, we recommend visiting Sangnim Park, designated as Natural Monument No. 154. * Pets are not allowed.

spot_at_1081744.title: Korean Traditional Food Culture Experience Center (Jeonggangwon)
spot_at_1081744.overview: Founded by Korean food researcher Cho Jung-gang, the Korean Traditional Food Culture Experience Center was established to promote and offer hands-on experiences with traditional Korean food culture. Located in Yongpyong-myeon, Pyeongchang-gun, it showcases traditional hanok stays, cooking classes, and formal Korean table d'hôte (hanjeongsik) to spread the taste and style of Korea. Nestled in an auspicious site surrounded by Mt. Geumgangsan's foothills and the flowing Geumgang Valley, the accommodation is divided into traditional hanok and modern rooms. The tiled hanok features traditional ondol flooring and views of Mt. Geumgangsan.

spot_at_125591.title: Odaesan National Park
spot_at_125591.overview: Designated as the country's 11th national park in 1975, Odaesan National Park spans an area of 327.904 ㎢. With Birobong Peak (1,563m above sea level) as its main peak, five grand peaks including Dongdaesan (1,434m), Durobong (1,422m), Sangwangbong (1,491m), and Holyeongbong (1,561m) stand like a folding screen. Below Noinbong Peak (1,338m), which breaks off to the east, lies the breathtaking Sogeumgangsan Scenic Area. To the west sits Mt. Gyebangsan (1,577m), renowned for its stunning snowscapes.

spot_at_125595.title: Mt. Cheongoksan (Pyeongchang)
spot_at_125595.overview: Named after the abundant wild cheongok greens growing natively in the area, Mt. Cheongoksan stands 1,256m above sea level and features a relatively flat ridge boasting the famous 'Yukbaekmajigi' plateau at its peak. The hike takes about 5 hours, and a headquarters for Samshin (Three Spirits) belief is located near the summit. Next to the Yukbaekmajigi Cheongoksan Observatory, a hiking trail leads to the summit, divided into a walking path and a barrier-free wooden deck sharing trail.

spot_at_125638.title: Naeunggyegok Valley
spot_at_125638.overview: Located in Naeung-ri, Pyeongchang-eup, Naeunggyegok Valley is a wide valley featuring abundant water as the Pyeongchanggang River meanders in an S-shape. Steep cliffs interspersed with the river create exceptionally stunning scenery. Sandy patches and pebbles spread throughout make it an ideal spot for water play and camping. With its wide river and crystal-clear waters teeming with native freshwater fish like mandarin fish, torrent catfish, and catfish, as well as freshwater snails, it is a wonderful place for fishing and enjoying nature. Nearby guesthouses offer rural experience programs such as picking chili peppers and digging potatoes.

spot_at_125771.title: Sangwonssa Temple (Odaesan)
spot_at_125771.overview: Sangwonssa Temple is a millennium-old temple located near Woljeongsa Temple, serving as a branch temple of Woljeongsa, the head temple of the 4th District of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism. Known to have been founded by Monk Jajang during the reign of Queen Seondeok of Silla, it was actually reconstructed by King Seongdeok in 705 and named Jinyeowon. It is the only temple in the country housing a statue of Munsu Bodhisattva (Manjusri) and is famous for the anecdote where King Sejo visited to cure his skin disease and was healed. The current temple was rebuilt following a fire in 1946, leaving no ancient buildings except for Yeongsanjeon Hall. It preserves precious cultural heritage including a National Treasure bronze bell, a Munsu Child Bodhisattva statue, a Munsu Bodhisattva statue, and King Sejo's handwritten restoration appeal, and is ideal to visit along the 9km Sunjae-gil trail starting from Woljeongsa.

spot_at_125772.title: Woljeongsa Temple & Fir Tree Forest
spot_at_125772.overview: Woljeongsa Temple was founded in 643 (the 12th year of Queen Seondeok of Silla) by Monk Jajang on Mt. Odaesan, an entire mountain designated as a Buddhist sanctuary. As the head temple of the 4th District of the Jogye Order, it oversees some 60 temples and 8 hermitages, holding countless cultural treasures including the National Treasure Octagonal Nine-Story Stone Pagoda, and Treasures such as the Seated Stone Bodhisattva and Seated Wooden Munsu Child Bodhisattva of Woljeongsa. A roughly 1km stretch from Woljeongsa's Iljumun Gate to Geumganggyo Bridge unfolds into a magnificent fir tree forest housing about 1,700 fir trees.

The fir tree forest is a representative tourist attraction of the millennium-old temple Woljeongsa, loved by visitors across all four seasons, making it a must-visit spot when coming to Woljeongsa. Woljeongsa operates Templestay programs divided into rest-oriented and experience-oriented types, allowing visitors to leave the secular world behind and recharge their weary bodies and minds deep in the mountains. Alongside Templestay, there is the Woljeongsa Chulga School for ordinary people to experience the life of a novice monk. Additionally, the Odaesan Meditation Village (OMV), spanning approximately 99,170㎡—about 14 times the size of a soccer field—features accommodations, cultural experience facilities, restaurants, gardens, and forest trails to help escape daily life.

spot_fo_134359.title: Sumvawi (Shumbawi Rock)
spot_fo_134359.overview: Located about 2.5 hours from Seoul, Sumvawi sits at the foot of Gyebangsan Mountain, South Korea's 5th highest peak known for its pristine nature at the 'Happy 700' highland (where human biological rhythms are said to be most active). Gyebangsan is currently popular for winter trekking due to its snow-covered landscapes and yew tree clusters, and an auto-camping site right below the hiking trail makes it great for family leisure. Nearby attractions include the Lee Seung-bok Memorial Hall, Bangadari Mineral Spring, Woljeongsa Temple in Odaesan, Bongpyeong Buckwheat Flower Village, Yongpyong Ski Resort, and Phoenix Park. Visitors can enjoy seasonal sports like skiing in winter and rafting or mountain ATVs in summer.

spot_at_125649.title: Naeri Valley

Surrounded by mountains, it features crystal-clear waters and aquatic life such as local fish species.

spot_at_125659.title: Yeongwol Orayeon (Gangwon Paleozoic National Geopark)
spot_at_125659.overview: Orayeon, part of the Donggang River section, is a pristine scenic area where fluvial landforms are intensively developed, serving as a representative site for entrenched meandering rivers. It features a continuous distribution of various micro-fluvial landforms such as river cliffs (vertical cliffs around Orayeon), canyon topography (Orayeon Valley) formed by river erosion, abandoned channels (Sangseonam, Jungseonam, Haseonam) showing traces of past river flows, and pools, riffles, and runs.

These fluvial elements harmonize with the vegetation landscape blending rivers, exposed rock outcrops, and forest zones, demonstrating the representative scenic perfection of the Donggang River basin.

In particular, the spatial contrast created by river flows and rock terrain highlights Orayeon as one of the most scenic areas in the upper Donggang River. Orayeon is a geological site based on the Mesozoic Jurassic Bansong Formation distributed around Geoun-ri, Yeongwol-eup, Yeongwol-gun, Gangwon-do, primarily consisting of clastic sedimentary rocks such as sandstone and shale.

spot_at_125724.title: Gossigul Cave (Gangwon Paleozoic National Geopark)
spot_at_125724.overview: Offering a glimpse into 400 million years of mystery, Gossi Cave is one of South Korea's representative caves. It was named after the Go family, who took refuge here during the Japanese invasions of Korea (Imjin War), and is also said to have been used as a ascetic training ground. In the past, visitors crossed the 130m-wide Namhangang River by ferry to reach the entrance, but a bridge now connects directly to the cave. Designated as a Natural Monument on June 4, 1969, Gossi Cave is nationally protected for its exceptional academic and natural heritage value, opening to the public on May 15, 1974.
spot_at_125724.pull_quote: Offering a glimpse into 400 million years of mystery, Gossi Cave is one of South Korea's representative caves. It was named after the Go family, who took refuge here during the Japanese…
paragraphs: Offering a glimpse into 400 million years of mystery, Gossi Cave is one of South Korea's representative caves. It was named after the Go family, who took refuge here during the Japanese invasions of Korea (Imjin War), and is also said to have been used as a ascetic training ground. Designated as a Natural Monument on June 4, 1969, Gossi Cave is nationally protected for its exceptional academic and natural heritage value, opening to the public on May 15, 1974.

Gossi Cave is a classic limestone cave featuring a multi-layered structure. The lower layer takes the form of a horizontal cave where groundwater flows like a small stream, and passages extend southwest from the entrance. The total main tunnel length is about 950m and branch tunnels measure about 2,438m, bringing Gossi Cave's total length to 3,388m, of which only a 500m section is developed and open to the public. Most of the main tunnel has developed along joint planes within the limestone.

spot_at_125758.title: Beopheungsa Temple (Yeongwol)
spot_at_125758.overview: Nestled in the foothills of Sajasang Mountain in Yeongwol, Gangwon-do, Beopheungsa Temple was founded in 643 (the 12th year of Queen Seondeok of Silla) by Master Jajang Yulsa to pray for national prosperity and the well-being of the people. Initially started as Heungnyeongsa Temple housing Buddha's true sarira (relics), it later became a central temple of the Sajasang Mountain school—one of the Nine Mountain Schools of Seon—when Jinghyo Jeoljung, a disciple of Silla Seon master Doyun, opened a Seon gate. Rebuilt in 1163 during the reign of King Uijong of Goryeo, it has preserved its Buddhist lineage through numerous destructions and reconstructions up to the Joseon Dynasty.

Initially started as Heungnyeongsa Temple housing Buddha's true sarira (relics), it later became a central temple of the Sajasang Mountain school—one of the Nine Mountain Schools of Seon—when Jinghyo Jeoljung, a disciple of Silla Seon master Doyun, opened a Seon gate. Rebuilt in 1163 during the reign of King Uijong of Goryeo, it has preserved its Buddhist lineage through numerous destructions and reconstructions up to the Joseon Dynasty.

Surrounded by dense pine forests, Beopheungsa is one of South Korea's five Jeokmyeolbogung (sanctuaries housing Buddha's relics), offering a deep sense of Buddhist culture in a tranquil atmosphere. Within the temple grounds remain three stone pagodas, a seated guardian stone Buddha, a grotto where Master Jajang practiced asceticism, and the Jeokmyeolbogung shrine. Various cultural heritage items, such as the Saritap stupa, the Monument for Master Jinghyo of Heungnyeongsa, the Stupa of Master Jinghyo, and the Heungnyeongseonwonji site, showcase the temple's profound history and tradition.

spot_at_125783.title: Yeongwol Hyanggyo (Confucian School)
spot_at_125783.overview: Yeongwol Hyanggyo is a local educational institution founded in 1398 (the 7th year of King Taejo) during the Joseon Dynasty. During Joseon, it functioned as a national educational institution responsible for educating and enlightening local citizens. Although all buildings except the Daeseongjeon Shrine were destroyed during the Korean War in 1950, it maintains its current appearance through multiple renovations and repairs. Yeongwol Hyanggyo is arranged in a 'jeonhak humyo' layout, with the Myeongnyundang lecture hall in the front and the Daeseongjeon ritual hall in the rear. Myeongnyundang, where Confucian students studied, is a gable-roofed building measuring 3 bays wide and 2 bays deep.

paragraphs: This is a Three Kingdoms period mountain fortress located on Jeongyangsan Mountain in Yeongwol-eup. Built with stones by cleverly utilizing the natural terrain of Jeongyangsan protruding toward the Namhangang River, it is estimated to have been first constructed in the late 5th to early 6th century when the Three Kingdoms vied for the Han River basin. It remained in continuous use until the early Joseon Dynasty. Along with the Jungwon Goguryeo Stele in Chungju and Ondalsanseong Fortress in Danyang, it is one of Goguryeo's cultural heritage sites located in the central region.

Situated on a steep mountain peak at an elevation of 550m at the end of the Bonghwangsan Mountain ridge, it boasts excellent locational conditions as a fortress. The overall flat layout forms a wide trapezoid facing northwest. The fortress is largely divided into an inner wall (1,060m in circumference) and an outer wall (570m in circumference), with a total wall length reaching 1,630m. It is comparable in scale to Samnyeonsanseong Fortress in Boeun, which is considered one of the largest among ancient Korean mountain fortresses based on wall size alone. The outer wall was constructed after the Goryeo Dynasty to increase the inner wall's capacity, utilizing natural cliffs for many sections and building artificial walls where necessary during emergency situations.

spot_at_125611.title: Taegisan Mountain

According to legend, King Taegi, the last king of Jinhan, was chased by Silla forces, built Taegisan Fortress (1.8km), and made his last stand—remnants of which still remain. The deep mountain valley, home to abundant primitive plant life and scenic spots like Mulhangari Waterfall and Chotdaebawi (Candlestick Rock), is breathtaking. spot_at_125646.title: Byeongjibang Valley
spot_at_125646.overview: Byeongjibang Valley in Hoengseong is a stunning valley located in Gapcheon-myeon, Hoengseong-gun, Gangwon-do, also known as Byeongjibangri Valley or Sandi Valley. Surrounded by lofty peaks such as Eodapsan, Taeuisan, and Balgyosan, the scenery is magnificent, and the crystal-clear, icy stream water flows from the source of the Seomgang River, a tributary of the Namhangang River. The name 'Byeongjibang' originates from a folktale stating that the soldiers of King Taegi, the last king of Jinhan who fled from King Park Hyeokgeose, once stayed here.

The name 'Byeongjibang' originates from a folktale stating that the soldiers of King Taegi, the last king of Jinhan who fled from King Park Hyeokgeose, once stayed here.

A paved road stretches approximately 10km along the valley, with large free parking lots set up roadside. As one of the most remote valleys in Hoengseong-gun, the area boasts lush foliage, and the Seonnyetang (Fairies' Pond) area features various strange rock formations and wildflowers. Smaller tributaries like Garakgol, Godeonggol, Semgol, and Jujutgol flow nearby. With abundant water, it is a popular summer retreat. The general campsite near Byeongjibang Valley is equipped with auto-camping sites, parking, drinking fountains, and sports facilities, making it ideal for family camping. Visitors can camp freely or use the paid campsites.

spot_at_125807.title: Pungsuwon Catholic Church
spot_at_125807.overview: Pungsuwon Catholic Church in Hoengseong traces its origins to the early 1800s, when around 40 believers led by Shin Tae-bo (Peter) settled here to escape religious persecution from Yongin, Gyeonggi-do. The Pungsuwon parish once oversaw 29 branch churches across 12 counties, including Chuncheon, Wonju, Hwacheon, Yanggu, Hongcheon, Hoengseong, Pyeongchang, and Yangpyeong. Separation of the Wonju parish began in 1896, followed by Chuncheon in 1920 and Hongcheon in 1948.

Located in Yuhyeon-ri, Seowon-myeon, Hoengseong-gun, Gangwon-do, Pungsuwon Catholic Church was designated as a Gangwon-do Tangible Cultural Heritage in 1982. Facing southwest on a low hill, the church building features a three-aisled plan where the nave and aisles are divided by colonnaded arcades and ceiling structures. The composition of the protruding main entrance at the front center, the second-floor circular window, and the bell tower with third-floor twin arched windows and louvered vents emphasizes verticality with upward-narrowing buttresses, leaving a striking impression on the central facade.

spot_at_127516.title: Holocene Eco School
spot_at_127516.overview: The Holocene refers to the geological epoch following the Pleistocene of the Quaternary period, spanning from about 10,000 years ago to the present, also known as the Alluvial or Recent epoch. This period is also when humans began agriculture and pastoral activities, systematically threatening all ecosystems. Most species went extinct due to human activity during this era, known as the Holocene extinction—the sixth extinction caused by destructive humans, raising major ecological concerns.

This period is also when humans began agriculture and pastoral activities, systematically threatening all ecosystems.

Most species went extinct due to human activity during this era, known as the Holocene extinction—the sixth extinction caused by destructive humans, raising major ecological concerns. Accordingly, to raise awareness of the current ecological crisis and provide an opportunity to deeply reflect on nature and life, the school goes beyond breeding and restoring endangered species. It serves as a practical model for environmental conservation through maintaining biodiversity via basic research such as insect species preservation, classification of insect resources, and ecology.

spot_at_127734.title: Cheonmunin Maeul (Astronomers' Village)
spot_at_127734.overview: Located at an altitude of 650 meters at the edge of Chiaksan Mountain in Hoengseong, Gangwon-do, Cheonmunin Maeul is a place where the universe meets pure nature amidst high skies and clean air, allowing visitors to see countless stars flowing across a night sky free of light pollution. It is used as an observation site by many amateur astronomers both domestically and abroad, and serves as a regular spot for observations and research by amateur astronomy clubs, astrophotography clubs, and school teachers.

It is used as an observation site by many amateur astronomers both domestically and abroad, and serves as a regular spot for observations and research by amateur astronomy clubs, astrophotography clubs, and school teachers.

To help visitors understand stars and the universe, the village is equipped with related videos, slide photos, and books, allowing guests to see and hear seasonal constellations and the beautiful stories woven into them. Visitors can observe the night sky through a large 14-inch astronomical telescope and appreciate various astrophotographs. Cheonmunin Maeul will remain a long-cherished hometown of the heart for anyone who loves stars, serving as an optimal observation spot for amateur astronomers and a memorable place for the general public to keep a beautiful night sky in their hearts.

spot_fo_134368.overview: Hoengseong Hanwoo (Korean beef) is renowned for its exceptional quality and taste, as evidenced by the large number of tourists attending the annual Hanwoo Festival. Geumgangsan Sutbulgui uses only grade 1 or higher beef certified by the Hoengseong Livestock Cooperative, and grills it exclusively over Gangwon pine charcoal to showcase the clean and savory flavor of charcoal-grilled Hanwoo. spot_fo_2822688.overview: Cottage Saengun is an emotional cafe located in Hoengseong, Gangwon-do, with drip coffee and Americano as its most popular menus.
