spot_at_1146400.title: Wirari Seven-Story Stone Pagoda
spot_at_1146400.overview: The Wirari Seven-Story Stone Pagoda is a Goryeo-dynasty stone pagoda located in Hwacheon-gun, Gangwon-do. At the time of excavation, the base and up to the third story retained their original form, but from the fourth story onward, the main bodies (oksin) were missing, leaving only the roof stones (okgaeseok). The scattered pieces of the base, pagoda body, and roof stones were collected and re-erected. The roof stones and the body stones of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd stories are original, while those of the 4th story and above were supplemented during restoration in 1975.
spot_at_1146400.pull_quote: The Wirari Seven-Story Stone Pagoda is a Goryeo-dynasty stone pagoda located in Hwacheon-gun, Gangwon-do. At the time of excavation, the base and up to the third story...
paragraphs: The Wirari Seven-Story Stone Pagoda is a Goryeo-dynasty stone pagoda located in Hwacheon-gun, Gangwon-do. At the time of excavation, the base and up to the third story retained their original form, but from the 4th story onward, the main bodies were lost, leaving only the roof stones. The scattered base members, pagoda body stones, and roof stones were collected and re-erected. The roof stones and body stones of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd stories are original, while the body stones above the 4th story were added during the 1975 restoration. The shape of the pagoda features a 7-story pagoda body placed on a large foundation stone.

The body stones of the pagoda have pillar shapes carved on each corner, and the 2nd story decreases significantly in height compared to the 1st story, after which it decreases very gradually. The roof stones have 3-tier supports on the underside, and the eaves are horizontal, lifting slightly upward at the four corners. The top finial ornaments are entirely gone, leaving only a single round stone. Although small in scale, the carving of pillars on the body stones and the 3-tier roof stone supports show a style and technique very similar to the Namgyewon Seven-Story Stone Pagoda, suggesting that the two pagodas were built around the same period.

spot_at_125599.title: Yonghasan Mountain (Gangwon Peace Region National Geopark)
spot_at_125599.overview: Granite is a plutonic rock formed when magma solidifies deep underground. Rocks formed under high-temperature and high-pressure conditions deep underground experience 'weathering', where they easily break down as temperature and pressure decrease when they rise near the earth's surface. In particular, weathering occurs actively when rocks come into contact with moisture underground.
spot_at_125599.pull_quote: Granite is a plutonic rock formed when magma solidifies deep underground. Rocks formed under high-temperature and high-pressure conditions deep underground near...
paragraphs: Granite is a plutonic rock formed when magma solidifies deep underground. Rocks formed under high-temperature and high-pressure conditions deep underground experience 'weathering', where they easily break down as temperature and pressure decrease when they rise near the earth's surface. In particular, weathering occurs actively when rocks come into contact with moisture underground.

This is a type of chemical weathering (a phenomenon where the bonds of minerals constituting rocks break down and crumble) that occurs underground, hence called deep weathering (or chemical deep weathering). When such deep weathering processes accelerate, even hard rocks become weak enough to be easily crushed by human hand power, and the material generated is called saprolite. However, when granite that has undergone little or no weathering is exposed above the ground, it has a short contact time with moisture and does not undergo further deep weathering, thus forming large-scale rock quarries. In other words, Yonghasan Mountain formed its fracture structures after the weathered and weakened material (saprolite) was washed away following deep weathering.

spot_at_127965.title: Bimok Park
spot_at_127965.overview: Located in Hwacheon-gun, Gangwon-do, Bimok Park is a place honoring the sorrow and sacrifice of the Korean War. It is also the birthplace of the beloved Korean national song, 'Bimok' (Wooden Cross). The song originated in the mid-1960s when a young officer in the Baegamsan valley, north of Peace Dam, discovered an overgrown stone grave of an unknown soldier and wrote lyrics commemorating his youthful soul.

spot_at_128094.title: Bisugumi Village
spot_at_128094.overview: Hidden by Lake Paroho, Bisugumi Village is a secret destination where you can immerse yourself in untouched natural beauty rather than crowded tourist spots. Formed right after the Korean War when evacuees settled down to cultivate slash-and-burn fields, the village became known as an 'island within the land' after overland routes were blocked by the construction of Hwacheon Dam. While it once housed 100 households, only 3 families have guarded this place since the 1970s.

Located at the entrance of the valley, this 10-meter-deep basin flows with a swirling motion resembling a dragon's movement.

spot_fo_2844154.overview: Located in Sanae-myeon, Hwacheon-gun, this makguksu (buckwheat noodles) restaurant has only 4 tables. The restaurant's makguksu features easily breakable noodles and a mild style reminiscent of Pyongyang naengmyeon. It can be enjoyed with either water or mixed style by pouring broth to your liking. Side dishes like suyuk (boiled pork slices), acorn jelly, and handmade tofu pair wonderfully together.

spot_at_126357.pull_quote: According to the historical records of Muwisa Temple, it was first established in 875 (the 1st year of King Heongang) by National Master Doseon as Galoksa Temple. Shortly after, around 905 (the 9th year of King Hyogong) and onward...
paragraphs: According to the historical records of Muwisa Temple, it was first established in 875 (the 1st year of King Heongang) by National Master Doseon as Galoksa Temple. Shortly after, around 905 (the 9th year of King Hyogong) and onward, National Master Seongak Hyeongmi (864–917) of the Gajisanmun Seon (Zen) school stayed at Muwigapsa Temple at the request of King Taejo Wang Geon of Goryeo. He restored the temple and widely propagated Buddhist teachings, gaining massive public support. Thus, it is known that Muwisa was founded as Muwigapsa Temple before the early 10th century when Monk Hyeongmi resided there.

However, according to the temple's historical records, Hyeongmi renamed it Maoksa Temple during his third reconstruction in 946 (the 1st year of King Jeongjong) of the Goryeo Dynasty. Yet, 946 was already 30 years after Hyeongmi passed away, and it was the year the 'Stupa Monument of National Master Seongak of Muwigapsa Temple in Goryeo', written by Choi Eon-wi, was erected, making this date hard to believe. This is likely a misunderstanding by later generations regarding the fact that Hyeongmi extensively restored Muwigapsa with the support of Wang Geon and propagated his teachings. Muwisa was founded before the early 10th century and was reconstructed by Hyeongmi.

Yeongrang's birthplace was traded a few times after Yeongrang moved to Seoul in 1948, but it was purchased and managed by Gangjin-gun in 1985. The main building, which had been partially altered, was restored to its original form in 1992, and the gate quarters, which had been demolished, were restored in 1993 based on historical research by Yeongrang's family. The birthplace still preserves the well, camellia tree, jar platform, and persimmon tree that served as subjects for his poems, and is widely planted with peonies.

After falling into decline, National Master Wonmyo Yose reconstructed it on the old site in the 7th year of King Huijong of Goryeo, and it became widely renowned through the Baengnyeon Association, leading to its current name, Baengnyeonsa. It is also well-known as a space where Dasan Jeong Yak-yong, who was exiled to Gangjin during the Joseon Dynasty, communicated and interacted with Master Aam Hyejang, transcending religion and age.

Mandaksan Mountain, where Baengnyeonsa and Dasanchodang are located, has an abundance of wild tea plants and has been called Dasan (Tea Mountain) since ancient times. Jeong Yak-yong adopted the pen name 'Dasan' in reference to his exile and stay here, which became his representative moniker. Flowers starting to bloom from late November reach full bloom around late March, and in April, they fall to the ground, dyeing the forest red once again. If you ask locals in Gangjin which Korean restaurant they visit most often, they will undoubtedly recommend Myeongdong Sikdang without hesitation.

Once you receive your table spread, the natural characteristics of Gangjin—blending mountains, fields, and the sea—are vividly revealed before you. Seafood delicacies like sliced raw fish, raw abalone, giant clam soup, and grilled eel, alongside tteok-galbi (grilled short rib patties), yukhoe (beef tartare), and Gangjin's specialty fried shiitake mushrooms, form a true feast of rare delicacies. Their homemade fermented salted small octopus (toha-jeot) and soy-sauce marinated crab are so popular that guests often ask to pack up the leftovers, while the samhap (fermented skate, boiled pork slices, and aged kimchi) is also counted among regulars' favorite menu items.

paragraphs: Located in Gangjin, a region renowned for Namdo-style Korean set meals, Haetae Sikdang is a representative local restaurant that serves healthy meals prepared with ingredients nurtured by pristine nature. Featured in Yu Hong-jun's travelogue 'My Cultural Heritage Tour', this traditional Namdo restaurant offers the Haetae Jeongsik (set meal) for 1 to 4 people. The dishes changes depending on the season, weather, and market availability, allowing visitors to enjoy fresh seasonal flavors.

Spring brings Gangjin's specialty giant surf clams; summer features freshwater eel; gizzard shad and raw spot prawns take center stage in autumn; and maseengi (hair seaweed) soup warms up the winter. To preserve the freshness and natural flavors of the ingredients, dishes are prepared with minimal seasoning. spot_at_126241.pull_quote: Duryunsan is a scenic tourist destination rich in temples and historical sites, standing 700 meters tall at the southern tip of the Korean Peninsula. Its forests of subtropical evergreen and temperate deciduous trees...
paragraphs: Rising 700 meters high at the southern tip of the Korean Peninsula, Duryunsan is a scenic tourist destination rich in temples and historical sites. It holds significant botanical value as a forest of subtropical evergreen broad-leaved trees and temperate deciduous broad-leaved trees. It is also a provincial park in Jeonnam Gwangju Metropolitan City that embraces Daeheungsa Temple, a UNESCO World Heritage site. Formed by eight rocky peaks, Duryunsan features a lotus-shaped mountain topography. Its ridge is formed by eight peaks, including Garyunbong, Duryunbong, Gokgebong, and Noseungbong.

These eight peaks form a rounded circle, resembling a giant holding up their right hand toward the South Sea. Duryunsan was also historically called Daedunsan; this name is interpreted as deriving from 'Handeum' (combining 'deum' meaning mountain and the modifier 'han' meaning big), which evolved into Daedeum and then Daedun. The ridge connecting Daedun Mountain to the main peak and the Changchungdong Valley leading into Daeheungsa Temple form the center of the provincial park. Covered in lush silver grass, the summits of the eight large and small peaks offer panoramic views of the West and South Seas dotted with islands. paragraphs: Situated on the western side of Dalmasan Mountain (489m), often called the Geumgangsan Mountain of the southern region, Mihwangsa is the southernmost mainland Buddhist temple in Korea, founded in the 8th year of King Gyeongdeok's reign (749) during the Silla Dynasty. Once prosperous enough to oversee 12 hermitages, it gradually declined after monks who set out to restore the temple 100 years ago suffered a disaster at sea. Left vacant for a long time, the temple began to breathe again in 1989 when monks Jiun, Hyeongong, and Geumgang arrived. Following a decade of restoration projects, buildings such as Myeongbujeon Hall, Daeungbojeon Hall (a Treasure), and Eungjingak Hall (a Treasure) now stand orderly, renewing its status as one of Korea's most beautiful temples.

Mihwangsa always offers a fantastic landscape blending the sunset over the West Sea with the bizarre rocks of Dalmasan Mountain. Notably, the foundation stones of Daeungbojeon Hall feature rare carvings of marine creatures like turtles and crabs, adding to the intrigue. At the Budo (stupa) field, reached by a 10-minute walk along the forest path, you can also encounter simple carvings of child monks and goblin faces. The mountain peak is about a 1-hour walk away, offering panoramic views of the Dadohae archipelago...

entered the valley of Daeheungsa, built Iljiam Hermitage, and devoted himself solely to ascetic practice for over 40 years. This established Daeheungsa as the sacred site of Korea's tea culture. paragraphs: Dadohaehaesang National Park is a national park in the Jeolla region centered around coastal areas and islands, stretching from Hongdo Island in Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated City through Sinan-gun, Jindo-gun, Wando-gun, and Goheung-gun to Dolsan-eup in Yeosu-si. It was designated as the 14th national park on December 23, 1981. Dadohaehaesang National Park is divided into 8 districts depending on the region (Heuksan/Hongdo, Bigeum/Dochodo, Jodo, Soan/Cheongsando, Geomun/Baekdo, Narodo, Geumodo, and Palyeongsan districts).

The park and its surroundings consist of various rock formations formed by Paleozoic schist and gneiss, Mesozoic Gyeongsang Basin sedimentary layers, and volcanic activity such as tuff and granite. Geological landmarks where these features can be observed include Mulneomimok in Geomundo Island and Heuksando Island. It is also an excellent place to observe sea cliffs, a typical coastal landform of the Korean Peninsula. (Source: Korea National Park Service)

spot_at_126372.title: Neung-gasa Temple
spot_at_126372.addr: 21, Palbong-gil, Jeomam-myeon, Goheung-gun, Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated City
spot_at_126372.overview: Neung-gasa Temple, a branch temple of Songgwangsa Temple (the head temple of the 21st Parish of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism), is one of the four major temples in the Honam region, boasting a large scale on flat terrain. Originally founded in 417 by Buddhist Monk Ado and named Bohyeonsa, it was completely burned down during the Japanese Invasions of Korea, then reconstructed in 1644 (the 22nd year of King Injo's reign of the Joseon Dynasty) by Master Byeokcheon Jeonghyeon, who renamed it Neung-gasa. Master Byeokcheon was originally practicing asceticism at Jirisan Mountain at the age of 90 when a Buddha appeared in his dream and gave him a revelation to build a temple to save all sentient beings.

paragraphs: Neung-gasa Temple, a branch temple of Songgwangsa Temple (the head temple of the 21st Parish of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism), is one of the four major temples in the Honam region, boasting a large scale on flat terrain. Originally founded in 417 by Buddhist Monk Ado and named Bohyeonsa, it was completely burned down during the Japanese Invasions of Korea, then reconstructed in 1644 (the 22nd year of King Injo's reign of the Joseon Dynasty) by Master Byeokcheon Jeonghyeon, who renamed it Neung-gasa. Master Byeokcheon was originally practicing asceticism at Jirisan Mountain at the age of 90 when a Buddha appeared in his dream and gave him a revelation to build a temple to save all sentient beings, leading him to newly construct Neung-gasa here.

Existing temple buildings include Daeungjeon Hall (Treasures No. 1307), which features a 5-bay front, 3-bay side, and a hip-and-gable roof, as well as Eungjingak Hall, the bell pavilion, Cheonwangmun Gate, and monks' quarters. Neung-gasa runs a Temple Stay program for southern sea meditation travel. Situated at the foot of Palyeongsan Mountain, it allows visitors to explore the mountain, and right past the temple is the adjacent Palyeongsan Auto Camping Ground.

spot_at_126423.title: Heungyang eupseong Fortress Site & Okhari Honggyo Bridge in Goheung
spot_at_126423.addr: Okhari, Goheung-eup, Goheung-gun, Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated City
spot_at_126423.overview: The Heungyang eupseong Fortress Site is where the Heungyang-hyeon district office was located from its establishment in 1441 until its administrative name was changed to Goheung-gun in 1914, leaving traces of the fortress built during the Heungyang-hyeon period throughout Goheung-eup. Walking up the sloped village road behind the Goheung Jonsimdang History and Culture Park, you can see remnants of the fortress walls on the upper ridge. The site preserves fortress gates, walls, defensive bastions (chiseong), and wells, playing a crucial role in understanding the history and culture of Goheung-gun.

Walking up the sloped village road behind the Goheung Jonsimdang History and Culture Park, you can see remnants of the fortress walls on the upper ridge. The site preserves fortress gates, walls, defensive bastions (chiseong), and wells, playing a crucial role in understanding the history and culture of Goheung-gun. The Okhari Honggyo Bridge in Goheung is a rainbow-shaped stone bridge constructed during the late Joseon Dynasty. Designated as a Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated City Tangible Cultural Heritage, there are two rainbow bridges flowing through Okhari. The upper bridge is relatively large, featuring a dragon head carved on the front of the rainbow shape and a dragon tail on the reverse side.

The lower bridge is larger in scale than the upper one. While similar in shape, it differs from the front bridge in that a dragon head is attached to the center of the underside ceiling. Both bridges were built during the late Joseon Dynasty and are grand in scale. Currently, the tops of both bridges are much higher than the ground level, which is due to changes in the topography over later generations.

spot_at_126890.title: Jeokdaebong Peak
spot_at_126890.addr: Seokjeong-ri, Geumsan-myeon, Goheung-gun, Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated City
spot_at_126890.overview: Located on Geogeumdo Island, Jeokdaebong Peak (592m above sea level) is the second highest peak in Goheung-gun after Palyeongsan Mountain. Unlike its broad and gentle mountain shape, it boasts exceptionally stunning views. Standing at the summit, the seas and islands around Wando to the west, Geomundo to the south, and Yeosu to the east come into view at a glance. On a clear day, the view is so clear that even Jeju Island can be seen in the distance. Due to these geographical characteristics, a large beacon mound measuring 34 meters in circumference and 7 meters in diameter sits at the summit, which was used during the Joseon Dynasty to transmit emergency signals such as invasions by Japanese raiders.
spot_at_126890.pull_quote: Located on Geogeumdo Island, Jeokdaebong Peak (592m above sea level) is the second highest peak in Goheung-gun after Palyeongsan Mountain, boasting exceptionally stunning views...
paragraphs: Located on Geogeumdo Island, Jeokdaebong Peak (592m above sea level) is the second highest peak in Goheung-gun after Palyeongsan Mountain. Unlike its broad and gentle mountain shape, it boasts exceptionally stunning views. Standing at the summit, the seas and islands around Wando to the west, Geomundo to the south, and Yeosu to the east come into view at a glance. On a clear day, the view is so clear that even Jeju Island can be seen in the distance. Due to these geographical characteristics, a large beacon mound measuring 34 meters in circumference and 7 meters in diameter sits at the summit, which was used during the Joseon Dynasty to transmit emergency signals such as invasions by Japanese raiders.

The foothills of Jeokdaebong are also known to be the site of a Mokjangseong (Joseon-era ranch fortress). It is recorded as a tax ranch where a 30-ri long fortress was built around Jeokdaebong to raise 116 horses. Traces of the ranch fortress still remain in various places along the forest road connecting Seokjeong-ri and Eojeon-ri, crossing Geogeumdo from north to south. Nearby tourist attractions around Jeokdaebong include Ikgeum Beach in the southern part of Geogeumdo, where the water is so clear that seafood can be seen 2 to 3 meters deep, and Geogeum Ecological Forest on the southeastern foothills of Jeokdaebong.

With its excellent value for money, even solo travelers can enjoy a hearty meal without burden. Dongbang Gisikdang's bulgogi set meal provides a separate grill so you can cook it yourself. Alongside the thinly sliced pork belly, twelve delicious side dishes are served.

While pork belly is delicious wrapped in ssam vegetables with ssamjang, it tastes even better when accompanied by the side dishes served alongside. The side dishes mainly consist of pickled vegetables (jangajji) and kimchi. In particular, the onion kimchi available exclusively at Dongbang Gisikdang is as refreshing and flavorful as water kimchi, offering a clean finish when eaten with the meat. Additionally, the blue crab stew (kkotge-jjigae) is a unique specialty only tasted here. The broth, flavored with doenjang (soybean paste) and a hint of red pepper powder, contains a large piece of blue crab and tofu. Because green onions and onions provide the foundational broth flavor, it is spicy yet refreshing and clean.

Jungang Sikdang hides a special flavor you cannot experience anywhere else: dipping conger eel sashimi in citron (yuja) ade/syrup and dried conger eel steamed dish made exclusively with conger eels that cannot be served fresh to customers. The refreshing citron syrup and savory seafood decorate your mouth with a fresh yet mild harmony.

spot_at_126289.overview: Opened in 1925, this beach is located 24 km west of Yeonggwang-eup. It features a 1 km long, 200 m wide crescent-shaped sandy beach, backed by a lush pine forest of over 2,000 trees that creates a cozy atmosphere. With clear water and a shallow depth of 1-2 meters, it is celebrated as one of the three major beaches in the Honam region. The name 'Gamami' originates from Geumjeongsan Mountain behind it, whose ridge is said to resemble the tail of a harnessed horse (駕馬尾). Natural monuments like yellow-billed egrets and black-tailed gulls inhabit the area.

As a branch temple of Baekyangsa, the head temple of the 18th parish of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism, it was named 'Bulgapsa (佛甲寺)' carrying the significance of being the first Buddhist doctrinal center established by Marananta when Buddhism was introduced during the reign of King Chimnyu of Baekje (384 AD).

spot_at_126415.pull_quote: A Confucian academy established to commemorate Gang Hang (1567–1618), a civil official of the mid-Joseon dynasty. While serving as a junior official, the Jeongyu War broke out...
paragraphs: This Confucian academy was established to commemorate Gang Hang (1567–1618), a civil official of the mid-Joseon dynasty. While serving as a junior official in the Ministry of Taxation and Ministry of Justice, the Jeongyu War broke out, prompting him to gather a militia to fight before being captured as a prisoner of war by Japanese troops and escorted to Japan. While in Japan, he gathered information on the country's history and geography to send back to his homeland while introducing Neo-Confucianism to Japan. After returning to his homeland in the 33rd year of King Seonjo's reign (1600), he declined official posts and dedicated himself solely to reading and nurturing future generations. The academy was bestowed the name 'Yonggyesa' by the royal court in the 13th year of King Injo's reign (1635) and was rebuilt in the 28th year of King Sukjong's reign (1702).

It was rebuilt again during the Japanese colonial period and has undergone several renovations since then to reach the present day. It follows a traditional layout with an educational space at the front and a sacrificial ritual space at the rear (Jeon-hak-hu-myo). The lecture hall, serving as the educational space, features a wooden floor in the center with heated ondol rooms on both sides. Passing through the inner three-gate in the back leads to a small shrine housing Gang Hang's spirit tablet. On the left foothill lies Gang Hang's tomb. (Source: Korea Heritage Service)

spot_at_129215.pull_quote: The Christian Martyrs Site is a historic location commemorating 194 martyrs who sacrificed their lives while protecting their faith during the Korean War, recognized as a representative...
paragraphs: The Christian Martyrs Site is a historic location commemorating 194 martyrs who sacrificed their lives while protecting their faith during the Korean War, recognized as a representative martyrdom site recorded even in global church history. Near Seoldo Port in Yeomsan-myeon, Yeomsan Church features a martyr's monument, a joint burial site for martyrs, and an exhibition hall, while Yawol Church in Yawol-ri houses a martyr's memorial hall to honor the noble sacrifices and faith of the martyrs.

Yawol Church was the first church in the Yeomsan region established by missionary Eugene Bell in 1908, and later with the establishment of Yeomsan Church in 1939, it established itself as the center of local Christian culture. However, during the Korean War in 1950, a tragic event occurred where clergy and church members sacrificed their lives defending their faith, totaling 194 martyrs centered around Yeomsan Church and Yawol Church. Today, this place is visited by many pilgrims seeking to reflect on the meaning of Korean Christian martyrdom history and revisit the values of peace and harmony.

spot_at_1087619.title: Mahan Cultural Park
spot_at_1087619.overview: Mahan Cultural Park was created to offer a glimpse into the unique ancient history of the Yeongsan River basin by helping visitors understand the ancient jar coffins scattered throughout the region. The Tomb Exploration Museum is themed around the myth of birth from an egg, featuring restored models of the jar coffin excavation process and burial styles. When illuminated at night, it creates a fantastic spaceship-like atmosphere. The exterior of the exhibition hall is shaped like a jar coffin, and the inside houses a video hall showing various films and an administrative office. The Namhae Watchtower serves as an observatory offering panoramic views of the Sampo River streams, Wolchulsan Mountain, Mongdan in Muan, and Donggang in Naju. Inside the Mongjeon of the Tomb Exploration Museum, the excavation site of the Naedong-ri Chobung-gol Ancient Tomb Cluster is recreated, along with a fun artifact-hunting play space for children. The Mahan confederacy consisted of 54 states distributed across the central-southern region of the Korean Peninsula from the 3rd–2nd centuries BCE to the late 5th–early 6th centuries CE, until the remaining forces in the Yeongsan River basin were absorbed by Baekje in the mid-6th century.

spot_at_1214029.title: Yeongam Hyanggyo (Confucian School)
spot_at_1214029.overview: Yeongam Hyanggyo was first established in 1420 (the 2nd year of King Sejong's reign in the Joseon Dynasty). After being burned down during the Japanese Invasions of Korea and a fire in 1918, it was rebuilt, only to suffer the hardship of being completely destroyed once again during the Korean War. The current buildings include the Daeseongjeon Shrine reconstructed in 1951, the Dongjae and Seojae student dormitories in 1963, and the Myeongnyundang Lecture Hall in 1969, with the remaining structures built sequentially afterward. The layout uniquely features the educational and ritual spaces arranged side by side on the east and west.

The current buildings include the Daeseongjeon Shrine reconstructed in 1951, the Dongjae and Seojae student dormitories in 1963, and the Myeongnyundang Lecture Hall in 1969, with the remaining structures built sequentially afterward.

The layout uniquely features the educational and ritual spaces arranged side by side on the east and west. Myeongnyundang, the lecture hall where students gathered to study, was built with a scale of 4 bays in the front and 2 bays on the sides. Daeseongjeon, which enshrines the ancestral tablets of Confucius and other sages of China and Korea, is decorated with modest elegance. In addition, there is a Naesammun Gate separating the two spaces and a neat, square pond.

spot_at_126361.title: Dogapsa Temple
spot_at_126361.overview: Nestled on a wide mountain slope facing Jujibong Peak with Dogapbong Peak on the southern side of Wolchulsan Mountain—often called the 'Mount Geumgang of the Southern Province'—Dogapsa Temple is a historic Buddhist sanctuary originated when National Master Doseon, one of the four great eminent monks of Silla, grandly rebuilt the original Munsuasa Temple. In 1456 (the 2nd year of King Sejo's reign in Joseon), Royal Preceptor Sumi built an enormous complex consisting of 966 halls, pavilions, and 12 hermitages by royal command. Generations of eminent monks and masters, including Master Yeondam, Master Heoju, and Master Cho-ui, resided here to spread the true principles of enlightenment, establishing Dogapsa as a vibrant sanctuary where spiritual practice and teachings never cease.

spot_at_126413.overview: Dr. Wangin traveled to Japan during the reign of King Geunchogo of Baekje to spread Baekje's advanced culture, and he is revered in Japan as the cultural patriarch who introduced civilization. Located on the foothills of Munpilbong Peak east of Gurim Village, the Dr. Wangin Historic Site restores his legacy as his historical significance has been newly illuminated. It consists of Dr. Wangin's Tomb, the inner and outer gates, Munsanjae, Yangsajae, an exhibition hall, a statue of Dr. Wangin, and a study cave. Among them, Dr. Wangin's Tomb enshrines his portrait and ancestral tablet, where memorial rites are held annually. Munsanjae and Yangsajae are where Dr. Wangin studied and nurtured future generations; they have been restored after only their foundations remained on the middle slopes of the western side of Wolchulsan Mountain.

spot_at_126741.title: Yeongamho Lake (Migratory Bird Habitat)
spot_at_126741.overview: Yeongamho Lake is a large-scale lake created following the completion of the Yeongam-Geumho seawalls. The Yeongam and Geumho seawalls connect Samho-eup in Yeongam-gun with Hawon-myeon and San-i-myeon in Haenam-gun, with construction beginning in 1985 and completed in 1996. Thanks to its nutrient-rich mudflats, expansive water surface, and warm climate, Yeongamho Lake serves as a migratory route and intermediate stopover for migratory birds. Among the winter migratory birds visiting the habitat, ducks and geese finish breeding in Siberia, travel down through areas like Cheonsuman Bay on the west coast and the Geumgang Estuary starting in October to reach the reclaimed lands of the southwestern coast, and head north again in March.

Among the winter migratory birds visiting the Yeongamho Migratory Bird Habitat, ducks and geese finish breeding in Siberia, travel down through areas like Cheonsuman Bay on the west coast and the Geumgang Estuary starting in October to reach the reclaimed lands of the southwestern coast, and head north again in March. Summer migratory birds, such as egrets, spend the winter in Southeast Asia, move to Korea in April to breed, and migrate southward again around September. Ecological surveys conducted by the Ministry of Environment since October 1996 have reported it as a migratory bird habitat inhabited by 34 species of winter birds, transforming this area into a new tourism landmark. Nearby attractions include Wolchulsan National Park, Dogapsa Temple, the Dr. Wangin Historic Site, and the Jeollanam-do Agricultural Museum.

spot_at_127672.title: Wolchulsan National Park
spot_at_127672.overview: Designated as Korea's 20th national park in 1988, Wolchulsan Mountain was formed when massive granite rock masses of the Honam Jeongmaek mountain range clashed with the Southern Sea and rose up over countless years of weathering. Although Wolchulsan has a relatively small area of 56.22 ㎢, it is home to a diverse distribution of flora and fauna, and boasts high-caliber cultural heritage including national treasures. The peak of Wolchulsan is Cheonhwangbong (809m), known as a sacred place where ancestral rites to the heavens have been held since the Silla Dynasty. Centered around Cheonhwangbong Peak, the northern and eastern sides feature magnificent scenery created by huge boulders perched atop bold ridge lines, while the southern and western areas showcase formations where large and small rocks resemble stacked pagodas.

paragraphs: Standing at 807 meters, Jeamsan Mountain is located at the end of the Sobaeksan Mountains, forming the border with Boseong-gun northeast of Jangheung-eup. With numerous large valleys and springs, it is called the 'King's Rock (Jeam) Mountain' because the surrounding rocks appear to bow toward the peak's rock. It is a famous mountain in Honam featuring gentle strange rocks and stones, hiking trails overlooking the South Sea, and native pine trees, royal azaleas, and various wild herbs. The soaring peak truly matches the name King's Rock, and the ridges on both sides stretch out vigorously.

In addition, deep in the mountain are the 'Brother Rocks,' named after a sad legend of poor brothers who fell to their deaths while picking wild herbs and turned into rocks. About 50 meters below the Brother Rocks are the Uisangam and Wonhyo hermitages. At the summit sits Jeamdan altar where rain-praying rituals were held, offering views of Mudeungsan, Wolchulsan, Cheonwansan, Jonjesan mountains, and the South Sea in the distance. In spring, the ridge stretching from Gomjaesan to Sajasand is so brilliantly covered with royal azaleas that its reddish glow reaches toward the Dadohae (Archipelago). Azaleas begin to bloom in late April after azaleas fade, reaching full bloom in mid-May under the warm sea breeze of the South Sea.

spot_at_126367.title: Borimsa Temple (Jangheung)
spot_at_126367.overview: Borimsa Temple is an ancient temple located in Bongdeok Valley on Gajisan Mountain. As one of the three major Borim temples in the East (India, China, and Korea), it is also the place where Seon (Zen) Buddhism first entered and settled in Korea. When Wonpyo Daedeok laid its foundation in 759, it seems to have remained in the form of a modest thatched hermitage, and its founding legend adds interest for visitors. Place names related to the tale remain scattered throughout the area.
spot_at_126367.pull_quote: Borimsa Temple is an ancient temple located in Bongdeok Valley on Gajisan Mountain. As one of the three major Borim temples in the East (India, China, and Korea), it is also the place where Seon Buddhism first entered...
paragraphs: Borimsa Temple is an ancient temple located in Bongdeok Valley on Gajisan Mountain. As one of the three major Borim temples in the East (India, China, and Korea), it is also the place where Seon (Zen) Buddhism first entered and settled in Korea. When Wonpyo Daedeok laid its foundation in 759, it seems to have remained in the form of a modest thatched hermitage, and its founding legend adds interest for visitors. Place names related to the tale remain scattered throughout the area.

In the past, Borimsa Temple was grand and magnificent. Although it declined due to the Joseon Dynasty's Confucian-supremacist and anti-Buddhist policies and suffered war damage during the Korean War, it has since been restored. The North and South Three-Story Stone Pagodas of Borimsa enshrine the true sarira (relics) of the Buddha, and the stone lantern between them signifies that the light of the Buddha shines in all directions. The Stele for State Preceptor Bojo's Changseong Pagoda records the state preceptor's achievements, the Seon state of mind, and the founding legend. In the middle of the courtyard is a mineral spring that never dries up even during severe droughts, and the nutmeg tree forest surrounding the temple offers fresh and divine energy.

spot_fo_133637.title: Bada House
spot_fo_133637.overview: A local culinary hotspot situated right in front of the breakwater between Sumun Beach and Sumun Port in Jangheung. Although it gained widespread fame after being featured on SBS's 'Mat-dae-mat' (Taste vs. Taste), it has long been renowned locally for its seasoned ark shell (cockle/manila clam) sashimi. Clam meat is tossed with water dropwort (minari) and onions in gochujang and vinegar, offering a unique sweet taste that follows a non-irritating tartness. Refreshing clam soup is also served in between to soothe the palate.
spot_fo_133637.pull_quote: Representative Delicacy: Samhap (Beef, Pen Shell, Shiitake Mushrooms) / Seasoned Clam Sashimi Set / Gizzard Shad Course / Spicy Rockfish Stew, etc.
paragraphs: A local culinary hotspot situated right in front of the breakwater between Sumun Beach and Sumun Port in Jangheung. Although it gained widespread fame after being featured on SBS's 'Mat-dae-mat' (Taste vs. Taste), it has long been renowned locally for its seasoned ark shell sashimi. Clam meat is tossed with water dropwort and onions in gochujang and vinegar, offering a unique sweet taste that follows a non-irritating tartness. Refreshing clam soup is also served in between to soothe the palate.

The secret to the famous seasoned clam sashimi lies in the vinegar used exclusively by this restaurant. Kept secretly in a large Cheongju (refined rice wine) bottle in a corner of the kitchen, the vinegar is reportedly made by fermenting makgeolli (rice wine). Homemade makgeolli is aged once more to extract the vinegar. The gochujang is also homemade, blended with the makgeolli vinegar to create the chojang (chili paste sauce). While Bada House specializes in pen shells and clams, it also serves seasonal raw fish like gizzard shad, sea bass, and conger eel depending on the time of year.

spot_at_125447.title: Nolbeundle Hakwon Farm
spot_at_125447.overview: A rare large-scale farm featuring a vast 150,000-pyeong green field cultivated into a single massive barley field. In spring, visitors can witness the nation's largest barley field, and in autumn, fields of blooming buckwheat. After the farm was authorized as a tourist farm and its scenic beauty became widely known, it established itself as a popular destination visited by numerous tourists and photographers, also gaining attention as a filming location for various dramas, movies, and commercials. Accordingly, Hakwon Farm dedicates itself to landscape agriculture to provide even more beautiful scenery.

spot_at_126236.title: Seonunsan Mountain (Jeonbuk West Coast National Geopark)
spot_at_126236.overview: The Nakjodae and Cheonmabong areas of Seonunsan Mountain, known for their stunning sunsets, are composed of rhyolite, a type of volcanic rock. Rhyolite is harder, denser, and more resistant to weathering than the surrounding tuff. Consequently, differential weathering between the rhyolite and tuff creates near-vertical rock cliffs primarily formed of rhyolite, offering magnificent natural scenery. This makes the Seonunsan area an important site for observing stunning natural landscapes while understanding the characteristics of rock weathering.

spot_at_126262.title: Dosolgokgyo Valley (Seonunsan Mountain)
spot_at_126262.overview: Along with Naejangsan Mountain, Gochang is renowned as one of the best spots for autumn foliage in the Honam region. In particular, Dosolgokgyo Valley around Seonunsan Mountain in Gochang is said to bloom with red flowers three times a year. In spring, the Natural Monument camellia forest flaunts its vibrant red hues, followed by red spider lilies in early autumn, and finally, brilliant autumn foliage once the lilies fade. Walking from Seonunsa Temple to Dosolam Hermitage along the Dosolcheon Stream, visitors can enjoy gorgeous autumn leaves and picturesque snowy winter landscapes. Designated as a Scenic Site in 2009, the Dosolgokgyo Valley area is beautiful in all four seasons.

spot_at_126286.title: Dongho Beach
spot_at_126286.overview: Dongho Beach is famous for its long, expansive sandy shore. Stretching over 4 km with fine sand and a gentle slope, it attracts numerous vacationers during the summer. spot_at_126290.title: Gusipo Beach
spot_at_126290.overview: Gusipo Beach is the largest beach in Gochang-gun, featuring a long, wide sandy shore and a dense pine forest. With its gentle slope, it is the perfect summer getaway for families. To the south of the beach lies a natural cave where dozens of residents and hundreds of rock doves reportedly took refuge for half a year during the Jeongyu War, and bizarre rock formations are scattered along the coastline. Beautiful islands, including Gamakdo Island, float gracefully in the open sea, and at dusk, you can witness a stunning sunset that paints the West Sea's Chilsan Sea in brilliant shades of red. It is also a popular spot for auto-camping enthusiasts, with various convenience facilities well-equipped nearby.

spot_at_126340.title: Munsubsa Temple (Gochang)
spot_at_126340.overview: Munsubsa Temple is nestled on the mid-slope of Munsubsan Mountain (621m), which forms the border between Gochang and Jangseong in Jeollanam-do. Passing the Gosu Pottery Site from Gosu-myeon township and heading upward leads to Josan Reservoir; following the left valley for about 6 km brings you to Munsubsa Temple. It is said to have been founded by Master Jajang. Legend has it that while returning from practicing at Mount Qingliang in Tang China, Jajang passed by Mount Munsu in Baekje territory, felt it resembled Mount Qingliang, and offered prayers in a stone cave. There, he discovered a stone statue of the Bodhisattva of Wisdom underground and built the temple.

Treasures housed here include the Daeungjeon Hall of Munsubsa, the Wooden Seated Shakyamuni Triad Buddha, the Wooden Seated Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva and Ten Kings Statues of Munsubsa, alongside Jeollabuk-do Tangible Cultural Heritages such as Munsubu Pavilion and Munsubsa Stupas, as well as Myeongbujeon Hall and Hansanjeon Hall. The Natural Monument baby maple tree forest at Munsubsa is planted along an 80-meter section from the Iljumun Gate to the temple entrance. Around 500 baby maple trees, aged between 100 and 400 years old, grow naturally here. In autumn, the colorful foliage harmonizes with the gently rolling mountain scenery around the millennium-old temple.

spot_fo_1017691.title: Woojin Eel
spot_fo_1017691.overview: Located in Gochang, Woojin Tidal Flat Eel specializes in pungcheon eel. The term 'pungcheon' does not refer to a local region, but rather to the point where freshwater and saltwater meet in rivers connected to the West or South Sea, where tidal variations are large. Raised in tidal flats where the sea and river meet without artificial feed, these eels are uniquely chewy in texture compared to others. You can savor the plump and savory tidal flat pungcheon eel dipped in a sweet and salty soy sauce.

spot_fo_134343.title: Sindeok Sikdang
spot_fo_134343.overview: Located at the three-way intersection at the entrance of Seonunsa Temple, this famous pungcheon eel restaurant has been passed down through two generations since the late 1960s. Eel is a stamina food, long symbolizing blood and vitality replenishment, making it great as a snack for the elderly and children as well as for women's skin beauty. The eel sauce is made from a base broth boiled down from eel bones, mixed with gochujang (chili paste) and various seasonings, then simmered for hours, holding over 30 years of culinary secrets. After being pre-grilled and allowed to absorb the flavors, the eel is grilled a second time before serving, melting softly in your mouth.

Two campsites are provided, and the parking lot covers an area of 6,300㎡ with a capacity of about 200 vehicles. Additional amenities include a foot volleyball court, volleyball court, hiking trails, a water play area, and an ecological pond. The hiking trails within the recreation forest are free for everyone to use. The animal enclosure houses 116 animals across 12 species, including fallow deer, blue peacocks, white peacocks, golden pheasants, silver pheasants, and Lady Amherst's pheasants. The natural observation garden features 224 plants of 12 species such as Japanese red pines, while the flower garden contains 2,424 plants of 7 species including oak-leaf hydrangeas. At the Bakdaljae pass summit, there is an octagonal pavilion and a spring.

spot_at_125814.overview: Mt. Woraksan is located in the middle section where the Baekdudaegan mountain range connects Mt. Sobaeksan to Mt. Sokrisan. With rugged mountain terrain and soaring rock cliffs resembling fierce tigers, it boasts breathtaking scenery harmonized with deep mountain valleys, waterfalls, and pools. Woraksan National Park was designated as the 17th national park on December 31, 1984. Spanning across Jecheon-si, Chungju-si, Danyang-gun, and Mungyeong-si, it is surrounded to the north by Chungju Lake and Cheongpung Lake, and to the east by the 8 Scenic Views of Danyang...
spot_at_125814.pull_quote: Mt. Woraksan sits centrally along the Baekdudaegan between Mt. Sobaeksan and Mt. Sokrisan, boasting rugged terrain, towering cliffs like fierce tigers, and stunning scenery with deep valleys, waterfalls, and pools...
paragraphs: Mt. Woraksan is centrally located where the Baekdudaegan connects Mt. Sobaeksan to Mt. Sokrisan. Its rugged terrain and towering rock cliffs, rising like fierce tigers, blend with deep valleys, waterfalls, and pools to boast magnificent scenery. Woraksan National Park was designated as the 17th national park on December 31, 1984. Spanning the administrative districts of Jecheon-si, Chungju-si, Danyang-gun, and Mungyeong-si, it is embraced by Chungju Lake and Cheongpung Lake to the north, and surrounded by scenic natural landscapes such as the 8 Scenic Views of Danyang and Sobaeksan National Park to the east, and Mungyeong Saejae and Sokrisan National Park to the south.

The main peak of Mt. Woraksan, Yeongbong, is also called Guksabong and has been revered as a sacred mountain since ancient times. Centered around Mt. Woraksan, there are numerous picturesque peaks including Haseulsan, where snow reportedly lingers even in summer, Munsubong, and Mansubong. Upon reaching the summit (Yeongbong), resilient pine trees that have weathered countless storms remain evergreen across all four seasons, and open skies stretch out refreshingly in all directions. In addition, the stunning views of Chungju Lake and Cheongpung Lake can be seen at a glance. In summer, the abundant valley water offers a refreshing escape from the sweltering heat.

spot_at_125828.title: Deokdong Valley
spot_at_125828.overview: Deokdong Valley is a 5km-long stream originating from Mt. Baegunsan (1,087m) and Mt. Sipsabong (984.8m) flowing down to Wondeokdong. Though less well-known than nearby Yongha Gugok or Songgye Valley, its beautiful rock formations, lush forests, and crystal-clear water are second to none. The valley is shallow and clear, making it ideal for water play, and its dense foliage makes it a supreme summer retreat secretly cherished and frequently visited by locals from Jecheon during the summer months. Fishing and gathering activities are prohibited by local residents to preserve the valley. Portable restrooms and deck paths are placed here and there for the convenience of visitors.
spot_at_125828.pull_quote: Deokdong Valley originates from Mt. Baegunsan (1,087m) and Mt. Sipsabong (984.8m) and flows 5km to Wondeokdong. Though less famous than Yongha Gugok or Songgye Valley...
paragraphs: Deokdong Valley is a 5km-long valley originating from Mt. Baegunsan (1,087m) and Mt. Sipsabong (984.8m) down to Wondeokdong. Compared to nearby Yongha Gugok or Songgye Valley, it is relatively unknown, but its beautiful bizarre rocks, dense forests, and pristine water are second to none.

The valley is not deep and its water is crystal clear, making it perfect for water play. With its lush woods, it is an unbeatable summer retreat that Jecheon locals keep closely guarded and frequently visit in the summer. All fishing and gathering activities in the valley are prohibited by the residents. Portable restrooms and wooden deck paths are installed throughout to ensure the convenience of summer vacationers.

spot_at_125834.title: Songgye Valley
spot_at_125834.overview: Songgye Valley is a representative valley tourist destination in Jecheon, located within Woraksan National Park. Surrounded like a folding screen by the foothills of Mt. Woraksan (1,094m), it effectively helps visitors forget the summer heat. In particular, the clear water flowing through the valley is ice-cold, drawing numerous vacationers looking to cool off during the summer. Popular among those seeking refuge from the heat in lush forests and deep valleys in summer, it also shines as a vibrant autumn foliage destination connected with Chungju Lake.
spot_at_125834.pull_quote: Songgye Valley is located within Woraksan National Park and stands out as Jecheon's premier valley destination. Encircled like a screen by Mt. Woraksan (1,094m)...
paragraphs: Songgye Valley is located inside Woraksan National Park and is considered Jecheon's representative valley tourist spot. The foothills of Mt. Woraksan (1,094m) surround it like a folding screen, making it a wonderful place to forget the summer heat. In particular, the clear water flowing through the valley is ice-cold, attracting many summer vacationers seeking relief from the warmth. It is popular in summer for its dense woods and deep gorges, and in autumn, it gains acclaim as a foliage-viewing spot linked with Chungju Lake.

The Mt. Woraksan area was designated as a national park on December 31, 1984. It is dotted with tourist attractions such as the natural monument Manggaenamu tree, Deokjusa Temple, and Mireukri Temple Site, which capture the attention of hikers. The scenic spots around the valley, including Wolgwang Waterfall, Haksodae, Jayeondae, Cheongbyeokdae, Waryongdae, Palrangso, Mangpokdae, and Sukyeongdae, are collectively known as the 8 Scenic Views of Songgye. Jayeondae, located at the entrance of Songgye Valley, impresses visitors with its clear valley water, wide bedrock, and deep pool. Wolgwang Waterfall is a 3--tier waterfall about 30 meters high, and Sukyeongdae is a historical site where the Woraksan Shrine was established and rituals were held since the Silla Dynasty.

spot_at_125876.title: Jeongbangsa Temple
spot_at_125876.overview: A thousand-year-old temple located on the ridge of Sinseonbong peak in the Geumsusan mountain range at an elevation of 1,016m, Jeongbangsa Temple is a subsidiary temple of Beopjusa Temple on Mt. Sokrisan of the Jogye Order, reportedly founded by Master Uisang during the Silla Dynasty. Reaching the temple offers panoramic views of Cheongpung Lake and surrounding mountains that resemble a wonderland, instilling a sense of natural wonder. A rock cliff covers one-third of the main hall's roof, and its grand and peculiar appearance evokes the greatness of nature. The temple grounds house the main hall, monk quarters, and Hyeonhyemun Gate.
spot_at_125876.pull_quote: Jeongbangsa Temple is a millennium-old temple on the Sinseonbong ridge of Geumsusan (1,016m), a branch temple of Beopjusa, reportedly founded by Master Uisang of Silla...
paragraphs: Jeongbangsa Temple is a thousand-year-old temple situated on the Sinseonbong ridge of the Geumsusan range at an elevation of 1,016m. A branch of Beopjusa Temple on Mt. Sokrisan under the Jogye Order, it was reportedly founded by Master Uisang during the Silla period. Upon climbing to the temple, visitors can overlook Cheongpung Lake and surrounding mountains, which resemble an ethereal fairyland and evoke a deep sense of natural wonder. An imposing rock cliff covers one-third of the main hall's roof, and its grand, unique shape inspires awe at the greatness of nature. The temple precinct includes the main hall, monk quarters, and Hyeonhyemun Gate.

Built in 1825, the main hall is a 12-kan wooden tiled building, and the monk quarters consist of a 5-kan structure. Hyeonhyemun is the main gate of the temple, also known as Iljumun (One-Pillar Gate), constructed as a 1-kan wooden gate. Inside the main hall sits the presiding Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva statue, 60cm in height and 30cm in shoulder width, with a post-Buddha painting behind it. The Seated Wooden Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva and Votive Relics of Jeongbangsa Temple in Jecheon refer to the wooden Avalokitesvara statue enshrined in the main hall and the relics discovered within it. This seated statue is enshrined as the main Buddha and clearly exhibits the typical characteristics of mid-Joseon Dynasty bodhisattva sculptures.

spot_at_125877.title: Muamsa Temple
spot_at_125877.overview: Climbing up the valley heading east from Seongnae-ri village in Jecheon, Kachiseongsan Mountain stretches its ridge on the left and Donsan Mountain on the right, nestled deep within which lies Muamsa Temple. Although said to have been founded during the Silla Dynasty, the exact founding year is unknown, though it is estimated to have existed since before the early Joseon Dynasty. However, the current main hall, Geuknakjeon, has been confirmed to have been reconstructed in the 16th year of King Yeongjo's reign (1740), and the seated wooden Tathagata statue here is estimated to have been crafted around the same time. Alongside the Buddha statue, Muamsa preserves relics such as a bronze bodhisattva head and Jeonpae.
spot_at_125877.pull_quote: Ascending the eastern valley from Seongnae-ri village in Jecheon, between Kachiseongsan and Donsan mountains, lies the deeply embraced Muamsa Temple...
paragraphs: Climbing the valley running east from Seongnae-ri village in Jecheon, Kachiseongsan stands on the left and Donsan on the right with long ridges, and deep in their embrace sits Muamsa Temple. While said to be built in the Silla period, the precise founding date is unknown, though it is presumed to predate the early Joseon Dynasty. The current main hall, Geuknakjeon, was verified to have been rebuilt in 1740 (the 16th year of King Yeongjo), and the wooden seated Tathagata statue inside is believed to have been created concurrently. Muamsa also preserves relics such as a bronze bodhisattva head and wooden tablets (jeonpae).

A rocky peak sits southwest of the temple resembling an old monk, so it is called Nojangam (Old Monk Rock). Legend says this rock only appears when fog rolls in, which inspired the temple's name, Muamsa (Mist Rock Temple). Existing structures include Geuknakjeon, Chilseonggak, Sansingak, monk quarters, guest rooms, and guardian rooms. Geuknakjeon preserves a seated wooden Amitabha Buddha, a post-Buddha painting, and a Jijang (Ksitigarbha) painting. Four stupas, Buddhist utensils, candlesticks, and ancestral tablets are designated cultural heritage assets, among which the Suwoldang stupa is...

spot_at_125448.title: Anmyeondo Natural Recreation Forest
spot_at_125448.overview: Anmyeondo Natural Recreation Forest is the country's only single-species pine forest, where a dense cluster of native Anmyeon pine trees, about 100 years old, thrives across 430ha. Since the Goryeo Dynasty, they were mainly used to build palaces and ships, but as illegal logging worsened, the royal family placed them under special management, and Chungcheongnam-do has managed them since 1965. Currently, the recreation forest is located on a pine forest ridge that appears after passing the wide plains of Bangpo Village past the Anmyeon-eup township.

Inside the path paved with interlocking blocks, a wonderful building comes into view: the Forest Exhibition Hall, which also serves as the management office. The Forest Exhibition Hall is organized so that visitors can easily understand the timber production process, uses of wood, and utility value of forests. paragraphs: Taean Haean National Park was designated as South Korea's 13th national park in 1978. It spans a total area of 377.019㎢ with 27 beaches spread across a 230km coastline embracing the Taean Peninsula and Anmyeondo Island from north to south. Since ancient times, the region was named Taean (meaning 'Peace and Comfort') because life was not harsh, thanks to the absence of major natural disasters, a mild climate, and abundant food.

The geology of the Taean Haean National Park area mainly consists of Precambrian ancient metamorphic sedimentary rocks and Mesozoic igneous rocks intruding upon them, and the coastal zone mostly comprises alluvial deposits made of medium to fine silt, appearing in the form of sandy beaches and coastal dunes. Topographically, the Taean coast consists of tidal flats, dunes, wetlands, bizarre rock formations, and large and small islands along a ria coastline of approximately 230 km from Hakampho in the north to Yeongmok in the south. Because of this, it is considered one of the representative places showcasing the unique and beautiful scenery of the West Coast. (Source: Taean Haean National Park Website)

spot_at_125840.title: Euihang Beach
spot_at_125840.overview: Walking past the Sowon-myeon township toward Mallipo Beach, you will find Euihang Beach on the right. Named because its topographical shape resembles an ant's neck, it features a gentle slope and maintains clean seawater even during high tide. The sandy beach, entirely composed of pebbles, sparkles brightly under the sunlight, and the cozy, curved shoreline boasts stunning beauty. Mainly recognized as an undeveloped tourist destination favored for family or educational camping trips, visitors arriving without special preparations can easily use the local homestays (minbak). Like typical West Coast beaches, the shore is gentle and spread with colorful pebbles. Along the Sowon-myeon coast, Baekripo Beach, Cheonripo Beach, Mallipo Beach, Eoeundol Beach, and Padori Beach continue southward from Euihang Beach.

spot_at_125843.overview: Bangpo Beach features excellent sand quality and is great for camping, making it an optimal quiet family getaway. On both sides of the beach stand legendary rock peaks such as Halmi Rock (Grandmother Rock) and Halarbi Rock (Grandfather Rock), and the area is home to a colony of golden rain trees designated as Natural Monument No. 138. Additionally, to the southwest lie Naepasudo and Oepasudo islands, which act as natural breakwaters. Bangpo Port is famous for fresh raw fish caught abundantly, including ray, conger eel, rockfish, and mackerel, and neighbors various beaches like Kkotji and Sambong.

Additionally, to the southwest lie Naepasudo and Oepasudo islands, which act as natural breakwaters. Bangpo Port is famous for fresh raw fish caught abundantly, including ray, conger eel, rockfish, and mackerel, and neighbors various beaches like Kkotji and Sambong. Nearby, attractions such as the Anmyeondo Natural Recreation Forest and an arboretum housing 208 species of natural flora from the central coastal region make it suitable for family relaxation and mental-physical refreshment.

spot_at_125845.title: Mongsanpo Beach
spot_at_125845.overview: Part of Taean Haean National Park, Mongsanpo Beach is surrounded by sandy shores and dense pine forests. With an auto-camping site located within the pine forest spreading widely along the beach, many campers visit to enjoy forest bathing and the fragrance of nature. The beach features a vast tidal flat, drawing frequent crowds looking to catch clams and crabs when the tide goes out. Well-developed sand dunes also make it perfect for tidal flat experiences and natural organism observation with children.

spot_fo_135110.title: Iwon Sikdang
spot_fo_135110.overview: Iwon Sikdang is a renowned 50-year traditional eatery and the original birthplace of Bak-sok Mil-guk Nakji-tang (octopus soup with gourd and wheat noodles). Selected as an exemplary restaurant designated by Chungnam, it is a representative dining spot for Taean tourism. Primarily using tidal-flat octopus caught in Iwon-myeon, Taean-gun, this local food restaurant uses agricultural produce from the Chungnam region. You can enjoy the local specialty of Wonbuk and Iwon-myeon—Bak-sok Nakji-tang, made by slicing the inside of a bottle gourd, adding vegetables and tidal-flat octopus for a clear, refreshing broth, served here with kalguksu (knife-cut noodles) and sujebi (hand-torn dough soup).

spot_fo_135411.title: Jeonggane Bak-sok Nakji-tang
spot_fo_135411.overview: Jeonggane Haemul Son-kalguksu has been specializing in bak-sok nakji-tang and seafood knife-cut noodles since opening in 1998. Bak-sok nakji-tang is a traditional Taean dish born from the old days when locals boiled tender tidal-flat octopus—commonly found along the Taean coast—with gourd instead of expensive meat to create a refreshing soup. Using only fresh mud-flat octopus from the Taean region, the meat remains tender rather than tough, and kalguksu noodles can be added to the broth. Made exclusively with domestic Korean wheat, the noodles ensure both great taste and health.

spot_fo_135903.overview: Located right in front of Anmyeon-do Recreational Forest, this is a specialty restaurant for soy sauce-marinated raw crabs (ganjang gejang). Anheung Ggot-gejang highlights the savory and light flavor of blue crab without being overly salty. It is complemented by about 13 neat and clean side dishes, including snail soybean paste stew, squid, and bulgogi. spot_at_1041580.title: Seondori Ssangdo Coast, Biin
spot_at_1041580.overview: Seondori in Biin-myeon got its name because it was historically a bustling route for boats. Though times have changed and boats are no longer seen, the beach, waves, and islands remain to preserve its scenic beauty. Off the coast of Seondori lie two small uninhabited islands called Ssangdo (Twin Islands). Legend has it that a widower with twin sons went out to sea, encountered a storm, and perished; when the twin sons waited anxiously for their father and died, they turned into rocks. The beach features the Seondori Tidal Flat Experience Center, allowing visitors to walk across to Ssangdo about 300 meters from the shore during low tide. Grilled clams and knife-cut noodles around Biin Beach, along with the gorgeous West Sea sunset, are unmissable highlights.

spot_at_1055245.title: Yi Ha-bok's Old House in Seocheon
spot_at_1055245.overview: Preserved in its original form as a modest, traditional folk farmhouse typical of Korea's central region, Yi Ha-bok's Old House in Seocheon was designated as a National Folk Cultural Heritage in 1984 in recognition of its historical value. Built in the late 19th century by a descendant of the scholar Mogeun Yi Saek—who constructed the 3-room main quarters—the house was expanded in the early 20th century with the addition of the sarangchae (men's quarters), lower wing, and upper wing, alongside a major expansion of the main quarters. Considered an auspicious site in geomancy, the property's sense of enclosure is further enhanced by neatly planted juniper, Chinese parasol, and evergreen trees.
spot_at_1055245.pull_quote: Preserved in its original form as a modest, traditional folk farmhouse typical of Korea's central region, Yi Ha-bok's Old House in Seocheon was designated as a National Folk Cultural Heritage in...
paragraphs: Preserved in its original form as a modest, traditional folk farmhouse typical of Korea.s central region, Yi Ha-bok's Old House in Seocheon was designated as a National Folk Cultural Heritage in 1984 in recognition of its historical value. This house was built in the late 19th century by a descendant of Mogeun Yi Saek, who constructed a 3-room main wing. Later, in the early 20th century, the sarangchae (men's quarters), lower wing, and upper wing were newly built, and the main wing was substantially expanded to take its current form. Geomantically, this location is considered an auspicious site, and rows of juniper, Chinese parasol, and evergreen trees further define its secluded ambiance.

Today, it is managed by the Cheongam Cultural Foundation, which carries on the legacy of Cheongam Yi Ha-bok—an educator and rural enlightenment activist from Seocheon. An exhibition hall displaying folk artifacts and books has been built right next door for visitors to explore alongside the old house. Programs such as 1-night 2-day stays, farming experiences, and photography tours are also operated here. Nearby attractions include Seocheon Yi Saek Experience Village, Seocheon Botanical Art Museum, Munheonseowon Confucian Academy, Hansan Hyanggyo, Hansan Ramie Fabric Cultural Center, Hansan Fortress, Geonjisanseong Fortress, and the Hansan 5-Day Market.

spot_at_1055310.overview: Seocheon Botanical Art Museum is located inside Yi Saek Experience Village, a rural tourism village honoring the loyalty and scholarship of Yi Saek, a loyal subject of the late Goryeo Dynasty. The museum features a lotus garden, maze garden, sotdae (pole) garden,onggi (traditional earthenware) exhibition hall, bonsai exhibition hall, open-air café, and an experiential learning center. Opened by a retired elementary school principal in 2003, the gardens showcase bonsai, trees, and oonggi jars collected and nurtured over 40 years.

spot_at_125929.title: Five-Story Stone Pagoda in Seongbuk-ri, Seocheon
spot_at_125929.overview: Standing at 6.2 meters tall, the Five-Story Stone Pagoda in Seongbuk-ri was built during the Goryeo Dynasty. However, reflecting the characteristics of the Seocheon region—which was formerly Baekje territory—it adopts the Baekje architectural style, resembling the Five-Story Stone Pagoda at Jeongnimsa Temple Site in Buyeo. This pagoda faithfully follows the Baekje stone pagoda style, featuring a single-layer foundation and a five-story body. In particular, each side tapers narrower at the top and wider at the bottom, forming a trapezoidal shape that clearly marks it as a Baekje pagoda.

Here, 85 camellia trees, approximately 500 years old, form a dense forest across 8,265㎡. Climbing up to Dongbaekjeong Pavilion at the summit offers a panoramic view of the blue West Sea and beautiful sunsets.

In particular, the scenery of the sea harmonizing with the landscape of Oryeokdo Island right in front gives the joy of appreciating a piece of oriental painting. Due to strong winds on the western side of the Mallyang-ri Camellia Forest, only a few trees remain, while about 70 trees are distributed on the eastern side. Camellia trees, belonging to the Theaceae family, are subtropical evergreen broad-leaved trees that grow up to 7m tall, but the camellia trees here are about 2m tall and spread sideways due to strong winds. spot_fo_135224.title: Seosan Hoegwan
spot_fo_135224.overview: Contrary to its name, Seosan Hoegwan is located in Seocheon, not Seosan, and specializes in Seocheon's famous webfoot octopus (juggumi). Located right in front of the tidal flat at Mallyangpogu Port in Seocheon, it is famous for serving fresh and delicious webfoot octopus caught live using conch shells in this region. The restaurant serves webfoot octopus cooked in iron-griddle stir-fry (cheolpan-bokkeum) and shabu-shabu styles, with peak season lasting from around February to early May. In addition, it offers various seafood menus such as rockfish soup and blue crab soup, with the webfoot octopus iron-griddle stir-fry being the main signature dish. Nearby tourist attractions such as Dongbaekjeong Pavilion above Mallyangpogu Port, Seocheon Marine Glamping, and Chunjangdae Beach are clustered around, making it a great place to combine for sightseeing.

spot_at_126149.title: Boriam Hermitage (Namhae)
spot_at_126149.overview: In 683, Master Wonhyo built a small thatched hermitage here to practice asceticism, and after seeing Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, he named the mountain Bogwangsan and the hermitage Bogwangsa. Later, Yi Seong-gye offered 100 days of prayers here before founding the Joseon Dynasty. In gratitude, King Hyeonjong designated this temple as a royal shrine in 1660 and renamed the mountain Geumsan and the temple Boriam. Perched on the peak of Geumsan Mountain, Boriam offers a panoramic view of Geumsan's unique rock formations and the azure Namhae sea.

paragraphs: In 683, Master Wonhyo built a small thatched hermitage here to practice asceticism, and after seeing Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, he named the mountain Bogwangsan and the hermitage Bogwangsa. Later, Yi Seong-gye offered 100 days of prayers here before founding the Joseon Dynasty. In gratitude, King Hyeonjong designated this temple as a royal shrine in 1660 and renamed the mountain Geumsan and the temple Boriam. Perched on the peak of Geumsan Mountain, Boriam is a beautiful temple where you can take in the bizarre rock formations of Geumsan and the blue scenery of Namhae at a glance.

Inside the temple grounds, the 'Jwaseondae' rock where Master Wonhyo is said to have practiced seated meditation catches the eye, and the nearby rock cave called 'Ssanghongmun' is known as the best among the 38 scenic views of Geumsan. Along with Hongyeonam Hermitage at Naksansa Temple in Yangyang, Gangwon-do, and Bomunsa Temple on Ganghwado Island, Incheon, it is one of the three major prayer sites in Korea, visited by endless streams of devotees. Geumsan is called a 'rock zoo' due to its outstanding scenery, the 'Geumgang Mountain of Namhae,' and numerous animal-shaped rocks. Founded by Master Wonhyo at the summit of Geumsan, where you can look down upon the harmony of the indigo sea and green fields to fully enjoy the beauty of Hallyeohaesang National Park, it is one of the nation's top three prayer sites.

spot_at_126949.title: Seolheulsan Mountain

Historically, beacon mounds were placed in locations with wide panoramic views, allowing visitors to overlook the Hallyeo Waterway, Anggangman Bay, and the endless open sea.

spot_at_126026.title: Jirisan National Park (Hadong)
spot_at_126026.overview: Jirisan is a sacred mountain located at the southern end of the Sobaek Mountain Range, boasting mysterious mountain terrain with large and small peaks and rich tourism resources that attract visitors throughout all four seasons. Spanning three provinces and five cities/counties—including Hadong-gun, Hamyang-gun, and Sancheong-gun in Gyeongsangnam-do, Namwon-si in Jeollabuk-do, and Gurye-gun in Jeollanam-do—it is one of the three major sacred mountains (Samsinsan) along with Geumgangsan and Hallasan. Regarded as Korea's premier natural realm once called Duryusan or Bangjangsan, Jirisan is where the Baekdudaegan mountain range heads south and stands tall, blocked by the Seomjinjin River.

spot_at_126070.title: Bulil Waterfall
spot_at_126070.overview: Bulil Waterfall is one of the eight scenic views of Jirisan, located 3 km away from Ssanggyesa Temple. Along the hiking trail from Ssanggyesa, there is a small hermitage called Guksaam. Right beside Bulilam Hermitage, Bulil Waterfall cascades down a cliff like a stream of water pouring from the sky. Standing 60 meters high and 3 meters wide, this naturally formed two-tier waterfall never dries up year-round, although the volume of water varies by season. Below the waterfall are Yongchu Pool and Hak Pool, adding a deep sense of natural mystery.

spot_at_126185.title: Chilbulsa Temple (Hadong)
spot_at_126185.overview: Perched at an altitude of approximately 800 meters on Banyabong Peak of Jirisan, Chilbulsa Temple is said to have been founded after the seven sons of King Suro—the founder of Geumgwan Gaya in the Nakdong River basin around the Gimhae area in the early Three Kingdoms period—came here to practice asceticism and all attained enlightenment. Growing into a central temple of Gaya Buddhism, Chilbulsa became even more famous for building 'Ajabang' (a hypogeum room where a single fire could keep the room warm for 100 days) during the reign of King Hyegong of Silla about 1,100 years ago. The original structures were destroyed by war and later rebuilt in 1978 by Venerable Jewoldang Tonggwang.

spot_at_126221.title: Hadong Goseong Fortress
spot_at_126221.overview: This is a stone fortress built during the Silla Dynasty, featuring a nearly pentagonal shape along the mountain ridge. The 'Hadong-gun Eupji' (Gazetteer of Hadong-gun County) is the sole historical source regarding the fortress's history. Based on records, location, and scale, it is believed to have been constructed by Silla for military purposes. However, recent opinions suggest it may be a fortress of Goguryeo origin, built when Gwanggaeto the Great of Goguryeo marched south through Silla to subdue Japanese forces in the early 5th century.

paragraphs: This is a stone fortress built during the Silla Dynasty, featuring a nearly pentagonal shape along the mountain ridge. The 'Hadong-gun Eupji' is the sole historical source regarding the fortress's history. Based on records, location, and scale, it is believed to have been constructed by Silla for military purposes, though recent opinions suggest it may be a Goguryeo-style fortress built when King Gwanggaeto the Great moved south in the early 5th century.

The walls were solidly built using squared stones and natural rocks. While the fortress walls remain mostly intact, the section overlooking the Seomjin River to the southwest has collapsed, leaving only piles of stone. Located on a high ridge halfway up the mountain chain stretching from Jirisan, the fortress has a ladder-like cross-section, solidly built with processed rectangular stones and featuring two gates on the north and south.

spot_at_126233.title: Hadong Songnim Park (Pine Tree Forest)
spot_at_126233.overview: Created in 1745 (the 21st year of King Yeongjo's reign in the Joseon Dynasty) by Dohobusa Jeon Cheon-sang, this pine forest was planted to protect Hadong-eup (then Cheongha-eup) by blocking the sea breeze from Gwangyang Bay and the sandy winds of the Seomjin River. About 1,500 pine trees were planted at its creation, and today around 900 trees, including successor saplings, carry on its legacy. The 260-year-old aged pines, clear Seomjin River, and expansive white sandy beach combine to resemble a landscape painting, drawing poets and scholars since ancient times.

The 260-year-old aged pines, clear Seomjin River, and expansive white sandy beach combine to resemble a landscape painting, drawing poets and scholars since ancient times.

Because of this, Hadong is called the home of 'Baeksacheongsong' (white sand and green pines) and 'Baeksacheongjuk' (white sand and green bamboos). Historically, Hadong Songnim was a venue where women held spring flower-viewing picnics, and the sandy beach in front of the forest served as an inland beach when seawater flowed in and out. Today, it is loved as a space offering natural education and relaxation to both locals and tourists. In particular, on the first full moon of the lunar year (Jeongwol Daeboreum), a 'Daljip Taeugi' (moonhouse burning) event is held on the sandy beach to harbor the wishes of Hadong residents, fostering harmony with neighbors from the Jeolla region.

spot_at_126631.title: Samsingung Palace
spot_at_126631.overview: Located in Muggye-ri, Cheongam-myeon, Samsingung sits at an elevation of 850 meters after winding through the mountain path of Cheonghakdong deep within Jirisan, the sacred mountain of the Korean people. The official name of Samsingung is Baedal Seongjeon Samsingung. Established in 1983 by local native Kang Min-ju (Venerable Hanpul), it restores the 'Sodo' (sacred ritual area) of the Gojoseon era. As a sacred shrine of the Baedal people enshrining Hwanin, Hwanung, and Dangun—the founding ancestors of the nation—it has established itself as a national sanctuary preserving Korea's orthodox Taoist lineage and practicing Seon (immortal) arts.

paragraphs: Located in Muggye-ri, Cheongam-myeon, Samsingung sits at an elevation of 850 meters after winding through the mountain path of Cheonghakdong deep within Jirisan, the sacred mountain of the Korean people. The official name of Samsingung is Baedal Seongjeon Samsingung. Established in 1983 by local native Kang Min-ju (Venerable Hanpul), it restores the 'Sodo' (sacred ritual area) of the Gojoseon era. As a sacred shrine of the Baedal people enshrining Hwanin, Hwanung, and Dangun—the founding ancestors of the nation—it has established itself as a national sanctuary preserving Korea's orthodox Taoist lineage and practicing Seon (immortal) arts. Over 1,500 stone towers, piled up by Venerable Hanpul—who inherited the ancient Seon traditions—and his disciples through training, harmonize with the surrounding forest to exude an exotic ambiance.

These stone towers are called 'Wonryeok Sostae' here. In the Samhan period, 'Sodo'—sacred grounds where sacrifices were offered to heavenly deities—were marked with 'Sostae' (tall wooden poles topped with wild goose carvings) to prevent ordinary people from approaching. Just as prayers are embedded in a village shrine, wishes are made while stacking Sostae with stones from the foot of Jirisan to restore the ancient Sodo. By building 3,333 Sostae to form a sanctuary, it aims to revive our nation's unique spiritual culture and realize the ideal of 'Hongik Ingan' (broadly benefiting humanity).

spot_fo_134111.title: Dongheung Sikdang
spot_fo_134111.overview: Located in Hadong-gun, Gyeongsangnam-do, Dongheung Sikdang is a specialty restaurant specializing in freshwater clam (jaecheop) dishes. Jaecheop is widely known as a hangover cure because it activates liver function, relieves fatigue, and restores vitality. spot_fo_2782730.overview: Sweetfish (ayu) primarily inhabit clear streams. Born in rivers, the young fish head to coastal waters and return the following spring to the river where they were born to complete their life cycle. It is a premium raw fish dish that is savory, non-fishy, and uniquely fragrant with a subtle scent of cucumber or watermelon. It can be enjoyed grilled, fried, or in spicy fish stews. Because Hadong's Hwagaecheon Stream is a protected area, freshwater fishing requires a permit. The owner of Beodeul Hoetjip holds a fishing license and directly serves fresh raw fish and seafood dishes made with wild freshwater fish, including sweetfish, making it immensely popular.

spot_at_126027.title: Gajisan Provincial Park (Miryang)
spot_at_126027.overview: Spanning the borders of Sannae-myeon in Miryang-si, Gyeongsangnam-do, Sangbuk-myeon in Ulju-gun, Ulsan, and Unmun-myeon in Cheongdo-gun, Gyeongsangbuk-do, Gajisan Provincial Park was designated in November 1979. It encompasses areas around Gajisan Mountain and Yeongchuksan Mountain—collectively known as the 'Yeongnam Alps'—along with Cheongsongsan Mountain. Due to its vast scope, it is divided into Seoknamsa Temple and the adjacent Yangsan-gun district. Peaks such as Gohongsan, Gajisan, Unmunsan, Cheonhwangsan, Ganjolsan, Sinbulsan, and Chwiseosan rise together to form this magnificent mountain cluster.
