Peaks such as Gohongsan, Gajisan, Unmunsan, Cheonhwangsan, Ganjolsan, Sinbulsan, and Chwiseosan rise together to form this magnificent mountain cluster known as the Yeongnam Alps. Gajisan and Unmunsan mark the boundary between Gyeongsangnam-do and Gyeongsangbuk-do, with Gajisan being the highest among these peaks.

Gajisan features rocky peaks and silver grass fields blended throughout, forming a mountain ridge that connects to Unmunsan, allowing hikers to traverse the ridgeline. In autumn, the silver grass fields stretching from Seoknam-gogae Pass to the summit present a magnificent spectacle, while bizarre rock formations and Ssalbawi (Rice Rock) catch the eyes of climbers. The area around the summit of Gajisan is dotted with rocky ridges and sparse trees, offering a wide, unobstructed view. Nearby are Baegunsan Mountain, which feels just within reach, and Hobakso Valley, a pond shaped like a traditional Korean pumpkin mortar.

paragraphs: Located about 32 km from downtown Miryang in Sile Village, Nammyeong-ri, Sannae-myeon, Eoreumgol (Ice Valley) extends from Jaeyaksan (Cheonhwangsan) Mountain. About 3 km from there lies Hobakso Valley, a branch stream originating from Gajisan Mountain. Washed by valley waters for hundreds of thousands of years, the jade-like granite bed pours forth white foam, creating stunning natural scenery that earned it a spot among Korea's 100 Best Clear Water Streams. According to the Dongguk Yeoji Seungnam, Hobakso is a deep pool carved out by a waterfall dropping from a height of over 10 meters, named 'Hobakso' because its shape resembles a traditional mill mortar called 'hobak'.

It has a circumference of about 30 meters and is also called Sile Hobakso, Guyeon Waterfall, or Baekryeon Waterfall. It is said that Hobakso historically served as a rain-prayer site during prolonged droughts. Locals of the past reportedly tested its depth by tying a stone to a full spool of silk thread and dropping it, but the thread ran out without ever touching the bottom—testifying to its incredible depth. Composed of a white rock bed, this waterfall valley is a pristine, unpolluted zone surrounded by Baekryeon-sa Temple, Hyeongjeso Pool, and Ocheonpyeong Flat Rock, offering exceptionally scenic views.

spot_at_126063.title: Miryang Eoreumgol (Ice Valley)
spot_at_126063.overview: Known since ancient times as Sile Binggok (Ice Valley), Eoreumgol is nestled in an open-air valley on the northern mid-slope of Jaeyaksan Mountain. Ice begins to form in early March when the earth's heat starts to rise, typically lasting until mid-July, and the chilling air from the rock crevices gradually subsides after Cheoseo (the end of the heat) following the dog days of summer. In winter, the valley stream rarely freezes; instead, warm vapor with temperatures above freezing rises from the rock crevices, allowing ferns and mosses to maintain their vivid green appearance in this mysterious region.

paragraphs: Known since ancient times as Sile Binggok (Ice Valley), Eoreumgol is nestled in an open-air valley on the northern mid-slope of Jaeyaksan Mountain. Ice begins to form in early March when the earth's heat starts to rise, typically lasting until mid-July, and the chilling air from the rock crevices gradually subsides after Cheoseo following the dog days of summer. In winter, the valley stream rarely freezes; instead, warm vapor with temperatures above freezing rises from the rock crevices, allowing ferns and mosses to maintain their vivid green appearance in this mysterious region.

From April onward, the more clear days and intense heat there are, the more ice freezes within the rock crevices and the longer it lasts. Due to recent climate anomalies causing more rainy days, the ice-covered period is not as long as it used to be, but a chilling breeze that gives you goosebumps still blows as soon as you step into the valley entrance. The rock crevices where ice forms maintain an average summer temperature of around 0.2°C, and the stream flowing through the valley averages 4–8°C, making it difficult to keep your feet dipped in the water for more than two minutes. The terrain around Eoreumgol features stunning cliff walls folding like a folding screen around rocky boulder fields and valleys where ice forms.

spot_at_126065.title: Gumangok Valley (Miryang)
spot_at_126065.overview: Located in Miryang, Gumangok Valley sits at the foot of Gumangsan Mountain and derives its name from the legend that 90,000 citizens sought refuge here to escape the ravages of war during the Japanese invasions of Korea (Imjin War). Flanked by vertical rock walls to the east and west with a narrow gorge opening north and south—a place known as Tongsu-gol—the valley features Gumang Falls, a stunning 40-meter-tall vertical waterfall that creates a breathtaking landscape, complete with a deep pool about 15 meters in diameter forming beneath it.

Gumangok Valley is dotted with bizarre rock formations and wide bedrock areas such as Byeorakdeumi, Adeulbawi (Son Rock), Sangyeobawi (Bier Rock), and Byeongpungbawi (Folding Screen Rock), along with numerous pools and ponds, drawing comparisons to Cheonbuldong Valley in Seoraksan Mountain. Famous tourist attractions such as Eoreumgol, Seokgolsa Temple, and Unmunsan Mountain are located nearby.

spot_at_126174.title: Pyochungsa Temple (Miryang)
spot_at_126174.overview: Housing numerous cultural heritages, Pyochungsa Temple is a nationally designated temple built to honor the loyal spirit of Master Samyeongdaesa, who made distinguished contributions during the Japanese invasions of Korea (Imjin War). Although reconstructed in 1715 (the 41st year of King Sukjong's reign), all buildings except the Eungjinjeon Hall were destroyed by fire in 1926 and subsequently rebuilt to form the temple complex seen today. Major cultural assets and structures include the National Treasure Bronze Incense Burner with Silver-Inlaid Patterns, the Three-Story Stone Pagoda (a Treasure), as well as provincial cultural heritages such as stone lanterns, Pyochung Seowon Confucian Academy, and Daegwangjeon Hall, along with 25 buildings and around 300 relics of Master Samyeongdaesa.

spot_fo_1921793.title: Dangoljib
spot_fo_1921793.overview: Located in Naeil-dong, Miryang-si, Dangoljib is a specialty pork soup restaurant (dwaeji-gukbap) situated inside the Miryang Traditional Market. They serve a variety of menus including dwaeji-gukbap, sundae-gukbap (blood sausage soup), and naejang-gukbap (offal soup). The dwaeji-gukbap is served in the traditional toryeom style (scalding rice in hot broth), and their mixed soup blends meat and offal harmoniously for a deep, rich flavor. It is widely known as a famous restaurant in Miryang, having been featured in various media outlets. The seating area offers a mix of Western-style tables and traditional low tables. Be sure to use the restaurant's exclusive parking lot to avoid parking fees.

spot_at_126022.addr: 1200, Gayasan-ro, Gayasan National Park Office, Hapcheon-gun, Gyeongsangnam-do
spot_at_126022.overview: Gayasan National Park was designated as a national park on October 13, 1972. Covering a total area of 76.256㎢ across the border of Gyeongsangnam-do and Gyeongsangbuk-do, its soaring Sangwangbong Peak, also known as Udusan Mountain, proudly displays its majestic presence. Since ancient times, this place has been renowned as one of the top 10 scenic spots in Haedong (Korea) or one of the eight scenic views of Joseon. It is also home to Haeinsa Temple, the fundamental temple of Korea's Hwaeom sect and the guardian of the Tripitaka Koreana (Palman Daejanggyeong).

spot_at_126066.overview: Hongryudong Valley is a 4km valley stretching from Gayasan National Park to the entrance of Haeinsa Temple. It is called Hongryudong because the autumn foliage is so intensely red that it casts a crimson reflection on the flowing water. The sound of water flowing through the surrounding pine forests and crashing against strange rock formations is said to have made the great scholar Choi Chi-won deaf, and legend has it that he disappeared, becoming a Taoist immortal, leaving behind only his hat and shoes. There is Nongsanjeong Pavilion and a large rock inscribed with poetical verses by Choi Chi-won.

spot_at_126118.title: Hapcheonho Lake
spot_at_126118.overview: Hapcheonho Lake is an artificial lake created in 1988 by damming the Hwanggang River, a tributary of the Nakdonggang River, to build the Hapcheon Dam. While completing the dam brought the pain of submerging several villages, Hapcheon-gun gained the magnificent scenery of Hapcheonho, which embraces the reflections of surrounding famous mountains in a single embrace. The surrounding area is famous for local specialties such as braised crucian carp (bungeo-jjim), icefish, and catfish stew (megi-tang), and visitors can enjoy fishing and water leisure sports. Additionally, cherry trees line the Hapcheonho Dulle-gil trail, offering dazzling cherry blossoms in spring, cool shade in summer, and brilliant autumn foliage in fall. The atmospheric scenery in the early morning where mountain mist and water vapor mingle is the highlight of the Hapcheonho Dulle-gil.

spot_at_126175.title: Haeinsa Temple (Hapcheon)
spot_at_126175.overview: Haeinsa Temple is one of Korea's three major temples, founded in the 3rd year of King Aejang of Silla by two monks, Sun-ung and I-jeong. Its name originates from the 'Haein Samadhi' in the Avatamsaka Sutra (Hwaeomgyeong), and it was built as one of the ten Hwaeom temples to widely propagate Hwaeom philosophy. King Taejo of Goryeo designated this place as a state temple and bestowed 500 gyeol of farmland in return for Master Hirangdaesa's help. Meanwhile, Haeinsa is called the Temple of the Dharma (Beopbojongchal) among the Three Jewels Temples because it enshrines the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks, a UNESCO Memory of the World, in the Daejanggyeong Panjeon (Depository). The temple grounds also feature various halls such as Daejanggyeong Panjeon, Daejeokgwangjeon, and Myeongbujeon. Subordinate hermitages include Wondangam, Hongjeam, Yongtapsinwon, Gounam, Ganworam, and Cheongnyangsa.

spot_at_129530.title: Monument for State Preceptor Wongyeong, Bonyasa Temple Site, Hapcheon
spot_at_129530.overview: Erected to honor State Preceptor Wongyeong, this stele was originally located at the old site of Bonyasa Temple before being moved in 1961 to its current location inside the grounds of Haeinsa Temple. Built in 1125 (the 3rd year of King Injong's reign during the Goryeo Dynasty), the monument well exhibits the sculptural techniques and simple roof stone designs characteristic of the mid-Goryeo period. Standing 2.3 meters tall and 1.2 meters wide, it is made of granite and features a tortoise pedestal, stele body, and roof stone, with the thinness of each component being a distinct characteristic.

According to the inscription, State Preceptor Wongyeong traveled to Song Dynasty China alongside State Preceptor Daegak, returned home, and became a prelate (Seungtong) in 1104 (the 9th year of King Sukjong's reign). He also served as a teacher to King Yejong. After residing at Guwibasa Temple, he passed away, and the king bestowed upon him the posthumous title 'Wongyeong.' The inscription was composed by Kim Bu-il and written in calligraphy by Lee Won-bu.

spot_at_126012.title: Deogyusan National Park (Namdeogyu Branch)
spot_at_126012.overview: Located in the heart of the Baekdudaegan mountain range, Mt. Deogyusan was designated as the 10th national park in 1975. Spanning across four counties bridging the Yeongnam and Honam regions—Muju-gun and Jangsu-gun in Jeollabuk-do, and Geochang-gun and Hamyang-gun in Gyeongsangnam-do—a total area of 229.43㎢ is designated as parkland. Deogyusan National Park is surrounded by Mt. Gayasan to the east, Mt. Naejangsan to the west, Mt. Jirisan to the south, and Mt. Gyeryongsan and Mt. Soknisaksan to the north. Mt. Deogyusan is the fourth-highest mountain in South Korea (Hyangjeokbong Peak at 1,614m) with high ecological preservation value, and serves as a water source for the Geumgang River flowing north and the Nakdonggang River flowing east.

In the Geochang area, Wolseong Valley is located, renowned as a deep, clear, and beautiful valley that attracts many tourists. Centered around its main peak, Hyangjeokbong (1,614m), Mt. Deogyusan boasts majestic ridges around 1,300 meters high stretching southwestward for about 30 kilometers.

spot_at_126159.overview: Surrounded by clear valleys and dense forests at the foot of Bukdeogyusan Mountain, Songgyesa Temple is a branch temple of Haeinsa Temple, the head temple of the 12th parish of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism. Originally founded in 652 (the 6th year of Queen Jindeok's reign) by the monks Wonhyo and 의상 as Songgyeram after establishing Yeongchwisa Temple and five subordinate hermitages, the temple has produced many eminent monks over the centuries. After being completely burned down along with the five hermitages during the Japanese Invasion of Korea, it lay in ruins until Jinmyeong reconstructed Songgyeram during the reign of King Sukjong.

paragraphs: Surrounded by clear valleys and dense forests at the foot of Bukdeogyusan Mountain, Songgyesa Temple is a branch temple of Haeinsa Temple, the head temple of the 12th parish of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism. Originally founded in 652 (the 6th year of Queen Jindeok's reign) by the monks Wonhyo and Uisang as Songgyeram after establishing Yeongchwisa Temple and five subordinate hermitages, the temple has produced many eminent monks over the centuries. After being completely burned down along with the five hermitages during the Japanese Invasion of Korea, it lay in ruins until Jinmyeong reconstructed Songgyeram during the reign of King Sukjong.

It was burned down again during the Korean War and restored by Monk Seungmin in 1969. In 1995, Wonjeong dismantled the leaning Yeongchuiru Pavilion (built during the 1969 restoration) to rebuild it and renamed it Mungak. Existing buildings include Geuknakbojeon Hall, Daeungjeon Hall, Mungak (Bell Pavilion), and Yosachae (monks' quarters), while cultural artifacts include a Seated Amitabha Buddha, a small bronze bell, and three Buddhist paintings. From the Daeungjeon Hall of Songgyesa, visitors can enjoy a direct view of Surideom on Bukdeogyusan Mountain, and the winter snowscape of Songgyesa creates yet another magnificent scenery crafted by the mountain.

spot_at_127137.title: Wolseong Valley
spot_at_127137.overview: Wolseong Valley is formed along Wolseongcheon Stream on the eastern foothills of Namdeogyusan Mountain. Although the valley is not very wide, the surrounding mountain terrain is so majestic that it boasts abundant water flow. Scattered rocks provide great resting spots alongside water play areas, and the crystal-clear stream weaves between boulders to create small waterfalls and rapids as it flows down toward Wicheon Valley and Suseungdae Valley in Galgye-ri.

Heading upstream, visitors will find spots like Janggunbawi Shelter and numerous great locations for water play all the way up to Wolseong Bridge 1. Wolseong Valley ends at Hwangjeom Ticket Office, the starting point for hiking Namdeogyusan Mountain. Following the paved road past the ticket office leads over Namnyeongjae Pass to Yeonggaksa Temple in Seosang-myeon, Hamyang-gun, the starting point for the Deogyusan Mountain ridge traverse, making it a wonderful driving course due to its stunning mountain scenery.

spot_at_127509.title: Geumwonsan Mountain

Another legend suggests it originates from a tale where a golden monkey living on this mountain was captured and trapped in a rock called Wonam. Geumwonsan sits on the Baekdudaegan mountain ridge extending from the Namdeogyusan Mountain branch, and following the ridge stretching southeast leads to Gibaeksan Mountain.

spot_at_127530.title: Geoyeolsanseong County Park
spot_at_127530.overview: Geochang-gun is an inland mountainous region in the northwestern part of Gyeongsangnam-do, bordering Gyeongsangbuk-do and Jeollabuk-do across Deogyusan National Park. To the north rise Deogyusan, Wolbongsan, and Sudosan mountains; to the west, Gibaeksan and Geumwonsan mountains; and to the east, Uisangbong and Bigyasan mountains. The south is surrounded by relatively low Boroksan and Cheolmasan mountains, forming an intermountain basin. Geoyeolsanseong County Park is located about 3 km west of Geochang-eup and centers around Geoyeolseong Fortress, built by Baekje loyal martyrs and volunteer armies to rebuild the nation.

Geoyeolsanseong County Park is located about 3 km west of Geochang-eup and centers around Geoyeolseong Fortress, built by Baekje loyal martyrs and volunteer armies to rebuild the nation.

Geoyeolseong Fortress is a historic open-air educational site where a fierce battle took place: after resisting for three years following the fall of Baekje, it fell in the 3rd year of King Munmu of Silla (663) to Silla generals Kim Heum-sun and Cheonjon, resulting in the decapitation of some 700 Baekje revival soldiers. Existing ruins include a 2.1 km-long, 7 m-wide fortress wall that partially retains its original form, along with 7 watchtower sites and 2 wells. In addition, Geochang Sculpture Park is located along the bicycle-only road, allowing visitors to appreciate the beauty of great nature.

spot_at_126024.title: Yeonhwasan Provincial Park (연화산도립공원)
spot_at_126024.overview: Located 12 km northwest of Goseong-eup, Yeonhwasan Mountain was named because its mountain contours resemble a blooming lotus flower. Originally called Biseaksan, its name was changed to the current one during the reign of King Injo of the Joseon Dynasty. Consisting of three peaks—Oknyebong, Seondobong, and Mangseonbong—it stands at 524 meters, making it a relatively low mountain, yet it attracts many hikers with its beautiful natural scenery, including lush forests and deep valleys. It was designated as a Gyeongsangnam-do Provincial Park in 1983, and on its northern foothills stands Okcheonsa Temple, founded in 670 (the 10th year of King Munmu of Silla) by the great monk Uisang.

spot_at_128490.title: Samgye Village (삼계마을)
spot_at_128490.overview: Estimated to have been formed about 500 years ago, Samgye Village was formerly called Gakkye or Gaekgi, but was later named Samgye ('Three Streams') due to its topography where three streams converge. Nestled at the foothills of Nojeokbong Peak in Cheonwangsan Mountain, Samgye Village features lush forests of zelkova, hackberry, and hornbeam trees over 300 years old, making the village panorama even more atmospheric and allowing for forest bathing. Daejujeosuji Reservoir, the largest reservoir in Gyeongnam located right in front of the village, has walking trails built around it, allowing visitors to breathe in plenty of clear rural water and fresh air.

spot_at_128568.overview: Donghwa Village completed the establishment of experience village infrastructure in March 2005, and all fishermen are joining forces to create an advanced experience village aimed at providing a safe yet special resting space for urbanites looking to enjoy their leisure time. spot_at_128658.overview: This park offers a panoramic view of the Goseong-eup area and the South Sea. At the park entrance, commemorative monuments detailing the deeds of predecessors are neatly arranged, and climbing 84 steps leads visitors to Bogwangsa Temple, a branch temple of Okcheonsa Temple under the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism. To the left of Bogwangsa Temple stand the Memorial Tower built to honor the spirits of patriotic martyrs, a enshrinement hall, and the June 25 Anti-Communist Monument. On the ridge above Bogwangsa Temple, living sports facilities and a magnolia rest area have been established, providing a complete relaxation space combined with physical training utilized by local town residents.

spot_at_1044187.title: Sancheong and Hamyang Incident Memorial Park
spot_at_1044187.overview: The Sancheong and Hamyang Incident Memorial Park is a joint graveyard for the victims of the Sancheong-Hamyang civilian massacre. On February 7, 1951, during the Korean War, the 3rd Battalion, 9th Regiment, 11th Division of the South Korean Army massacred 705 innocent civilians in Gahyeon and Banggok villages in Geumseo-myeon, Sancheong-gun, and Jeomchon village in Hyucheon-myeon and Seoju village in Yurim-myeon, Hamyang-gun, while carrying out the Jirisan communist-suppression operation known as 'Gyeonbyeokcheongya'. This park enshrines the spirits of those unjustly sacrificed.

The creation of the joint graveyard and the erection of the memorial tower were realized following the promulgation of the Special Act on Restoring the Reputation of Persons Related to the Incident on January 5, 1996, and the determination of the deceased and bereaved families by the Geochang Incident and Other Related Persons Reputation Restoration Deliberation Committee on February 17, 1998. Following the groundbreaking of the joint graveyard project on December 13, 2001, construction was completed over four years. This graveyard serves as a living educational site where visitors can reaffirm with a solemn heart that under any circumstances, the people are like the sky, history is on the side of justice, and human life has absolute value, while reflecting on the precious values of true peace and human rights left to our descendants by the sacrificed spirits.

spot_at_126041.title: Hwangmaesan Mountain (Sancheong)
spot_at_126041.overview: Hwangmaesan Mountain, the final major peak of the Taebaek Mountain Range, is known as the place where the Goryeo Dynasty's national guardian monk Muhak practiced asceticism. Together with nearby Hwangmaebong Peak, its southeastern side features bizarre rock cliffs, making it as beautiful as a 'mini Geumgangsan.' Upon reaching the summit, the surrounding scenery resembles fully bloomed plum blossom petals, giving a mystical feeling as if floating alone inside a plum blossom, hence the name Hwangmaesan.

spot_at_126594.title: Jirisan National Park (Sancheong)
spot_at_126594.overview: Designated as South Korea's national park on December 29, 1967, Jirisan Mountain spans administrative districts across three provinces and is the largest mountainous national park in the country. Literally translated, Jirisan (智異山) means 'Mountain of Wise Extraordinary Beings.' Perhaps for this reason, more hermits have cultivated and practiced asceticism here than on any other mountain, and the number of hermits deeply hidden in the valleys of Jirisan is said to be uncountable.
spot_at_126594.pull_quote: Designated as South Korea's national park on December 29, 1967, Jirisan Mountain spans administrative districts across three provinces and is the largest mountainous national park in the country...
paragraphs: Designated as South Korea's national park on December 29, 1967, Jirisan Mountain spans administrative districts across three provinces and is the largest mountainous national park in the country. Literally translated, Jirisan (智異山) means 'Mountain of Wise Extraordinary Beings.' Perhaps for this reason, more hermits have cultivated and practiced asceticism here than on any other mountain, and the number of hermits deeply hidden in the valleys of Jirisan is said to be uncountable.

Since ancient times, Jirisan has been revered alongside Geumgangsan and Hallasan as one of the Three Spirit Mountains (Samsin-san), serving as a spiritual sanctuary of national faith. At Cheonwangbong, the main peak of Jirisan, a shrine called Seongmosa was built and a stone statue of the Holy Mother was enshrined, while at Nogo-dan, Namaksa Shrine has worshiped the Seongdo Holy Mother since the Silla Dynasty. Names like Banyabong, Jongsakdae, Yeongshindae, and Nogodan also symbolize this faith. In Gyeongsangnam-do, it extends across Hadong, Hamyang, and Sancheong, and its rich flora and fauna have shaped a diverse yet distinct cultural sphere between the east and west.

spot_at_126595.title: Tomb of King Guhyeong, Sancheong
spot_at_126595.overview: This stone tomb is known to be the burial site of King Guhyeong, the 10th and final ruler of Geumgwan Gaya. King Guhyeong was the great-grandfather of General Kim Yu-sin. He became king of Garakguk (Gaya) in 521 and reigned for 11 years until surrendering his territory to King Beopheung of Silla in 532. There are two theories regarding this mound: one is that it is a stone pagoda, and the other is that it is a royal tomb. The theory of it being a pagoda is based on similar structures distributed in the Andong and Uiseong regions, while the evidence supporting it as a royal tomb comes from records in the 'Dongguk Yeoji Seungnam' (Augmented Survey of the Geography of Korea).
spot_at_126595.pull_quote: This stone tomb is known to be the burial site of King Guhyeong, the 10th and final ruler of Geumgwan Gaya. King Guhyeong was the great-grandfather of General Kim Yu-sin. He became king...
paragraphs: This stone tomb is known to be the burial site of King Guhyeong, the 10th and final ruler of Geumgwan Gaya. King Guhyeong was the great-grandfather of General Kim Yu-sin. He became king of Garakguk (Gaya) in 521 and reigned for 11 years until surrendering his territory to King Beopheung of Silla in 532. There are two theories regarding this mound: one is that it is a stone pagoda, and the other is that it is a royal tomb. The theory of it being a pagoda is based on similar structures distributed in the Andong and Uiseong regions, while the evidence supporting it as a royal tomb comes from records in the 'Dongguk Yeoji Seungnam', San-eum-hyeon section, which states that there is a nine-dragon stone formation 40 ri deep in the mountains of the district with tiered steps on all four sides, traditionally passed down as a royal tomb.

The record attaching the royal title to this tomb first appears in 'Wansansimneung-gi' by Hong Eui-yeong, a Joseon Dynasty literati, who stated that because there was a temple called Wangsansa to the west of the tomb, it was recorded as King Guhyeong's tomb in the temple's historical records. Unlike ordinary tombs, it consists of terraced stone tiers built in the middle of a sloped hillside.

spot_at_126756.title: Georim Valley
spot_at_126756.overview: Georim Valley is formed by the convergence of several streams: Georimgol as its main current, Dojanggol originating from Yeonhabong and Chotdaebong peaks along the main ridge of Jirisan Mountain, and Jappajingol originating from Hanbeotsaem spring located on the ridge connecting Seseok Plateau to Samsinbong Peak. Georimgol, whose main current alone stretches for some 60 li, draws so many hikers in spring when royal azaleas bloom that the sound of the flowing valley water is drowned out.

Continuing slightly uphill brings you to Yongchusa Temple, in front of which roars Yongchu Waterfall with thunderous water sounds. At the end of Yongchu Valley lies Yongchu Natural Recreation Forest established by Hamyang-gun, featuring cozy mountain cabins, a spacious parking lot, a water play area, and an observatory, along with hiking trails leading up Gibaiksan and Hwangseoksan mountains, ridges of Namdeokyusan Mountain.

paragraphs: Located along the Wicheon Stream on the western side of Hamyang-eup, Hamyang Sangnim is a historic forest created by scholar Choe Chi-won during Queen Jinseong's reign in the Unified Silla period to prevent flood damage in Hamyang-eup. Formerly known as Daegwanrim, the forest was divided into Sangnim (Upper Forest) and Halim (Lower Forest) when its central section was washed away by a flood.

Today, Halim is largely damaged with only traces remaining, while Sangnim preserves its original appearance. Dominated by oak and hornbeam trees, the intertwining wild grapes and kudzu vines evoke the natural vegetation of a deep valley. With around 120 species of trees planted along the embankment, it is also a wonderful natural learning center for children.

spot_fo_2843664.title: Daeseong Sikdang (대성식당)
spot_fo_2843664.overview: Daeseong Sikdang is a gukbap (soup with rice) specialty restaurant located in Hamyang-eup, Hamyang-gun, Gyeongsangbuk-do. An old house was remodeled into a restaurant, featuring traditional low-legged tables on the floor inside. Retaining old closets and wallpaper, it gives the cozy feeling of visiting a rural hometown home. There are only two items on the menu: gukbap and suyuk (boiled meat slices). Unlike regular suyuk, the Hanwoo (Korean beef) suyuk is served with thick meat and green onions piled atop a rich, red broth, while the Hanwoo gukbap is generously packed with large chunks of meat, taro stems, and other hearty ingredients.

spot_at_1180879.title: Gyeomamjeongsa House, Hahoe Village, Andong (안동 하회마을 겸암정사)
spot_at_1180879.overview: Gyeomamjeongsa is a pavilion located near Hahoe Village in Pungcheon-myeon, Andong-si, Gyeongsangbuk-do. It was built by Gyeomam Ryu Un-ryong (1539–1601), a mid-Joseon dynasty scholar and older brother of Seae Ryu Seong-ryong, for studying and fostering younger scholars. Situated on a cliff overlooking the meandering Nakdonggang River, it boasts exceptional natural scenery and is known as a scenic spot offering panoramic views of Hahoe Village and Buyongdae Cliff. The current building was reconstructed by descendants after being destroyed during the Imjin War, and features a sarangchae (men's quarters) and ancestral shrine centered around the main pavilion.

spot_at_1181011.title: Andong Jangseung Park (안동 장승공원)
spot_at_1181011.overview: Jangseung (traditional Korean totem poles) have long been placed at village entrances as guardian deities protecting villagers from evil spirits and diseases, and sometimes as objects of prayer, forming a familiar folk culture among commoners. Andong Jangseung Park was created at the entrance of Hahoe Village by Jangseung master Kim Jong-heung of the Hahoe Jangseung Village Mokseokwon. Around 250 jangseung, carved from discarded trees, gather together. With various names such as Cheonhadaejanggun (Great General Under Heaven), Jiyeohajanggun (Great Underground General), Jinseodaejanggun, Bukjanggun, and Dangjanggun...

Their expressions vary widely, from rugged, intimidating features with names like Cheonhadaejanggun, Jiyeohajanggun, Jinseodaejanggun, Bukjanggun, and Dangjanggun, to innocent and clumsy ones resembling country children. Dainty jangseung—such as bride-and-groom-shaped ones, a single tree with two distinct faces, or one utilizing a curved trunk to look like a shy maiden peeking out from behind a pillar—spark visitors' curiosity. However, what draws the eye most is the unique Andong-style Hahoe mask-shaped jangseung not found anywhere else.

spot_at_1181386.title: Samgwijeong Pavilion (삼귀정)
spot_at_1181386.overview: Samgwijeong is a Joseon Dynasty pavilion located in Andong, Gyeongsangbuk-do. It was built in 1496 (the 2nd year of King Yeonsan's reign) by the scholar Kim Yeong-su and his brothers to pray for the health and longevity of their mother, Lady Kwon of Yecheon. Sosan Village, where the pavilion stands, is a clan village for the Andong Kim family. The name 'Samgwijeong' originates from three turtle-shaped rocks to the left of the pavilion. As turtles symbolize longevity, the pavilion embodies deep filial piety toward parents. The current building was reconstructed in 1947.

spot_at_126157.title: Gaemoksa Temple, Andong (개목사)
spot_at_126157.overview: Gaemoksa Temple was originally named Heungguksa Temple and was reportedly founded by Master Uisang during the reign of King Sinmun of Unified Silla (reigned 681–692). According to legend, Master Uisang attained enlightenment through the miracle of a celestial maiden in Cheon-deunggul Cave behind the temple and subsequently established it. The name 'Gaemoksa' was reportedly given during the Joseon Dynasty. Wontongjeon Hall of Gaemoksa, which houses the Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, contains a record discovered during disassembly and repair work in 1969 bearing the phrase 'Cheonsun Wonnyeon', indicating it was built in the 3rd year of King Sejo (1457).

The name 'Gaemoksa' was reportedly given during the Joseon Dynasty.

It well preserves the architectural style of the early Joseon Dynasty and was designated as a Treasure on January 21, 1963.

spot_at_126158.title: Bongjeongsa Temple [UNESCO World Heritage] (봉정사)
spot_at_126158.overview: Located not far from the city center, Cheondeungsan Bongjeongsa is a serene temple ideal for stepping away from daily life and enjoying peaceful relaxation. It houses Korea's oldest wooden building and allows visitors to take walks and rest amidst clean air and the tranquil atmosphere of a mountain temple. It is also known as a place for spiritual practice, carrying on the traditions of Korean mountain Buddhism. Bongjeongsa was founded in the 12th year of King Munmu of Silla (672) by Neungin, a disciple of Master Uisang.

paragraphs: Located not far from the city center, Cheondeungsan Bongjeongsa is a serene temple ideal for stepping away from daily life and enjoying peaceful relaxation. It houses Korea's oldest wooden building and allows visitors to take walks and rest amidst clean air and the tranquil atmosphere of a mountain temple. It is also known as a place for spiritual practice, carrying on the traditions of Korean mountain Buddhism. Bongjeongsa was founded in the 12th year of King Munmu of Silla (672) by Neungin, a disciple of Master Uisang.

Cheondeungsan Mountain was originally called Daemangsan Mountain. The name 'Cheondeungsan' (Mountain of Heavenly Lantern) originates from a legend where a heavenly fairy lowered a lantern to illuminate the cave while Neungin was practicing asceticism inside a rock cave. Afterward, Neungin folded and released a paper phoenix, which landed and stayed here, leading to the name 'Bongjeongsa' (Temple of the Resting Phoenix). Since its founding, it has been renovated six times and preserves precious cultural heritage including National Treasures and Treasures such as Geungnakjeon Hall, Daeungjeon Hall, and post-Buddha murals, along with a wooden seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, Hwaeom Gangdang, and Gogeumdang. Other notable sites include Deokhwiru Pavilion, Muryang Haehoe, Samseonggak, a three-story stone pagoda, Yeongsanam Hermitage, and Jijoam Hermitage.

spot_fo_134381.title: Chuimsae (추임새)
spot_fo_134381.overview: Named after 'Chuimsae', the traditional exclamations of encouragement used by masters of Korean traditional music, this is a renowned traditional Andong restaurant. It is well-known as a hotspot where world cultural heritage exploration teams stayed for weeks, visited by celebrities from all walks of life (guestbooks available), and designated as an official restaurant for KEPCO training sessions, university MTs, and forums. Representative dishes include salted mackerel (gan-godeungeo) and soybean paste stew (doenjang-jjigae). Other Korean dishes like Andong jjimdak, Hanwoo sprout bibimbap, Hanwoo gukbap, and baechu-jeon (cabbage pancakes) are also available to suit various tastes.

spot_fo_134770.title: Mat 50-nyeon Heotjesabap (맛50년 헛제사밥)
spot_fo_134770.overview: As the person who commercialized 'heotjesabap' (fake ancestral ritual food), which is now widely popular in Korea, this restaurant is considered the pioneer of the dish. Passed down to her daughter-in-law, three generations have dedicated themselves to running the restaurant for over 50 years. Heotjesabap is a traditional local food of Andong where various seasoned vegetables are placed over rice and mixed with soy sauce, just like the food prepared for ancestral rites, but without actually holding a ritual. Since Andong has many famous Confucian academies (seowon), Confucian scholars used to gather here to enjoy literature and leisure. They would set up ancestral food, compose sacrificial texts and prayers as if holding a memorial service, and then share the food together. This is how the dish came to be called 'heotjesabap' (false ritual meal).

spot_at_126018.title: Palgongsan National Park (Eunhaesa District)
spot_at_126018.overview: Palgongsan Mountain was designated as a provincial park on May 13, 1980, and later as a national park on December 31, 2023. Spanning across five cities and counties including Dong-gu and Gunwi-gun in Daegu, as well as Gyeongsan-si, Yeong천-si, and Chilgok-gun in Gyeongsangbuk-do, the national park covers a total area of 126.058 ㎢. Palgongsan is a core high-altitude ecological axis in the Yeongnam region where the Palgongjicheon and Yubongjicheon ridges diverge from the Nakdong Jeongmaek.
spot_at_126018.pull_quote: Palgongsan was designated as a provincial park on May 13, 1980, and as a national park on December 31, 2023. Spanning Daegu, Gunwi-gun, Gyeongsan-si, Yeongcheon-si...
paragraphs: Palgongsan Mountain was designated as a provincial park on May 13, 1980, and later as a national park on December 31, 2023. Spanning across five cities and counties including Dong-gu and Gunwi-gun in Daegu, as well as Gyeongsan-si, Yeongcheon-si, and Chilgok-gun in Gyeongsangbuk-do, the national park covers a total area of 126.058 ㎢. Palgongsan is a core high-altitude ecological axis in the Yeongnam region standing at 1,192.8 meters above sea level, composed of majestic, folding screen-like granite peaks.

Centered around the main peak Birobong (1,192.8m), Dongbong Peak (1,167m) and Seobong Peak (1,153m) stand shoulder to shoulder, enclosing the northern side of the Daegu Basin in the center of the Yeongnam region like a folding screen. Home to dozens of temples and hermitages including the millennium-old Donghwasa Temple, the lush forests and multi-branched valleys feature delicate azaleas in early spring, royal azaleas in late spring, chaste trees in summer, and brilliant autumn foliage, alongside mystical winter snowscapes. The Eunhaesa District is located in Yeongcheon-si, Gyeongsangbuk-do, and houses Eunhaesa Temple.

spot_at_126925.title: Imgo Seowon Confucian Academy
spot_at_126925.overview: Imgo Seowon is a Confucian academy originally founded in 1553 in Gocheon-dong, Imgo-myeon, by local Confucian scholars to honor the virtue and loyalty of Jeong Mong-ju. It received royal naming [Imgo] in 1554. Destroyed during the Japanese Invasions of Korea, it was relocated to its current site in 1603 and received royal naming again the following year. It played a significant role in enshrining sages and educating local youth by additionally enshrining Jang Hyeon-gwang in 1643 and Hwang Bo-in in 1787, before being dismantled in 1871.

paragraphs: Imgo Seowon is a Confucian academy originally founded in 1553 in Gocheon-dong, Imgo-myeon, by local Confucian scholars to honor the virtue and loyalty of Jeong Mong-ju. It received royal naming [Imgo] in 1554. Destroyed during the Japanese Invasions of Korea, it was relocated to its current site in 1603 and received royal naming again the following year. It played a significant role in enshrining sages and educating local youth by additionally enshrining Jang Hyeon-gwang in 1643 and Hwang Bo-in in 1787, before being dismantled in 1871. In 1919, the Junyeonggak Pavilion was built to enshrine Jeong Mong-ju's portrait and hold ancestral rites.

Within the grounds are a shrine, a portrait pavilion (Junyeonggak), a lecture hall, a kitchen, and administrative rooms. The Mutchungsa Shrine houses Jeong Mong-ju's spirit tablet, while Junyeonggak preserves his portrait. The lecture hall consists of a central wooden floor and flanking rooms, used for various academy events, scholar gatherings, and scholarly lectures. Relics preserved in the academy include three sets of Jeong Mong-ju's portraits, 113 woodblocks of the Poeun Collection, 71 woodblocks of Jibong Yuseol, the Poeun Collection, 11 volumes of Eosa Seongri Gunseo, and over 200 other historical books.

spot_at_126933.title: Dolhalmae (Grandma Stone, Yeongcheon)
spot_at_126933.overview: Dolhalmae Park in Bukan-myeon, Yeongcheon features a mineral spring, a Buddha statue, a Dolhalmae (Grandma Stone) statue, the 12 zodiac animal statues, and a stone building housing the actual Grandma Stone. Dolhalmae is a granite stone weighing about 10 kg and measuring 25 cm in diameter used for divination. According to tradition, when you lift the stone with both hands, if it feels light your wish will not come true, but if it refuses to budge, your wish will come true—meaning it gives a yes-or-no answer to your prayers.
spot_at_126933.pull_quote: Dolhalmae Park in Bukan-myeon, Yeongcheon houses a mineral spring, Buddha statue, zodiac statues, and a stone building housing the Grandma Stone, a 10kg granite stone...
paragraphs: Dolhalmae Park in Bukan-myeon, Yeongcheon features a mineral spring, a Buddha statue, a Dolhalmae (Grandma Stone) statue, the 12 zodiac animal statues, and a stone building housing the actual Grandma Stone. Dolhalmae is a granite stone weighing about 10 kg and measuring 25 cm in diameter used for divination. According to tradition, when you lift the stone with both hands, if it feels light your wish will not come true, but if it refuses to budge, your wish will come true—meaning it gives a yes-or-no answer to your prayers. What makes this stone a subject of fascination is not necessarily any mystical prophetic power, but the fact that the stone feels light or heavy depending on the person and their earnest wishes.

The proper way to lift the stone is to first lift it without any specific thoughts, serving as a process to verify that it lifts easily without sincerity. Next, you state your date of birth, address, age, and name, and speak of your wish or trouble, after which whether the stone lifts or not indicates the answer. For about 350 years, local villagers have visited this stone to hold ancestral rites whenever fortunes or misfortunes arose, or when epidemics and tragedies struck the village.

spot_at_126934.title: Manbulsa Temple (Yeongcheon)
spot_at_126934.overview: Manbulsa Temple in Yeongcheon began when the monk Hakseong established propagation centers in Seoul, Busan, and Daegu in 1987 to fulfill a modern Buddhist vow distinct from the past, culminating in the completion of Manbulsan Mountain temple in 1995. Prior to its establishment, he carried out numerous grand Buddhist projects such as building the Manbulbojeon Hall, transferring the Buddha's true sarira (sacred relics), and enshrinement of an outdoor standing Amitabha Buddha, pouring immense effort into spreading modern Buddhism alongside culture, medical care, and welfare.
spot_at_126934.pull_quote: Manbulsa Temple in Yeongcheon was founded by monk Hakseong, beginning with propagation centers in 1987 and completed in 1995 on Manbulsan Mountain...
paragraphs: Manbulsa Temple in Yeongcheon began when the monk Hakseong established propagation centers in Seoul, Busan, and Daegu in 1987 to fulfill a modern Buddhist vow distinct from the past, culminating in the completion of Manbulsan Mountain temple in 1995. Prior to its establishment, he carried out numerous grand Buddhist projects such as building the Manbulbojeon Hall, transferring the Buddha's true sarira (sacred relics), and enshrinement of an outdoor standing Amitabha Buddha, pouring immense effort into spreading modern Buddhism alongside culture, medical care, and welfare.

Relics preserved here include the Amitabha Buddha, the Samjonbul (Triad Buddha) which is the largest indoor Jeonbul (statue-filled hall) in Korea, 5 grains of the Buddha's true sarira brought from Sri Lanka, and a Bodhi tree. In addition, there are the Yeongcheon Amitabha Great Buddha, stupas, a brass reclining Nirvana statue, the Great Bronze Manbul Peace Bell, the Indung Pagoda, Manbulbojeon Hall, Gwaneumjeon Hall, Daeungjeon Hall, the Beopseongge Dharma Wheel, the Medicine Buddha (Sujeong Yurigwang Yeoraebul), lucky pouches, and ancestral spirit tablets (Yuja Yeongga).

spot_at_4150321.title: Mokpojin History Park
spot_at_4150321.overview: First established in 1439 as Mokpojin, a Joseon naval garrison, this site firmly guarded the maritime routes of the Dadohae archipelago. Also called Manhojin as a 'manho' (naval commander) was stationed here, it was fortified with a castle wall around 1502. As a strategic stronghold for southwestern coastal defense and a meaningful historic site marking the genesis of modern Mokpo, the site was partially restored as a history park in 2014 after being abandoned in 1895. The neatly restored old government office harmonizes with the surrounding lush trees.
spot_at_4150321.pull_quote: First established in 1439 as Mokpojin, a Joseon naval garrison, this site firmly guarded the maritime routes of the Dadohae archipelago. Also called Manhojin...
paragraphs: First established in 1439 as Mokpojin, a Joseon naval garrison, this site firmly guarded the maritime routes of the Dadohae archipelago. Also called Manhojin as a 'manho' (naval commander) was stationed here, it was fortified with a castle wall around 1502. As a strategic stronghold for southwestern coastal defense and a meaningful historic site marking the genesis of modern Mokpo, the site was partially restored as a history park in 2014 after being abandoned in 1895.

The neatly restored old government office, Gaksa, harmonizes with the surrounding lush trees, its subtle depth of time naturally causing visitors to pause. Stroll leisurely along the well-organized outdoor walking trails and naturally feel the breath of the Joseon navy and the historical value of the space. Beyond Gaksa, stepping up to the observation deck at the top of the hill reveals a panoramic view of Mokpo-jin port with boats gliding across calm waters. Beyond the colorful old downtown housing, the majestic ridges of Mt. Yudal rise high, making it a great spot to take in both Mokpo's past and present scenery at a glance.

spot_mk_2773998.title: DMZ Market
spot_mk_2773998.overview: Every Saturday and Sunday, the DMZ Market is held in the Milky Way Bridge parking lot, focusing on local foods produced directly by Cheorwon residents. The variety is truly diverse, including native yam grown in Cheorwon, as well as agricultural products like aralia and balloon flower roots, mulberry ice cream, buckwheat rice cakes, wooden cutting boards, and straw crafts. All these products, sold by about 30 farms, are local specialties that have not undergone long-distance transportation, helping to reduce carbon emissions in one stone.

spot_mk_131992.overview: Baegam Market opens on dates ending in 1, 6, 11, 16, 21, and 26. spot_mk_2765103.title: Bongilcheon General Market, Paju
spot_mk_2765103.overview: Located in Bongilcheon, Jori-eup, Paju-si, Bongilcheon General Market is a commercial-residential complex market consisting of 197 stores. It holds 70 years of tradition, history, and the warm affection of merchants, having been together with the residents of Bongilcheon since 1945. It is large enough to be called one of the four major markets in Gyeonggi-do, famous for its cattle market since the Joseon Dynasty, and was also the site of the Gongreung Market Independence Movement in 1919. spot_mk_1257204.overview: This is a traditional market that formed naturally in 1983. It was approved as an official certified market in December 2005 under the 'Special Act on the Revitalization of Traditional Markets' promulgated on March 1, 2005. Yeokgok Nambu Market stretches about 300 meters from east to west toward the Yeokgok Police Substation from Yeokgok Station, featuring around 100 large and small stores lined up in a row. The number of workers reaches about 190. Bucheon City installed the first light-shielding tunnel here to enhance user convenience.

spot_mk_132787.overview: Bucheon Wonmi General Market is a traditional market that spontaneously formed in Wonmi 1-dong, Wonmi-gu, Bucheon-si in 1985. It also features a variety of food towns, bakeries, and more.

spot_mk_1807706.title: Sagang Market
spot_mk_1807706.overview: Sagang Market gets its name ('Sagang', meaning sandy river) from the days when sea tides reached the front of the village, leaving white sandy deposits like a river. It has long served as a crucial transportation hub and distribution center connecting southern regions like Songsan, Daebudo, Yeongheungdo, Suwon, and Ansan. Opened in 1915 with a history of periodic markets held even earlier, it expanded significantly in the 1980s. It is also a historically meaningful site tied to the March 1st Independence Movement in 1919.

The main offerings are centered around restaurants, along with butcher shops, hardware stores, and vegetable vendors. Each section offers unique items and local foods, such as tools at Gucheondong Tool Alley, hanbok (traditional clothing) at Yeongdong Market, sundae (blood sausage) at Jidong Market, and Korean fried chicken at Paldalmun Market. spot_mk_1804160.title: Yangsu-ri Traditional Market
spot_mk_1804160.overview: Yangsu-ri Traditional Market is one of the three major traditional markets in Yangpyeong, Gyeonggi-do, located at the confluence of the Bukhan River (originating from Mt. Geumgang) and the Namhan River (originating from Geomryongso Spring in Gangwon-do). Its origin lies in the Yangsu-ri ferry port. It flourished greatly due to its strategic location connecting Jeongseon and Danyang in Gangwon-do along the upper Namhan River water route with Ttukseom and Mapo Ferry, the endpoints of the waterway. Yangsu-ri Traditional Market is about 40 minutes away from Seoul.

spot_mk_131990.title: Yeoncheon 5-Day Market
spot_mk_131990.overview: Yeoncheon has long been famous as a collection and distribution center for beans and cattle. In particular, its beans, known as 'Yeoncheon-tae', are famous nationwide and make it the number one bean-producing region in the country. As one of the traditional markets in Yeoncheon, Gyeonggi-do, the Yeoncheon 5-Day Market opens on every 2nd, 7th, 12th, 17th, 22nd, and 27th of the month. Although smaller in scale compared to other markets, it offers a wide variety of items including foods such as fruits, vegetables, and seafood, as well as hats and arm sleeves useful for farming, plants, and potted seedlings.

Food-related businesses such as vegetables, fruits, dried fish, and mills account for about half of the stores, while clothing and daily sundries are also widely available. Centered around Miso Street (Mill Alley), the market's main gate, it features the freshness-filled Green Street (Ingredient Alley), Beautiful Street (Food Alley), and Mom's Street, which offers fun sights to explore.

spot_mk_2733837.overview: Joam Market in Hwaseong-si, Gyeonggi-do, was also known as Samgoe Marketplace. Because Joam was close to the sea and had a well-developed agriculture industry, seafood trading such as oysters and blue crabs, as well as agricultural crops, flourished here. In the 1980s, the cattle market disappeared, and with the construction of the Hwaseong Embankment, seafood trade decreased, gradually reducing the size of the market. spot_mk_2752650.title: Paldalmun Gate Market
spot_mk_2752650.overview: Paldalmun Market, along with Yeongdong Market, is known as a 'market created by a king.' King Jeongjo, the 22nd monarch of the Joseon Dynasty, summoned descendants of Gosan Yun Seon-do—who had settled in Haenam, Jeollanam-do and were engaged in the trading business—to Suwon. The market is said to have formed as merchants from all over the country began to eye Suwon. Initiated alongside the history of Suwon Hwaseong Fortress, Paldalmun Market has centered around Paldalmun Gate until today, following King Jeongjo's vision to establish Suwon as a center of commerce and economy.

It offers various herbs, wild greens, and vegetables from Jirisan, and dried persimmons are famous in winter, though traded goods have evolved over time.

spot_mk_132392.overview: Also called Samnangjinjang, Songji Market, or Songjijang, Samnangjin Songji Market is one of the remaining periodic markets as markets within Miryang gradually disappeared in the past. spot_mk_2770991.title: Donggwang Fish Market
spot_mk_2770991.overview: Located at Ganggu Port, Donggwang Fish Market is a great place to purchase fresh seafood from Yeongdeok at affordable prices. As a major habitat for Yeongdeok snow crabs, visitors can buy fresh, high-quality snow crabs at low prices, along with shops selling raw sliced fish (hwe), dried seafood, and other ocean delicacies. It offers the freshest seasonal mountain herbs and local specialties such as Mungyeong apples, Mungyeong Omija, Yakdol Hanwoo (medicinal stone-fed beef), and Yakdol Pork, alongside clothing and bedding.

Located 500m east of Oggeori, the center of Pohang, Jukdo Fish Market is the largest permanent market on the east coast. From around 2:00 AM to 5:00 AM, seafood brought in from various ports is distributed to other city markets and restaurants. The seafood here is exceptionally fresh and reasonably priced.

spot_mk_2488220.overview: The transformation of traditional markets in Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Special City began with the successful revitalization of Daein Market, which bustles with crowds every Saturday evening. Unlike the commercial centers of Chungjang-ro and Geumnam-ro, Daein Market is uniquely located downtown, making it extremely popular. As a wholesale market for fish and vegetables, it handles a large volume of seafood and dried goods, alongside fabric stores, silk shops, and brassware and rice shops.

spot_mk_1433867.title: Malbau Market (2nd, 4th, 7th, 9th)
spot_mk_1433867.overview: Malbau Market, a representative traditional market in Buk-gu, Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Special City, is named after a rock shaped like a horse's footprint (Malbau). Boasting a tradition of over 50 years, legend has it that during the mid-Joseon dynasty, Righteous Army General Kim Deok-ryeong shot an arrow here, rode his horse faster than the arrow, and left a hoofprint on the rock. Although the original rock is gone and buildings now stand in its place, the market thrives along the alleys between these buildings.

spot_mk_2783789.overview: Opened in 1964, Bia 5-Day Market is one of the three major public markets in Gwangsan-gu, Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Special City. Held every 5 days on dates ending in 1 and 6 along narrow alleyways, it is a compact yet remarkably well-stocked market. It features vegetables, grains, seafood, herbal medicines, meat, eateries, manufactured goods like shoes, and even a traditional blacksmith shop making hand-crafted farming tools. You can often see vendors carrying bundles of homegrown produce.

Located in a transportation hub near the 2nd Ring Road and Seogwangju Station, it is adjacent to logistics complexes and industrial tool centers, enabling one-stop shopping for agricultural, livestock, fishery, and manufactured goods. Notably, it houses an agricultural and fishery product inspection station.

spot_mk_1622550.title: Art Street Ant Market
spot_mk_1622550.overview: Held on the car-free street of Art Street every Saturday, Ant Market offers lively traditional performances and songs. As the nation's only traditional Pungmul (folk music) market, members of the Gwangju Antique Association voluntarily participate to exhibit and sell a variety of old books, antiques, and folk lifestyle items collected from all over. It is a wonderful landmark in Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Special City to experience traditional lifestyle and bygone eras.

spot_mk_2783840.overview: Located in Unam-dong, Buk-gu, Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Special City, Unam Market is a neighborhood-style traditional market situated in the center of dense residential and commercial areas, offering various foods and daily necessities. Boasting a history of over 40 years, it is not a large market. It is a straight, alley-style shopping area specializing in food, consisting of about 60 large and small stores selling vegetables, meat, chicken, seafood, rice, health drinks, and daily necessities.

Also called 'Madari' or 'Medari' because the village is located at the foot of a mountain, Wolgok Market sits right at its center. Though small, Wolgok Market is exceptionally well-organized. spot_mk_1608882.overview: Gwanmun Market is one of Daegu's top three traditional markets (along with Seomun and Chilseong Markets) and represents the western area of the city. Located right next to Seobu Bus Terminal Station on Daegu Subway Line 1, it offers excellent accessibility. Visitors can easily find a wide variety of street food, side dishes, vegetables, and fruits, as well as fresh produce brought in from nearby regions like Goryeong and Waegwan. The active street vendor area also offers practical clothing such as workwear.

spot_mk_2766801.overview: Located in Gwaneum-dong, Buk-gu, Daegu, Gwaneum Market is a permanent market that opened in 1994. It features small restaurants, rice cake shops, fruit stands, vegetable vendors, and dried seafood stores. Although the interior is narrow, numerous shops line the roads outside. Surrounded by dense apartment complexes and residential areas, it is frequently visited by local residents. It also allows for combined sightseeing with nearby attractions such as Palgongsan Provincial Park, Chilgok Hyanggyo Confucian School, and Unamji Reservoir.

spot_mk_132104.overview: Gunwi Market is a traditional 5-day rural market where a wide variety of goods are traded, ranging from seasonal agricultural produce, seafood, and livestock to clothing, food, and daily necessities at low prices. The market primarily features local agricultural products such as garlic, cucumbers, hot peppers, and Chinese cabbage produced in Gunwi, alongside produce gathered from neighboring areas sold at bargain or retail prices. It also hosts a cattle market, earthenware vendors, and a traditional blacksmith shop.

spot_mk_2766903.overview: Located in Myeongnyun-dong, Jung-gu, Daegu, Nammun Market is conveniently situated just 350 meters from Banwoldang Station. While it cannot compare in scale to well-known large markets in Daegu like Seomun, Chilseong, Gwanmun, or Daemyeong Markets, the merchants who have spent years here are true local fixtures. Nammun Market features raw fish restaurants and eateries, but it is especially famous for its three renowned rice cake shops: Seoul Tteokjip, Gyeongnam Tteokjip, and Nakwon Tteokjip.

spot_mk_2745686.overview: Located in Dalseo-gu, Daegu, Dalseo Market is a traditional market that first opened in 1986. It consists of a shopping mall-style building combining Dalseo General Shopping Center phases 1 and 2. Shopping carts are provided at the entrance for added convenience. Inside the market, various shops thrive, selling street food, vegetables, fish, meat, clothing, and household goods.

Despite its small size, it features a variety of shops including small eateries, snack bars, vegetable stands, and home fashion stores, with 72 stores operating as of October 2021. Surrounded by apartment complexes, it is popular among Dowon-dong residents, and its affordable raw fish slices and dried seafood have recently gained popularity. It attracts about 50–100 customers on weekdays and 150–200 on weekends.

spot_mk_2746376.title: Daegu Gyodong Market
spot_mk_2746376.overview: Gyodong Market is a traditional market situated between Daegu Station and Dongseongro. Following liberation and especially right after the Korean War, refugees gathered from all over, naturally forming the market. Unlike other large traditional markets in Daegu, narrow alleys remain, allowing visitors to feel a sense of nostalgia. For those who have visited the same pathways over many years, it is a market filled with memories and familiarity. Entering the alleys by following the cute goblin guide sign at the entrance, you will find friendly neighbors.

spot_mk_2679564.title: Daegu Beongae Market
spot_mk_2679564.overview: Daegu Beongae Market is a mid-sized, shopping-mall-style market located right next to Daegu Station. Its name, 'Beongae' (meaning 'lightning' or 'flash'), originates from the 1970s when itinerant merchants from rural areas near Daegu gathered spontaneously using early morning trains to sell vegetables and fruits from 3:00 AM to 11:00 AM. Formally established in 1988, its main traded items are agricultural and marine products, alongside clothing, fish, and general goods. The National Agricultural Cooperative Federation (Nonghyup) wholesale market is located right next door.

spot_mk_1610055.title: Bongdeok Market, Daegu
spot_mk_1610055.overview: Bongdeok Market is one of the representative traditional markets in Nam-gu, Daegu. Following the Korean War, the market overflowed with goods from nearby US military bases. Everything from C-rations, blankets, sewing machines, and frying pans to various second-hand goods and military supplies filled the market. Born naturally amidst such an unfortunate history, Bongdeok Market enjoyed its peak prosperity in the 1970s and 1980s, growing into one of Daegu's top four markets before the advent of large supermarkets.

spot_mk_999012.overview: Located midway along the path from Anjirang Five-way Intersection to Apsan Anjiranggol, Anjirang Market has moved past its glamorous past and gained new vitality with the recent influx of seasoned gopchang (beef/pork tripe) restaurants. Starting around 1979 with Chungbuk Sikdang near the market, the number of livelihood-supporting businesses increased after the IMF crisis, revitalizing the Anjirang Market. It has evolved into a comfortable resting place for ordinary citizens and, more recently, a youth street led by the younger generation.

Apples and agricultural products gathered here from Dongchon and Hayang, leading it to be once called Dongcheon Market. Established in 1946 as Bukmun Market under the market publicization policy, it is now a comprehensive market comprising several markets including Chilsung Market, fruit market, Samsung Market, Gyeongmyeong Market, Bukmun Market, Neunggeum Market, Chilsungwon Market, furniture market, Daeseong Market, and flower market.

Having continued for some 50 years since its emergence in the 1970s, Daegu Pyeonghwa Market is a small-scale market consisting of about 80 stores in a commercial-residential complex format. When it first opened in the 1970s, Pyeonghwa Market was not large. In the late 1970s, as surrounding hills and fields turned into residential areas, it began to take the shape of a market, and flourished starting in the 1980s.

spot_mk_132257.title: Daegu Herbal Medicine Wholesale Market
spot_mk_132257.overview: Located on Dongseong-ro in Jung-gu, the Daegu Herbal Medicine Wholesale Market is a global herbal medicine distribution hub with a 360-year tradition. Daegu Yangnyeongsi was certified as the country's top herbal medicine market by the Korea Guinness Committee in 2001 and designated as the first oriental medicine special zone in 2004, making it a cultural heritage of immense tangible and intangible value. After Daegu Metropolitan City designated it as a market wholesaler [Daegu Herbal Medicine Wholesale Market] in April 2020, it opened as a 3-story building in August 2020.

It offers a wide variety of goods including local street foods, agricultural products, seafood, livestock products, fruits, and daily necessities.

The market sells various freshly cooked foods such as kalguksu (knife-cut noodles) and buchimgae (Korean pancakes), alongside fresh fruits and vegetables. Nearby tourist attractions include Hwarang Park, Dongchon Amusement Park, Daegu Senior Experience Center, and Daegu Aquarium, making it a great spot to visit during a sightseeing tour.

spot_mk_2650890.overview: Bangcheon Market is a traditional market located next to Suseonggyo Bridge, one of the 12 bridges crossing Sincheon Stream which passes north-to-south through downtown Daegu. After the liberation in 1945, war refugees returning from Japan and Manchuria started selling goods here to make a living, and it came to be called Bangcheon Market because it was established along the Sincheon embankment. At the time, it stretched about 500 meters south from Suseonggyo Bridge along the stream bank.

It operates as both a permanent market and a periodic 5-day market, and until the early 1980s, its commercial area was so vibrant that it ranked among the top 5 periodic markets in Gyeongsangbuk-do. About 130 permanent shops run from the north to the south of the market, making it great for shopping even on non-market days.

Adjacent to the main road, the market features a wide variety of stores and houses Daegu's very first youth mall. Key items sold include clothing, miscellaneous goods, fish, dried fish, and side dishes. There is also an array of food stalls offering delicious treats like rice cakes, fried snacks, flat dumplings, tteokbokki, fish cakes, and jokbal (pig's trotters).

spot_mk_2766914.title: Sangdong Market
spot_mk_2766914.overview: Located in Sangdong, Suseong-gu, Daegu, Sangdong Market started out as a small market known as Sangdong Super Shopping Center. It was a thriving market until the IMF crisis in 1998, after which it gradually declined, leaving only roadside shops to show that it was once a bustling market. Despite being densely surrounded by apartment complexes, the commercial district has struggled to recover. A few restaurants serving pork soup with rice (dwaeji gukbap) and set meals remain deep inside the market, hinting at its past. Sangdong

spot_mk_2751569.title: Saegil Market
spot_mk_2751569.overview: Located in Naedang-dong, Seo-gu, Daegu, Saegil Market is a small commercial-residential complex market established in the 1970s with about 65 stores. Though small, it offers a variety of foods including vegetables, snacks (bunsik), various grains, and meat. Notable dishes at Saegil Market include duruchigi (spicy stir-fried pork) and bulgogi, with the duruchigi being especially famous for its great taste. Nearby attractions include Bangogae Muchimhoe Alley, Seomun Market, Dalseong Park, and E-World.

spot_mk_2745608.title: Seonam Sinmarket

spot_mk_2788455.overview: Gaegeum Alley Market naturally formed in the 1970s when several subsidiary food stores gathered to do business. It officially opened as Gaegeum Alley Market in 1975 and was registered as a traditional market on April 28, 2005. Starting with the groundbreaking ceremony for an environmental improvement project in 2005, construction to install arcade roofs inside the market was carried out in two phases until 2007. spot_mk_1608608.overview: Geoje Market is the largest conventional market in Yeonje-gu with a tradition of over 50 years. You can purchase a variety of items ranging from fresh seafood, raw fish, and various foods to clothing and general goods. There are many famous restaurants inside Geoje Market, with hand-cut noodles (son-kalguksu) being especially renowned. Specialized hand-cut noodle shops line the market alley, and with many other famous foods available, local residents and tourists constantly visit. If you want to leave special memories when visiting Busan, this is a must-visit spot.

spot_mk_1303759.overview: Located in Geumjeong-gu, Busan, Guseo Osige Market is a shopping district-style market near Exit 1 of Guseo Station. Once a bustling place visited by many customers with around 400 stores, it has declined as other commercial districts in Busan developed. However, it remains popular as a daily grocery shopping spot where you can purchase various foods and daily necessities in one place. Even nowadays, fresh agricultural products such as vegetables, wild greens, hand-made tofu, and acorn jelly grown and made directly by elderly women are sold.

spot_mk_132520.overview: Established in the mid-1960s, Gupo Livestock Wholesale Market specializes in meat and livestock products. Currently home to around 210 thriving stores, it was officially registered as a traditional market in 2006. Spanning 14,000㎡ with approximately 500 workers, the market handles all kinds of livestock products including Korean beef (Hanwoo), beef cattle, dairy cattle, imported meat, pork, by-products, and boiled pork slices (pyeonyuk), supplying and delivering them nationwide to maximize the efficiency and economic scale of meat distribution.

spot_mk_1250885.overview: Gupo Market is a large-scale traditional market that is hard to find in modern city centers. Historically developed around the Gupo-naru ferry on the Nakdonggang River, it has long been a vibrant commercial hub with active trade connecting neighboring regions like Gimhae and Yangsan. Operating as a hybrid of a permanent daily market and a periodic traditional 5-day market, it still buzzes with people buying and selling freshly delivered fruits, vegetables, seafood, and everyday goods on market days, offering the lively atmosphere of a nostalgic rural marketplace.

spot_mk_1013716.overview: Gukje Market Youth Street is a vibrant alley filled with large and small clothing stores. It is a unique specialty district packed with shops and sports stores targeting younger generations. Browsing through the numerous wholesale clothing boutiques makes it easy to find rare apparel and accessories. Affordable dress shops and men's suit stores, compared to other regions, are another point of pride for this street. Located inside Gukje Market, visitors can enjoy shopping alongside a wide variety of sights and street foods.

spot_mk_2788359.overview: Namgwang Market is a compact local market selling a variety of foods and ingredients. Located in Daeyeon 4-dong, Nam-gu, Namgwang Alley Market consists of about 30 stores offering diverse goods and food items. Street stalls and shops lining both sides of the market alley sell a wide range of products including fruits, vegetables, and livestock materials. The generous warmth of the merchants adds to the market's cozy charm. Small eateries scattered throughout offer a place to fill an empty stomach and rest for a moment.

spot_mk_2788830.title: Namsan Market (남산시장)
spot_mk_2788830.overview: Located in Geumjeong-gu, Busan, Namsan Market is a commercial-style traditional market featuring a variety of goods, ingredients, restaurants, and raw fish (hoe) restaurants. Situated near Beomeosa Station, the market offers great convenience with a dedicated parking lot right next to it that is free for market visitors. You can trust the freshness of all agricultural and marine products as well as ingredients sold here. Thanks to Busan's proximity to the ocean, visitors can enjoy raw fish at affordable prices comparable to specialized raw fish centers.

spot_mk_1303784.title: Namcheon Beach Market (남천 해변시장)
spot_mk_1303784.overview: Located in Namcheon-dong, Namcheon Beach Market is a comprehensive market filled with plenty of things to see and eat. Historically a coastal area, the land was reclaimed for residential development, leading to apartment complexes and street stalls that eventually formed the market. Opened in 1989, it is currently a multi-story commercial building market housing about 200 stores. Many vendors specialize in seafood such as live fish, fresh fish, and seafood pancakes, alongside agricultural produce, vegetables, groceries, raw fish restaurants (chojangjip), diners, snack bars, rice cake shops, imported goods, and more.

spot_mk_986063.overview: A traditional market deeply steeped in the salty scent of the Busan sea. While it has evolved from its past as a consignment trading hub into a market mostly run by retail merchants over time, it is a must-visit for anyone looking to experience Busan's savory and distinct coastal aroma. Located at the eastern end of Jagalchi Market, this wholesale market specializes in dried seafood. It houses Busan's only fisheries cooperative auction house, where about 200 stores sell items like dried anchovies, dried squid, seaweed, and kelp.

spot_mk_1942298.overview: Namhang Market formed in the 1960s when people began gathering to live in Yeongdo, Busan, following the Korean War. Boasting the third-largest scale in Busan with a tradition of over 60 years, Namhang Market blends the charm of a traditional market with modern, comfortable facilities for convenient shopping. It primarily handles agricultural, marine, and livestock products either directly sourced from local farms or homegrown. Alongside side-dish shops selling fish cakes (eomuk) and kimchi, you can also find daily necessities and clothing.

Opened in the 1970s, it features about 200 shops mainly selling agricultural products, seafood, livestock, ritual items, and hanbok. Although it is not as bustling as before due to nearby large supermarkets, visitors can still enjoy local delicacies like naengmyeon (cold noodles) and soup.

spot_mk_2796940.title: Daebyeon Market
spot_mk_2796940.overview: Located at Daebyeon Port, the representative hub for anchovies accounting for 60% of the country's driftnet anchovy catches, Gijang Daebyeon Market comes alive during the spring and autumn anchovy seasons. Stalls line the market, bustling with people buying fresh anchovies, salted anchovies, and various seafood. Along with anchovies, it also offers Gijang specialties such as seaweed, kelp, and dried fish. Visitors right by the sea can even watch fishermen shaking anchovies out of their nets.

spot_mk_3031356.title: Daesin Jonghap Market
spot_mk_3031356.overview: Opened in 1932, Daesin Jonghap Market is a mid-sized commercial-residential building market. Unlike most traditional markets that developed from open-air street stalls, it established itself as an indoor building-style traditional market relatively early on, and is particularly famous for its clothing alteration masters. More than half of the shops specialize in custom clothing and alterations, such as hanbok and Western-style suits. Even luxury designer clothes are said to be reborn when brought here.

spot_mk_2785611.title: Deokpo Market
spot_mk_2785611.overview: Located in Sasang-gu, Busan, Deokpo Market derives its name from 'Deok' (meaning hill) and 'Po' (meaning port), originally signifying a market located on a hill. The name was given because a large port once stood here, and a natural market naturally formed as crowds gathered around it. However, when Deokpo Market was registered as an official traditional market in 2007, its meaning was changed from 'market on a hill' to 'market full of blessings.' It offers abundant food and sights.

spot_mk_1608737.title: Dongnae Market
spot_mk_1608737.overview: Dongnae Market carries on the legacy of Dongnae Jangteo, the largest 5-day periodic market in the Busan region during the Joseon Dynasty, maintaining its large scale today. Many shops within the market have preserved their deep-rooted traditions for a long time. Surrounding the exterior of the building are herbal medicine stores, a restaurant alley with prices that rarely increase, and fashion accessories where gentle haggling is welcomed—with most businesses boasting at least 40 to 50 years of history. Rich in history and stories, it is a great place to visit with children and family.

spot_mk_1013694.title: Manmul-ui Geori (Street of Everything)
spot_mk_1013694.overview: Gwangbok-ro is directly adjacent to the front sea of Busan. Consequently, it was a site of Japanese colonial exploitation as well as a place burning with the aspiration for the anti-Japanese independence movement. After liberation, the people of Busan named a neighborhood in Jung-gu 'Gwangbok-dong' to remember the joy of liberation and anti-Japanese spirit. Located right next to the Street of Lighting, the Street of Everything ('Manmul-ui Geori') trades a wide variety of products across numerous shops, true to its name. Lined with unique and personality-filled items, this place...

spot_mk_2742601.title: Myeongji Market
spot_mk_2742601.overview: Myeongji Market is a representative traditional market in the Gangseo area of Busan with a 50-year history. Having evolved from a 5-day periodic market and a dawn market, it has been famous as a live fish market for the past 30 years. Thanks to its geographical advantage where the Nakdonggang River converges, it boasts abundant catches and short distribution distances from the production areas, keeping the live fish fresh across its 120-plus stores. In late summer every year, the market hosts its proud 'Gizzard Shad Festival,' establishing itself proudly alongside Jagalchi Market, Gukje Market, and Kkangtong Market as one of Busan's premier markets.

Mainly focusing on fresh foods such as agricultural, marine, and livestock products, as well as various daily necessities, it is closely tied to the daily lives of nearby residents. It was officially recognized as a traditional market in 2005. Inside the building, you will find stores selling dried seafood, supermarkets, and raw fish restaurants, while the surrounding area features shops selling vegetables, fruits, and everyday goods.

spot_mk_1756609.overview: Opened on September 18, 2008, at Gamcheon Port—a major international seafood distribution and logistics hub—this public wholesale market for seafood features a 71,587㎡ wholesale building, refrigerated and frozen storage facilities with a 25,000 M/T storage capacity, freezing, ice-storing, and ice-making facilities across 7 buildings. It also has a large dedicated pier capable of simultaneously accommodating two 20,000-ton vessels. Furthermore, it boasts modern, high-tech features such as automated logistics processing and computerization of transactions.

spot_mk_1117790.title: Busan Gijang Market
spot_mk_1117790.overview: Centered around Daera-ri in Gijang-eup, Gijang Market transformed into a modern permanent market in 1985 as part of a market modernization plan. Today, it has evolved into a famous marketplace where various goods, including seafood and agricultural products produced in Gijang, are traded. Gijang Market feels more like a traditional lively street market ('jeojatgeori') than a modern commercial market. Its main characteristic is that seasonal specialties define the market throughout the year: seaweed and anchovies in spring, and brown seaweed in fall.

It is divided into an energetic outdoor traditional market and a clean, neat indoor modern market. With the horizon of the South Sea as your view, you can taste fresh and diverse seafood, including a plate of fresh raw fish (hoe), deliciously grilled fish, and spicy seafood stew (maewontang).

The market building spans 1 basement floor to 5 floors above ground, covering about 10,000 pyeong with around 1,000 large and small stores. The building consists of 4 underground floors and 30 floors above ground, with shopping areas spanning from the 1st basement floor to the 3rd floor above ground. Later, following the trends of the times in the early 1970s, it transformed into a specialized clothing market, attracting about 40 wholesale merchants and over 100 clothing vendors. It converted the 3rd floor into a factory space for on-site production, securing competitiveness against similar traditional markets and laying the foundation for growth. Today, it serves as a major commercial district covering Busan as well as the Yeongnam and Honam regions.

Boasting a long history and tradition, it specializes in seafood auctions, playing a key role in upgrading seafood quality, ensuring smooth distribution, and maintaining fair prices. spot_mk_132189.overview: Busanjin Market is famous as a specialized market for wedding gifts and fabrics, and is counted among the top 3 markets nationwide along with Seoul Dongdaemun Market and Daegu Seomun Market. Around 1,350 stores operate here, offering a vast array of goods comparable to a department store. It started as a daily regular market in September 1913, and the merchants' association was launched in October 1930.
