spot_mk_132188.overview: Bujeon Market Town originally started as 'Gijang Alley Market'. Its origins trace back to after the Korean War, when peddlers carrying agricultural and marine products produced in nearby regions such as Gijang, Seosaeng, Ilgwang, and Wolnae unloaded their loads at Bujeon Station on the Donghae Nambu Line and began selling them. The Gijang Alley Market became Bujeon Market, which has now evolved into Bujeon Market Town. It brings together six markets including Bujeon Sangga, Bujeon Market, Seomyeon General Market, Bujeon Ginseng Market, Bujeon General Shopping Center, and Busan Electronics General Shopping Center.

spot_mk_1878218.overview: Bupyeong Kkangtong Market in Busan was formed after the Korean War as US military surplus goods and various imported items were distributed here. It is said to have earned the nickname 'Kkangtong (Can) Market' because many canned goods, such as fruits and fish, were imported. At the time, it supplied imported goods to major markets nationwide, earning it the name 'Dotegi Market' (a bustling flea market). It was large enough that you could find almost anything, including foreign goods, and has established itself as one of Busan's representative markets leading to today's International Market.

spot_mk_132180.overview: Brimming with vibrant energy where tradition and modernity coexist, Namdaemun Market welcomes an average of 300,000 visitors a day. Close to major Seoul landmarks like Shinsegae Department Store and the Bank of Korea, and adjacent to tourist attractions such as Jeongdong-gil, Myeong-dong, Namsan Seoul Tower, and Namsalgol Hanok Village, it is a favorite spot for foreign tourists visiting Seoul. Around 10,000 stores stretch out centered around Sungnyemun Gate. Sayings like 'If it's not in Namdaemun Market, it doesn't exist anywhere in Seoul' and 'Namdaemun Market even has cats'...

spot_mk_132225.title: Namdaemun Ginseng Market
spot_mk_132225.overview: Namdaemun Ginseng Market refers to the cluster of ginseng-selling shops located inside Namdaemun Market. About 20 stores face each other across the central market aisle. Operating as both wholesale and retail stores, general consumers can purchase high-quality ginseng at low prices. Prices vary slightly depending on the item, but they are usually 20-30% cheaper than market prices. The reason for these low prices is direct trading of ginseng and processed ginseng products with farmers and processing companies in the production regions.

spot_mk_2743745.title: Nanseong Sagye Market
spot_mk_2743745.overview: Nanseong Sagye Market is a traditional market located in Sadang-dong, Dongjak-gu, named after the area's former name, Nanseong-dong. Operating since 1966, it boasts a history of nearly 60 years. With large apartment complexes behind the market and great accessibility to subway stations and public transportation, it attracts over 50,000 visitors on a yearly average. Delivery services are available across Gwanak-gu, Dongjak-gu, and parts of Seocho-gu. At the market entrance, various jeon (Korean pancakes) and side dishes are displayed.

spot_mk_132216.title: Noryangjin Fisheries Wholesale Market
spot_mk_132216.overview: Originating next to Seoul Station on Eiju-ro in 1927, Noryangjin Fisheries Market boasts a long history of over 90 years and is Korea's largest inland wholesale market specializing in seafood. A new wholesale market was built in Noryangjin in 1971, and in 2002, the National Federation of Fisheries Cooperatives (Suhyup) acquired the market to promote fishermen's income and the development of the fishery industry. Through modernization projects, it has been reborn as Korea's representative seafood wholesale market where distribution and culture coexist, handling 5% of the capital area's transaction volume.

spot_mk_2751406.overview: Opened in the 1970s, this is the oldest traditional market in Gwangjin-gu, organized neatly as an alley-style market. It has great accessibility as it is a short walk from Konkuk University Station, and popular street foods like nostalgic tteokbokki and traditional snacks draw crowds. Walking a bit further toward the northern end of Yeongdonggyo Bridge connects directly to Yeongdonggyo Alley Market, allowing visitors to explore both simultaneously. Packed with delicious street food, it is frequently visited by people of all ages, and the stores located along the alleyways welcome visitors.

spot_mk_2037026.overview: Located in Daelim-dong, Yeongdeungpo-gu, Seoul, Daelim Central Market is often called a small China within Korea, where ethnic Koreans from China (Joseonjok), Chinese nationals, and South Koreans coexist. While it sells regular market goods such as agricultural, livestock, and marine products, and general groceries, the market also features restaurants run by local Chinese residents and street food stalls offering authentic tastes from China, providing a variety of Chinese culinary experiences alongside Korean food.

spot_mk_2753117.overview: This is a traditional shopping-mall-style market located in Singil-dong, Yeongdeungpo-gu, Seoul, with a history spanning nearly 60 years since opening in 1965. Singil-dong faces Yeouido across the Saetgang Stream and was historically a major transportation hub where a ferry crossing existed for travelers entering Seoul. Naturally, people and goods gathered here, leading to the formation of the market. Today, with many apartment complexes and residential areas densely packed nearby, it attracts numerous visitors with its cozy, welcoming atmosphere.

spot_mk_2782194.overview: Dogok Market is a traditional market located in Yeoksam-dong, Gangnam-gu, Seoul. It originated organically in the 1970s as merchants started doing business one by one. It is an alley-style market with shops lined up along both sides of a street leading from an urban road toward apartment complexes, and it attracts many visitors because it is connected with apartment shopping arcades. As apartment complexes moved into the surrounding area, the market grew in scale, at one point hosting hundreds of merchants.

spot_mk_2789102.overview: Formed near Dongnimmun in Seodaemun-gu during the 1960s, Yeongcheon Market is a traditional market with a history of over 50 years, formerly famous as Seoul's representative ricecake wholesale market. Located near residential areas, it is a quintessential neighborhood traditional market loved by locals. The area around 38 Yeongcheon-sijang-gil, Seodaemun-gu, was designated as Seoul's 'Future Heritage of July' in 2021. As a large-scale traditional market operating around 198 stores, it sells various street foods such as tteokbokki and twisted doughnuts (kwabaegi).

spot_mk_2743857.title: Doksan-dong Livestock Market
spot_mk_2743857.overview: Doksan-dong Livestock Market is a specialized meat market operating since 1974, supplying top-quality wholesale and retail meat from slaughtered cattle and pigs. Cattle and pig offal are directly supplied to processed food companies and restaurants. Currently, it receives fresh meat and offal daily from 73 slaughterhouses nationwide, including Hyeopjin Food, Nonghyup Bucheon, Nonghyup Eumseong, and Pyeongnong Co., Ltd. In addition, the Doksan-dong Livestock Market Merchants Association was established as an incorporated corporation in 2012.

From fabrics and modified 'life Hanbok' designed for modern functionality to various accessories and sub-materials, everything can be found in one place, making it a top souvenir shopping spot for foreign tourists and an educational site to experience Korean traditions.

It covers a wide variety of products from clothing, shoes, wallets to watches, electronics, old books, and movie posters. The items here are so cheap that they feel almost free. spot_mk_2745620.title: Ddukdo Youth Market

Ddukdo Youth Market was once one of Seoul's top three markets alongside Namdaemun Market and Dongdaemun Market, located on the route bringing goods from Gangwon-do since the Joseon Dynasty. Its current appearance was established in 1962. As a traditional local market located in Seongsu-dong, Seongdong-gu, it has recently grown alongside commercial development centered around Seongsu Station.

It was named 'Nanchang' because a warehouse storing grain during the Joseon Dynasty was located in the southern part of Ulsan. It came to be called 'Onggijonggi Market' as onggi (traditional earthenware) produced in the nearby Oegosan Onggi Village during the 1970s and 80s was distributed nationwide. It offers regional specialties such as Ulsan's Seosaeng pears, along with fruits, meat, and seafood.

Situated right in the middle of a densely populated residential area with apartments and multi-family homes, it is always bustling with visitors. spot_mk_2492108.title: Gyodongdo Daeryong Market
spot_mk_2492108.overview: Daeryong Market is an alley market created by displaced residents who fled from Yeonbaek-gun, Hwanghae-do to Gyodongdo Island during the Korean War. When the Han River estuary became a demarcation line preventing them from returning home, they recreated the Yeonbaek Market of their hometown to make a living. For over 50 years, it was the center of economic development on Gyodong도 Island. Today, as most of the elderly displaced founders have passed away and the population has sharply declined, the market's scale has also shrunk significantly. spot_mk_1049865.title: Gilsang Public Market
spot_mk_1049865.overview: Gilsang Public Market is held in Gilsang-myeon, Ganghwa-gun, Incheon. Gilsang-myeon was established in 1914 by incorporating Jeongdu-dong and Jeongha-dong (currently Dojang-ri and Giljeong-ri, Yangdo-myeon) into Yangdo-myeon and merging Donggeomdo Island of Bucheon-gun, Gyeonggi-do. On market days (every 4th and 9th), street vendors begin setting up around the Ganghwa Nambu Nonghyup area from early morning. It is filled with homegrown and foraged agricultural products and various local foods, offering a heartwarming atmosphere and rustic countryside hospitality.

spot_mk_1025514.title: Bupyeong General Market
spot_mk_1025514.overview: Bupyeong General Market is a traditional market with a long history. Its origins trace back to street vendor alleys that formed as the area around Bupyeong Station was developed and the population grew during the Japanese colonial period. It took on the true appearance of a market after the Korean War. As military supplies leaked from nearby U.S. military bases were traded here, it was called the 'Goblin Market' or 'Yankee Market,' and its scale gradually expanded. Later, with the establishment of a fruit and vegetable wholesale market in the 1970s, it grew into a major hub serving Incheon as well as Gimpo and Yeongdeungpo.

spot_mk_132267.overview: Soraepogu General Fish Market is a seafood market located in Incheon Metropolitan City. In spring, visitors can enjoy freshly caught blue crabs on the day boats arrive at Soraepogu, and during the Kimjang (kimchi-making) season, the market is filled with flavorful salted seafood (jeotgal). Unlike the old, crowded, and messy port, it is a neatly zoned modern fish market equipped with a seawater purification system to enhance customer satisfaction, featuring air conditioning and heating.

spot_mk_2465126.title: Singi Market
spot_mk_2465126.overview: A cultural tourism-type market frequently visited by both domestic and foreign tourists, Singi Market attracts crowds daily with its charming alleys and abundant shopping and food options. True to its name ('Singi' meaning fascinating/novel), there are many fascinating things here. One of them is 'Singi Tongbo,' which can only be used here. Shaped like ancient brass coins, Singi Tongbo is Singi Market's own currency system used instead of real money. Each Singi Tongbo is exchangeable for a value of 500 won, perfect for enjoying snacks in the food alley.

spot_mk_3061211.title: Jinheung General Market
spot_mk_3061211.overview: Jinheung General Market is a commercial building-style market established in 1979, and is currently Bupyeong's largest wholesale market. In 2019, it won the Ministry of SMEs and Startups Minister Award at the National Excellent Market Fair. The market consists of four buildings: Ga, Na, Da, and Ra, among which dried seafood is the most famous. In addition, it sells various items such as seafood, meat, diverse street foods, kitchenware, and daily necessities. In the past, it operated mainly as a wholesale market opening at dawn.

spot_mk_2766376.title: Tojigeumgo Market
spot_mk_2766376.overview: Tojigeumgo Market got its name after Tojigeumgo, the predecessor of the Korea Land Corporation, reclaimed salt pans and tidal flats in the 1970s to build a model housing complex, leading to the creation of a market in the area. Surrounded by apartment complexes, it is frequently visited by homemakers and operates about 130 stores. With well-organized roof arcades, walkways, and a home-delivery service, it is a very convenient market. It offers easy-to-go packed items.

spot_mk_2766402.title: Hagik Market
spot_mk_2766402.overview: Located in Hagik-dong, Michuhol-gu, Incheon, this traditional market was formed when factories moved into Hagik-dong in the 1960s, creating residential areas and merchants settling around them. Opened in 1962, it currently operates 65 stores. Although modernized and renovated, there are still many street vendors selling fish, vegetables, and fruits. It features small eateries such as dumpling shops, noodle houses, and gukbap (soup with rice) restaurants, alongside hardware stores and cosmetics shops typical of traditional markets.

spot_mk_132051.title: Gangjin Ogamtong Market
spot_mk_132051.overview: Gangjin Ogamtong Market is a premier cultural tourism-type market linked with tourism, infused with the traditional culture of Gangjin Bay under the vision of a wellbeing culture representing happiness, health, and life satisfaction. It connects Gangjin's 9 major tourist attractions—such as the poetry literature of Youngrang (famous for 'Until the Peonies Blossom'), Dasan Chodang, and the Goryeo Celadon Museum—with 5 major festivals including the Youngrang Literature Festival, Celadon Festival, and Maryang Port Festival. Discovering specialties and linked with the Ogamnuri Town, it is a wellbeing cultural tourism market full of happiness and life satisfaction.

spot_mk_132053.title: Goheung Traditional Market
spot_mk_132053.overview: Located in the center of Goheung-eup, Goheung Traditional Market bustles with merchants and residents on market days. Operating from early morning until afternoon, it mainly distributes food and clothing. The cattle market, which once had a narrow space, has been expanded and relocated to the outskirts. The market is rich in local specialties like reclaimed land rice, garlic, yuzu, pomegranates, and fresh seasonal seafood from clean waters. Among the various foods, charcoal-grilled fish is particularly famous, drawing many visitors.

spot_mk_1434518.title: Gokseong Train Village Traditional Market
spot_mk_1434518.overview: Established in 1956, the Gokseong Train Village Traditional Market is a medium-sized covered market held every 3rd and 8th day of the month. As part of a traditional market modernization project, the historic Gokseong 5-Day Market relocated to this new site in 2009 and continues its legacy. The market primarily deals in grains, cotton fabrics, bamboo crafts, chestnuts, bowls, daily sundries, and local specialties such as native honey and Dolsilmapo (traditional ramie fabric) from Seokgok-myeon.

spot_mk_132059.title: Gongsan Market
spot_mk_132059.overview: Gongsan-myeon is located about 12 km southwest of Naju City Hall, bordering Wanggok-myeon and Bannam-myeon to the east, Yeongam-gun to the south, Donggang-myeon to the west, and Hampyeong-gun to the north, with Mt. Gusubong and Mt. Gomunsan rising within the area. With the Yeongsan River flowing to the north and the Sampo River to the south, it is an agriculturally prosperous region blessed with convenient irrigation. Although smaller than in the past, a 5-day market still operates here on the 1st and 6th of every month, featuring grains and more.

spot_mk_132054.title: Gwaryeok Market
spot_mk_132054.overview: Held in Gwaryeok-myeon, Goheung-gun, the Gwaryeok 5-Day Market opens every 5th and 10th day. Famous for offering locally grown agricultural products and seafood at affordable prices, visitors can also enjoy various street foods and sights. True to its regional characteristics, seafood is traded at remarkably low prices here. You can purchase fresher seafood—ranging from fresh catches by small fishing boats and tidal flat marine life to sliced raw fish—than what is typically brought in from outside regions.

spot_mk_1976858.title: Gwangyang 5-Day Market
spot_mk_1976858.overview: Located in Gwangyang, Jeollanam-do, the Gwangyang 5-Day Market is a traditional market held every 1st, 6th, 11th, 16th, 21st, and 26th of the month. First opened in 1964, it boasts a proud history of over 50 years. It is a great place to purchase various food items and goods, including Gwangyang's famous grilled chicken and fresh agricultural and marine products. With bakeries and restaurants available as well, a visit is highly recommended to enjoy a hearty meal and dessert.

spot_mk_132057.title: Gurye 5-Day Market
spot_mk_132057.overview: Along with Hwagae Market, the Gurye 5-Day Market has long been one of the representative countryside markets in the Yeonghonam region. Considerably larger than 5-day markets in other areas, it bustles with lively crowds gathering from Hadong, Gokseong, Namwon, Suncheon, Gwangyang, and beyond. It is especially famous for wild mountain herbs and medicinal ingredients, offering various wild greens harvested from Mt. Jirisan and Mt. Baegunsan—such as pine mushrooms, bracken, deodeok, aster greens, and Jakseolcha tea—as well as aster scaber greens, herbal medicines, and Gurye's specialty, cornus fruits (sansuyu).

spot_mk_132072.title: Gurim Market
spot_mk_132072.overview: Opened on May 19, 1966, the Gurim 5-Day Market is held every 2nd and 7th day of the cycle (the 2nd, 7th, 12th, 17th, 22nd, and 27th of every month). Spanning a site area of 6,606㎡ with 66 store buildings, the market buildings were renovated in 1998 to serve as a gathering place for local residents and a specialty sales point near tourist attractions. Depending on the season, it offers fresh, clean local agricultural products such as garlic, chili peppers, persimmons, bracken, deodeok, aralia shoots, chamnamul (ormer greens), and bellflower roots.

spot_mk_1976875.title: Naju Moksa Goeul Market
spot_mk_1976875.overview: Naju Moksa Goeul Market is a traditional market that carries on Naju's long-standing market culture, where you can experience the region's rich local produce and heritage. As part of an urban restoration project, Seongbuk Market and Geumgye Daily Market in downtown Naju were integrated to create the current market in 2012, and it was selected as a Culture and Tourism-type Market in 2013. Operating various cultural programs such as the Saturday Cultural Market and Saturday Night Market, it has established itself as a vibrant space enjoyed by both locals and tourists alike.

spot_mk_132091.title: Namri Market
spot_mk_132091.overview: Market days are the 3rd, 8th, 13th, 23rd, and 28th of every month. Most merchants reside in Haenam-eup, with some from Hwangsan-myeon, totaling around 100 vendors. The types of goods are similar to other markets, but it barely keeps its traditions alive with one agricultural tool shop selling plows, A-frames, and rakes, and one traditional blacksmith shop. Since the market only opens in the morning, it is best to visit early.

spot_mk_2758168.title: Namoak Market
spot_mk_2758168.overview: Located inside a commercial building within Namak New Town, this market might not look like a traditional market from the outside, but stepping inside reveals an atmosphere just like any other alley market. Mainly tailored for urban residents looking for groceries, snacks, and dining options, it features stores selling various side dishes, seafood, raw fish restaurants, meat, Korean pancakes, rice cakes, fruits, and street food.

spot_mk_132092.title: Namchang Market
spot_mk_132092.overview: Opened shortly after 1945, this market is held every 2nd, 7th, 12th, 17th, 22nd, and 27th of the month. Most of the merchants reside in Bukpyeong-myeon, averaging around 100 and up to 150 during peak times. While most markets feature many clothing shops, Namchang Market stands right next to the sea, offering a wide variety of fresh fish and seafood ranging from butterfish and silver cutlassfish to octopus, alongside plenty of street food and snacks.

spot_mk_132167.title: Nampyeong Traditional Market
spot_mk_132167.overview: If you take a city bus from the Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Special City to Nampyeong-eup Terminal, the 5-day market is right in front of you. As one of Naju's top three 5-day markets (alongside Yeongsanpo Pungmul Market and Seongbuk Market), the market village is called 'Jang-giri' in Hanja, a name derived directly from Nampyeong Market. The market buildings comprise 50 structures and 171 bays, retailing rice, fish, groceries, vegetables, and clothing. It first opened as a 5-day market in 1925.

spot_mk_132093.title: Neungju Traditional Market
spot_mk_132093.overview: Neungju Traditional Market is a small, building-style market established in 1923, held every 5th and 10th of the month. The market mainly features agricultural products from Hwasun, offering plenty of sights to see during peach season. Due to various locally produced specialties, it is frequently visited by residents from nearby Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Special City. Although not large, it sells diverse items including fruits, vegetables, clothing, and side dishes. Enjoy the friendly and vibrant market atmosphere!

spot_mk_132060.title: Damyang Market
spot_mk_132060.overview: Damyang, home to world-famous bamboo groves, has been famous for bamboo since the Joseon Dynasty and is a primary production region for bamboo handicrafts. The oldest record of Damyang Market is found in the 'Dongguk Munheonbigo' compiled in 1770. While Damyang has a long history of bamboo product manufacturing, the market itself was formed during the Japanese colonial period. The bamboo market is a specialized market unique to Damyang-gun, Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Special City, held along the dikeside walkway in Damju-ri, Damyang-eup. Damyang's bamboo goods are renowned nationwide...

spot_mk_132061.title: Daechi Market
spot_mk_132061.overview: Located in Daechi-ri, Daejeon-myeon, Damyang-gun, Daechi Market is a traditional market primarily selling various agricultural goods and daily necessities. Main agricultural products of Daechi-ri include rice, barley, beans, and sesame, while specialties include cordyceps and cherry tomatoes. Although it once flourished, it now maintains its legacy on a 2,237㎡ site housing 25 stores. Daechi Market opens on days ending in 3 and 8.

spot_mk_132070.title: Deogyang Market
spot_mk_132070.overview: Located in Deogyang-ri, Sora-myeon, Yeosu-si, Deogyang Market was established in 1932. On market days, a small number of merchants conduct business, and restaurants selling beef gopchang (tripe) and beef cattle are particularly famous, drawing steady streams of visitors. Deogyang Market underwent an environmental improvement project in 2008 to upgrade restrooms and market building facilities, and is now well-known for its spacious parking lot, neat signboards, and delicious gopchang.

spot_mk_132073.title: Dokcheonjang Market
spot_mk_132073.overview: Opened on October 1, 1964, Dokcheon 5-Day Market is held every 4th and 9th day of the month (specifically on the 4th, 9th, 14th, 19th, 24th, and 29th). Spanning an area of 4,670㎡ with 934 stores, it thrives alongside some 200 nearby shops. Agricultural, marine, and livestock products are actively traded at this traditional market, which meets every five days. In the past, its cattle market was so bustling that 100 to 200 head of cattle were traded in a single day.

spot_mk_2752133.title: Maryang Noltto Fisheries Market
spot_mk_2752133.overview: Known as the Naples of Korea, Maryang Beautiful Port is a vital maritime transport hub connecting the mainland and Jeju Island. It is celebrated for its pristine living ocean, the evergreen forest of Maryang Gukam Island (a natural monument), and the scenic Maryang Gogeum Bridge. Held every Saturday, the Maryang Noltto Fisheries Market offers seafood of the 'highest freshness,' 'highest quality,' and 'lowest price.' It is a vibrant destination combining local Gangjin agricultural, livestock, and marine foods with cultural events like concerts.

spot_mk_132052.title: Maryangjang Market
spot_mk_132052.overview: Abundant in natural tourism resources and famed as a Grade-1 clean sea zone, Maryang Port receives various fruits and seafood produced in Wando—an area made up of numerous large and small islands—transported via boat on Maryang 5-Day Market days (every 3rd and 8th of the month). True to a traditional old market, Maryangjang particularly offers bamboo rakes, rice-straw baskets, various wild medicinal herbs, and everyday household items used by ancestors that are hard to find in other city markets.

General goods sold by outside merchants are also visible, retaining the nostalgic atmosphere of a classic marketplace.

spot_mk_4013366.overview: Located near Mokpo Port, Dried Seafood Street is where you can find an abundance of marine products from the Jeolla region all in one place. Lined with various dried seafood items such as brown croaker (mineo), fermented skate (hongeo), anchovies, and kelp, it is a popular shopping spot for locals and tourists alike. Many shops offer free samples, allowing visitors to taste various seafood before making a purchase.

spot_mk_1143723.overview: Mokpo Dongbu Market is the largest market in Mokpo, boasting a 60-year history that began when street vendors started gathering one by one in 1956. Following construction work between 2006 and 2008 to install an arcade roof, it overcame the drawbacks of traditional markets to enhance convenience. It continually evolves by diversifying its customer base through the issuance of nationwide Onnuri gift certificates. It also features great facilities including a spacious parking lot and restrooms.

spot_mk_1227095.title: Mokpo Sinjungang Market
spot_mk_1227095.overview: Established in 1999, Mokpo Sinjungang Market is a small, commercial-building-style market. About 10 years after opening as a temporary market, it was registered as a traditional market (certified market) under the Special Act on the Promotion of Traditional Markets and Shopping Districts, entering the legal system and paving the way for revitalization. Since then, like other traditional markets, it has expanded its food and specialty offerings, and is particularly known as a clothing-centric market. Inside, you will find restaurants and clothing stores such as raw fish restaurants, pocha snack bars, sundae gukbap (blood sausage soup) eateries, hanbok shops, and shoe stores.

spot_mk_1177225.title: Mokpo Jayu Market
spot_mk_1177225.overview: Mokpo Jayu Market is a merchant-run market established through an installment savings campaign initiated by the vendors themselves. Famous for its delicious food and high-quality products, it attracts customers not only from Mokpo but also from neighboring regions, boasting high sales. To impress customers, merchants wear name tags bearing store names alongside the phrase 'We will serve you with kindness,' and they have introduced a 100% exchange and refund policy to boost customer satisfaction. Furthermore, strong bonds among the merchants allow for autonomous operation.

spot_mk_1730879.title: Mokpo Chungho Market
spot_mk_1730879.overview: Mokpo Chungho Market is famous for its octopus, boasting the largest number of octopus vendors in the country. It is a vibrant market rich with a wide variety of seafood, including skate. Around 6 stalls specialize in skate, while most other seafood stalls focus primarily on octopus. Recognized as the top market among some 1,500 traditional markets nationwide for transparent country-of-origin labeling on seafood, it's a place where you can make purchases with confidence.

spot_mk_2765255.title: Mokpo Agricultural Wholesale Market
spot_mk_2765255.overview: Opened in December 2005, Mokpo Agricultural Wholesale Market is the largest agricultural wholesale market in Mokpo. Wholesale auctions are held here for fruits, fruit vegetables, root vegetables, and leafy vegetables. Agricultural products shipped by local distributors are auctioned off by the Mokpo Agricultural and Marine Products Corporation for intermediate wholesalers and trading participants.

spot_mk_132064.title: Muanjang (Muan 5-Day Market)
spot_mk_132064.overview: The representative specialties of Muan-gun are onions and sweet potatoes, better known as 'Muan Onions' and 'Muan Night Sweet Potatoes.' The Muan region is the first area in Korea to start cultivating onions, making its soil and climate ideal for onion farming. Muan is also famous for sweet potatoes, with over 60% of its farmland dedicated to them. Notably, the coastal areas feature reddish loamy soil, perfect for growing produce.

spot_mk_2748736.title: Muan Traditional Market
spot_mk_2748736.overview: Muan Traditional Market is a modernly remodeled convenience-enhanced market nestled between apartment complexes. Opened in 1983, it now boasts a history of about 40 years. The 5-day periodic market (held on dates ending in 4 and 9) and the permanent market are integrated into one place. Additionally, regularly operating shops offer side dishes and fresh seasonal agricultural and marine products, providing plenty of sights and foods. Through modernization in 2016, visitors can comfortably explore the market even during hot summers.

spot_mk_132066.title: Beolgyojang (Beolgyo 5-Day Market)
spot_mk_132066.overview: Around 1920, the Beolgyo Marine Products Corporation was established by the Japanese, centering around a daily fish market. By the 1930s, with the opening of the railway to transport agricultural and marine products from the nearby Goheung Peninsula to Japan, Beolgyo grew into a hub commercial city, naturally revitalizing its periodic market. After liberation, it was relocated to the Semang Market area in Beolgyo-ri in 1947.

spot_mk_132069.title: Seosijang Market
spot_mk_132069.overview: A traditional market primarily dealing in seafood and clothing. Notably, Seosijang is located close to the Yeosu Coastal Ferry Terminal and the Yeosu Fisheries Cooperatives Cooperative Market, facilitating the trade of fresh and diverse seafood. The Pungmul Street inside Seosijang is frequently visited by out-of-town tourists looking for fresh fish and sliced raw fish (hoe). You can also expect warm hospitality in the food alley selling Deokyang gopchang hotpot, boiled pork head meat, and jokbal (trotters).

spot_mk_132055.title: Seokgok Traditional Market
spot_mk_132055.overview: Established to increase national income through the smooth distribution of local agricultural products and to enhance the convenience of local residents. It is operated on a site spanning 5,371 square meters with wooden-tin buildings covering a total floor area of 952 square meters across 50 blocks, and is particularly famous for its cattle market. In the past, it was also called Dolsiljang or Dosiljang because there were many pebbles nearby.

spot_mk_2044930.title: Suncheon Araetjang Market
spot_mk_2044930.overview: Araetjang is located in Pungdeok-dong (along the Dongcheon stream) in Suncheon. As the largest traditional market in the Honam region, Suncheon Araetjang is the biggest among all 5-day markets nationwide. It has gained popularity as a food tourism destination where visitors can affordably purchase various agricultural and marine products produced around Suncheon, Yeosu, and Beolgyo. With a night market opening on Friday and Saturday nights, it has emerged as a hot spot favored by young people and tourists.

spot_mk_2765262.title: Suncheon Jungang Market
spot_mk_2765262.overview: Opened in 1981, Jungang Market is located in the heart of Suncheon's old downtown area, offering excellent accessibility. Surrounded by a trendy fashion street favored by the youth, the historic Gopchang (tripe) Alley, and the Okcheon waterfront cultural space, it blends shopping, local cuisine, and culture. Inside the market, you can find a variety of shops selling clothes, soft tofu (sundubu), mills, seafood, vegetables, fruits, rice cakes, bakeries, traditional sweets (yugwa), glutinous rice donuts, and dumplings.

spot_mk_132076.title: Sinbuk Market
spot_mk_132076.overview: Sinbuk Market is located along National Route 13 in Sinbuk-myeon toward the Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated City area, opening every 3rd, 8th, 13th, 18th, 23rd, and 28th of the month. Currently, it covers an area of 6,222m² with 104 storefronts. In the past, it was a bustling traditional market, but urban development and changes in distribution markets have led to a decline. spot_mk_132769.title: Namwon Terminal Market (남원 터미널시장)
spot_mk_132769.overview: Namwon Dongchung Terminal Market is a permanent market established and operated privately next to the express bus terminal when the urban area was developed in the early 1980s, designed for residents on the eastern side of Namwon. Thanks to its convenient transportation, it is frequented not only by Namwon locals but also by residents from neighboring Sunchang, Gokseong, Hamyang, Jangsu, Gurye, and Imsil regions. It is also known as Dongchung Arcade. Farmers from nearby rural areas directly trade vegetables and fruits they grew themselves.

spot_mk_132305.title: Namwon Inwol Market (남원인월시장)
spot_mk_132305.overview: Inwol Market is a traditional market utilized by residents of Jeolla-do and Gyeongsang-do since the late Joseon Dynasty. Opening every 5 days, it started with the sale of local agricultural specialties and the barter of daily necessities. Later, the current Inwol Traditional Market was established, serving residents of Inwol-myeon, Ayong-myeon, Sannae-myeon, Macheon-myeon, Unbong-myeon, Hamyang-myeon, and Beonam-myeon. Serving as a major transportation hub connecting Jeolla-do and Gyeongsang-do, it acts as a marketplace of harmony for residents of both regions. The market is located at the entrance of Jirisan Mountain.

spot_mk_132043.title: Namwon Market / Namwon Public Market (남원장 / 남원공설시장)
spot_mk_132043.overview: Namwon Public Market is Namwon's representative permanent traditional market, established in 1970 near Gwanghalluwan Garden by relocating the outer-castle market that used to open across the Yocheon Stream after the Japanese Invasions of Korea (Imjin War). It is fully stocked with all daily necessities including clothing, general merchandise, bowls, dried fish, fresh fish, fruits, and ancestral ritual items, while also selling local specialties such as Jirisan medicinal herbs, Namwon knives, and woodenware. Popular local foods include traditional sundae gukbap (blood sausage soup) unique to Namwon Market, sweetfish (uneo) sashimi, chueotang (loach soup), and wild vegetable set meals.

It is a small alley-style market with about 72 stores and an average of around 400 daily visitors. Mostly frequented by loyal regulars, the stores sell items such as fish, rice mills, vegetables, fruits, clothing, side dishes, meat, and dried fish.

spot_mk_132297.overview: Muju Bandibul Market is a traditional 5-day periodic market and permanent traditional market held on the 1st and 6th of every month. Its predecessor, Muju Market, was a traditional market formed around 1890 on the site of the current post office, which was once the government office site of Muju-gun, and served as a historic site of the March 1st Independence Movement in 1919. After the entire market building burned down during the Korean War, a 5-day market naturally formed around Muju Bridge, and in 1950, it relocated to its current marketplace in Eupnae-ri, Muju-eup. spot_mk_132299.title: Muju Anseong Market
spot_mk_132299.overview: Muju Anseong Market is a traditional market located in Anseong-myeon, Muju-gun, Jeollabuk-do. It serves as a living hub for locals and a cozy space where tourists can experience the nostalgic atmosphere of the Korean countryside. It has long been a center of exchange for daily necessities and agricultural products, and is currently developing in step with modern distribution trends and changing consumption patterns. Mainly fresh, pollution-free agricultural products are traded here, including omija (magnolia berry), wild durup (angelica shoots), apples, pears, and highland vegetables.

spot_mk_132416.title: Bokheung Market
spot_mk_132416.overview: Bokheung Market is a traditional market in Sunchang, Jeollabuk-do, held every 3rd and 8th day of the month. Situated near Naejangsan National Park, the Bokheung area offers vibrant autumn foliage. If you visit in October during the Jangseung (totem pole) Festival held at Churyeong Pass, you can stop by Bokheung Market in the town center to purchase shiitake mushrooms and highland vegetables at affordable prices.

spot_mk_132288.title: Bongdong Saengganggol Market
spot_mk_132288.overview: Located 15 km from Jeonju toward Daedunsan Provincial Park and 7 km from Iksan IC toward Jeonju, Bongdong Saengganggol Market is a traditional marketplace held every 5th, 10th, 15th, 20th, 25th, and 30th of the month. With thriving suburban commercial agriculture, fresh ginger, king grapes, cabbages, and strawberries are produced and sold here. Nationally famous for its ginger, which is cultivated and sold in large quantities, the market also offers a variety of seasoned herbs and vegetables.

spot_mk_132045.title: Buan Sangseol Market (Buan Market)
spot_mk_132045.overview: Located near the Buan Terminal, Buan Sangseol Market was selected as an exemplary market in 2015. It is gaining popularity as a traditional market revitalized through cultural tourism projects that allow visitors to enjoy sightseeing and hands-on experiences by leveraging Buan's unique local specialties, history, and culture. The Buan 5-day market opens on the 4th and 9th of every month. True to Buan's geographical trait of being surrounded by the sea on three sides, visitors can personally view, select, and taste fresh seafood, primarily sea bream.

spot_mk_1435147.title: Bukbu Market
spot_mk_1435147.overview: Bukbu Market is the largest traditional market in the Iksan area, located in Namjung-dong, Iksan-si, Jeollabuk-do. It operates as a regular market on weekdays, and on every 4th and 9th of the month, a traditional 5-day folk market is held, attracting about 10,000 visitors from neighboring regions like Gunsan, Gimje, Nonsan, and Wanju-gun. Known for its massive nationwide scale, it is considered one of top traditional markets right after Moran Market in Seongnam. The market offers a wide variety of goods, including fresh agricultural products from the Honam Plain and seafood brought in from Gunsan.

spot_mk_132050.title: Sanseo Market
spot_mk_132050.overview: Sanseo Market is a traditional market held every 2nd and 7th day in Jangsu-gun, Jeonbuk Special Self-Governing Province. Although convenience facilities were installed through a facility modernization project in 2010, it is currently a small-scale market used mostly by nearby local residents. Sanseo-myeon is known as the granary of Jangsu-gun and is famous for its rich, high-quality rice. In addition to grains, visitors can purchase agricultural products, general goods, and herbal medicines.

spot_mk_132300.overview: Established in the 1960s, Samrye Market was newly reopened in July 2018 as a modernized market equipped with comfortable facilities and ample parking space, keeping consumer convenience in mind. Alongside the regular market, a 5-day market opens on the 3rd and 8th of every month, offering a rich array of sights and foods through transactions of various items such as locally grown agricultural products, West Coast seafood, and imported fruits. Beyond its commercial role, the market serves as a vibrant cultural hub where local residents and visitors mingle.

spot_mk_132307.title: Samgeul Market
spot_mk_132307.overview: A deeply rooted traditional market that began in the 1910s, Samgeul Market operates in both 5-day periodic market and regular daily market formats. It holds a strong commercial sphere of influence, drawing shoppers not only from all over Jeongeup-si but also from Gochang, Buan, Sunchang-gun, and parts of Jeollanam-do. Market modernization projects were completed in 1978 to give it its current appearance, and in 2011, its name was officially changed from Jeongeup Market No. 1 to Jeongeup Samgeul Market. spot_mk_132325.title: Sunchang Market
spot_mk_132325.overview: Located in Namgye-ri, Sunchang-eup, Sunchang-gun, Jeollabuk-do, Sunchang Market was established with the construction of traditional market buildings in 1923 and is held every 1st and 6th of the month. It is famous for agricultural products like chili peppers, rice, and beans, as well as its 'Sundae Alley' selling Sunchang's specialty traditional blood sausage. In the 1960s and 70s, it thrived as one of the top 7 cattle markets in the country, attracting about 5,000 visitors a day, with embroidery merchants flocking from all over for its famous embroidery products.

Currently consisting of about 120 stores, it features rain-shielding facilities so visitors can conveniently shop even on rainy days. Products sold include Pacific saury, salted seafood, vegetables, yellow corvina, blue crabs, mackerel, tongue sole, and various shellfish.

spot_mk_132295.title: Yeosan Market
spot_mk_132295.overview: The exact origin of Yeosan Market is not precisely recorded, but since ancient times, it has served as a treasure trove of daily necessities. Historically, a wood market was held here alongside fish, dried seafood, fabrics, and general daily goods flowing in from Ganggyeong, as well as firewood for fuel. Today, the market primarily deals in vegetables, clothing, household goods, and miscellaneous items, with garlic and chili peppers as seasonal staples.

Although the old Gunsan Station—once the lifeline of Gunsan citizens—has been replaced by a parking lot and restrooms, the memories of citizens taking the train from the old station, transferring in Jeonju or Iksan to go to Seoul, still linger in a corner of the market.

Although it is now cleanly rebuilt with modern buildings, it originally started as a thatched-roof market. Through reconstruction projects over the past decade or so, it has taken on its current appearance. Osu Market days are held on the 5th, 10th, 15th, 20th, 25th, and 30th of every month.

Located along the route toward Jirisan's Jeongryeongchi Pass, it also attracts many outside tourists. Since a traditional 5-day market has been held in Unbong, a rural center since the Joseon Dynasty, one can easily guess its deep history. Opened as a regular market on March 3, 1965, it spans a site of 3,709㎡ with 43 store spaces.

spot_mk_132332.overview: Located in Geumsan-myeon, Gimje-si, Wonpyeong Public Market is a traditional market with a long history dating back to the reign of King Seonjo in the Joseon Dynasty. It is known as a historic site where the Donghak Peasant Revolution was actively centered around the Wonpyeong marketplace. Furthermore, it was a site of the March 1st Independence Movement during the Japanese colonial period, imbuing the market with the spirit of national autonomy and independence. Today, periodic 5-day markets are held here.

The 1st floor sells clothing, hanbok, accessories, and agricultural/marine products, while the 2nd floor houses shops for herbal medicines, rice cakes, side dishes, meat, and restaurants. Remodeled a few years ago to revitalize the traditional market, Jungang Market features rainproof ceilings, unique themed streets, and a variety of trusted local products.

spot_mk_2754762.overview: Iksan Agricultural and Fishery Products Wholesale Market is a large-scale wholesale market. Situated on a spacious plot of land, it features a parking lot, management building, fruit and vegetable building, vegetable building, and horticultural building in sequence. The market begins to bustle starting at 2 AM. As the earliest starting workplace in Iksan, it gathers seasonal fruits and vegetables shipped from famous production areas alongside agricultural products from the Jeonbuk region. spot_mk_132620.title: Imsil Market
spot_mk_132620.overview: Opened in 1977, Imsil Market is a traditional market operating daily as a permanent market, while also opening a 5-day periodic market (oiljang) on dates ending in 1 and 6. It handles a variety of items including local agricultural products such as chili peppers, rice, pumpkins, and garlic, as well as clothing, dried fish, and daily necessities. Due to Imsil's abundance of orchards, visitors can also find fresh fruits like peaches, watermelons, and berries. On market days, high-quality fish and fresh vegetables are abundantly displayed starting from early morning.

spot_mk_132414.overview: Serving as a transportation hub where the Gunsan-Daegu line and Namhae-Wonju line (former National Routes 26 and 19) intersect and adjacent to Gyeongsangnam-do and Jeollabuk-do, Janggye Market was bustling 20 years ago on market days with people gathering from various regions including Hamyang and Seosang in Gyeongsangnam-do, and Muju, Anseong, Jinan, Namwon, Geumsan, and Jeonju in Jeollabuk-do. Although it is said that its scale has shrunk as commercial areas have become locally revitalized, serving only residents and parts of Jinan and Anseong, the cattle market remains exceptionally vibrant.

spot_mk_132326.title: Jeonju Nambu Market
spot_mk_132326.overview: The history of Nambu Market dates back to the early Joseon Dynasty. It is known that the 'Nammun-bak Market' at that time was the base of Nambu Market. It was opened as a regular public market in 1905, after which the name 'Nambu Market' began to be used. Entering the 21st century, Nambu Market houses about 800 stores, with main items including silk and fabrics, furniture, dried seafood, vegetables, fruits, and medicinal herbs. Today, young people reviving traditional markets are breathing new vitality into Nambu Market.

spot_mk_3065483.overview: Jeonju Dokkaebi Market is a traditional market held in the vacant lot along the Jeonjucheon Stream between Maegokgyo Bridge and Ssaajeondari Bridge in front of Nambu Market, Wansan-gu. It earned the name 'Goblin Market' because it starts between 4 AM and 5 AM and disappears without a trace by dawn. As a representative traditional market of Jeollabuk-do, it is frequently visited by restaurant owners and locals alike because fresh agricultural and marine products grown directly or brought straight from production areas can be purchased at affordable prices. Gaining word-of-mouth popularity, it offers a lively atmosphere that is hard to see nowadays.

All around the market, visitors can taste Jeonju's various foods and experience the vibrant merchants and friendly atmosphere.

spot_mk_522069.overview: As the only market in the western region of Jeonju, it is a distribution market where clean groceries such as vegetables and fruits produced directly by farmers in Wanju-gun and Gimje-si are traded directly. In addition to groceries, visitors can purchase a variety of clothing and sundries. Located near large apartment complexes, it provides residents with a more convenient and reasonable shopping opportunity. Its excellent quality-to-price ratio captures the footsteps of many customers. A variety of rice cakes are sold here, making them popular as snacks or gifts. spot_mk_1334747.title: Jeongeup Shintaein Market
spot_mk_1334747.overview: During the Japanese colonial period, Shintaein was renowned as the city with the highest grain trade volume in the Honam region. Operating as a traditional 5-day periodic market since the 1910s, Shintaein Market was newly reopened on December 30, 2008, following a market modernization project. A key feature of the market is its generally affordable seafood prices. It is also located in a major chili pepper production hub, allowing visitors to purchase top-quality chili peppers and fine chili powder produced at the Shintaein Agricultural Cooperative processing plant.

spot_mk_522533.title: Jeongeup Yeonji Market
spot_mk_522533.overview: Jeongeup Yeonji Market is a historic traditional market that officially opened when its current market building was constructed in 1958. Continuing the traditional 5-day market culture, it opens on the 2nd and 7th of every month. Originally called 'Jeongeup 2nd Market,' it was renamed 'Jeongeup Yeonji Market' in July 2011 to better reflect the local identity and characteristics. Conveniently located near the Jeongeup Intercity/Express Bus Terminal, the market offers excellent transportation accessibility.

spot_mk_522463.title: Jeongeup Agricultural Products Wholesale Market
spot_mk_522463.overview: As a public wholesale market, Jeongeup Agricultural Products Wholesale Market plays a pivotal role in the distribution of agricultural goods in the southwestern region of Jeollabuk-do. It was established to ensure a stable supply of eco-friendly, premium produce and to improve the agricultural distribution system. Adjacent to the Honam Expressway, the market facilitates smooth logistics and provides ample parking space. Divided into fruit, vegetable, and chili pepper sections, it also features convenient facilities such as a bank, restaurant, lounge, and management office.

spot_mk_132046.title: Julpo Market
spot_mk_132046.overview: In the past, Julpo served as a major collection and distribution hub for agricultural and marine products in the southern part of Buan-gun. Alongside Beopseongpo in Jeollanam-do and Seocheon in Chungcheongnam-do, it was one of the three major ports on the southern west coast. During the yellow croaker fishing season, numerous brokers gathered from the Chilsan and Wido fishing grounds for active trade and distribution of croakers and salted seafood. Although the reclamation of Gomso Bay changed its landscape, the market continues its long tradition since the late Joseon Dynasty, actively trading grains, fish, and salted seafood.

spot_mk_132336.title: Jinan Plateau Market
spot_mk_132336.overview: Jinan, along with Muju and Jangsu, is part of the representative highland region commonly referred to as 'Mujinjang.' Being a region surrounded by mountains, exchange among residents and logistics distribution were historically difficult, which naturally led to the development of 5-day periodic markets. Jinan Plateau Market was reorganized into a building-style market in February 2010 and operates as a permanent market, while still hosting a traditional 5-day market every 4th and 9th day. On market days, over a hundred stalls fill the area, creating a vibrant and lively atmosphere.

spot_mk_132293.title: Hamyeol Market
spot_mk_132293.overview: Hamyeol Market originated in Geumseong-myeon during the late Joseon Dynasty and later developed at its current location during the Japanese colonial period after briefly operating near Hamyeol Station. From the 1950s to the 1970s, it flourished as a distribution hub for goods coming from Ganggyeong and Ungpo. However, with the introduction of city buses around 1975, commercial activity shifted heavily toward nearby Iksan, causing the market to shrink. Today, it operates as a 5-day periodic market offering vegetables, clothing, miscellaneous goods, fish, and fruits.

spot_mk_132296.title: Hwangdeung Market

Fueled by goods such as fish, salted seafood (jeotgal), and salt flowing in from Napo and Gomgae (now Ungpo), it was quite large for a rural market. During the 1940s to 1960s, its cattle market and horsehair headband (manggeon) market thrived together. Today, a permanent market has formed due to local industries like stone processing, but the 5-day periodic market still operates. Seasonal agricultural trading is particularly active, with spring sweet potato shoots enjoying great popularity.

Together with the Dongmun Seafood Market, it forms the most important and largest permanent traditional market in Jeju. It first formed right after liberation in August 1945, serving as Jeju's only permanent market at the time and acting as the base for all commercial activity on the island. After a massive fire in March 1954 reduced the entire market to ashes, it was rebuilt the same year.

spot_mk_2913835.title: Ganggyeong Daeheung Market
spot_mk_2913835.overview: Ganggyeong-eup in Nonsan-si, Chungcheongnam-do is famous for Ganggyeong Port and Ganggyeong salted seafood (jeotgal). The history of Ganggyeong Market dates back to the late 17th century around the Ganggyeongcheon Stream. By the late 19th century, it emerged as a major market, famously ranked alongside the markets of Daegu and Pyongyang as one of the 'Joseon Top 3 Markets' (1st Pyongyang, 2nd Ganggyeong, 3rd Daegu), boasting deep tradition and history. Ganggyeong Daeheung Market was established in October 1955 to carry on Ganggyeong's legacy as a commercial city, originating from the first 5-day traditional market.

spot_mk_132519.overview: Kanggyeong Jeotgal Market is a specialty market naturally formed within the town of Ganggyeong-eup, Nonsan. Reaching its peak in the 1930s, its geographic location on the lower Geumgang River and intersection with the Honam Railway made it a major transportation hub connecting both the West Sea and the inland. Consequently, it thrived as a bustling trading center for various seafood, centering around jeotgal (salted fermented seafood). Even after river transport on the Geumgang declined, this tradition continued, and today it has grown into the nation's largest jeotgal market, where visitors can purchase a wide variety of salted seafood at very affordable prices.

In 2012, it was chosen for the Specialized Market Promotion Project, making it a culture- and tourism-oriented market linked with nearby historical relics and tourist attractions. Notably, 'SoriMaru', a radio station run by the market merchants, plays a major role in revitalizing the market.

spot_mk_132743.overview: Seocheon Special Market is a historic market in downtown Seocheon where a 5-day periodic market has been held since the Joseon Dynasty. Consequently, the old market site is called 'Gu-jangteo' (old market), and the current one is called 'Sae-jangteo' (new market). A regular market is held on the 3rd and 8th of every month, serving as part of the 5-day market network around Oga-myeon, Yesan. Its main items include homegrown agricultural products such as chili peppers, sesame seeds, and Yesan apples. Notably, due to the increased distribution of fresh vegetables including Yesan apples and its convenient transportation right in front of Yesan Station, it is a place easily accessible to many visitors.

In the 1950s and 60s, it was a bustling market that even drew shoppers from neighboring areas, but its scale gradually shrank as the rural population declined from the 1980s onward. It offers a nostalgic glimpse into a traditional countryside market, making it a great stop during your travels. Located close to Yangchon (Hipass) IC.

Because of this, Cheonan has naturally developed a thriving market culture as a transportation hub since ancient times. A 5-day market was held here on the 3rd and 8th of every month starting in 1931. Later, Cheonan Central Market—which began as Namsan Central Market in 1918—merged with Central Market and Cheonil Market to be reborn as Cheonan Central Market.

Connected to the Seoul Metropolitan Subway Line 1 via Cheonan Station, it is easily accessible by public transport and blends traditional charm with modern elements. Linked with youth entrepreneurship and urban regeneration projects, the market features youth-run stores, bakeries, cafes, multicultural eateries, fashion apparel, and various retail shops.

Today, it operates simultaneously as a permanent market and a 5-day periodic market held on days ending in 2 and 7. Cheongyang-gun is a mountainous, remote area with limited farmland, featuring the rugged and deep Chilgaksan Mountain, the highest in the county. Gogi-ja (goji berries) harvested from the foothills of Chilgaksan Mountain are Cheongyang Market's signature specialty. Goji berries are known to purify the blood, help clear acne or boils, and prevent adult diseases.

The cattle market here was also widely known, and it is said that up to 100 cattle were traded in a single day at one time. Although registered as a regular market in 1956, it is said to have been established before the Joseon Dynasty. At the vegetable street near the market entrance, you can find a rich variety of vegetables and mixed grains such as spinach, radishes, carrots, shepherd's purse, and mugwort. Because it is not far from the sea, a wide variety of seafood can also be found alongside plenty of manufactured goods necessary for daily life. Built in a commercial-residential building style, the market area originally consisted of fields and paddies, but grew and established its current commercial district after the intercity bus terminal was relocated from downtown. spot_mk_132012.title: Gwan-gi Traditional Market
spot_mk_132012.overview: Gwanteo Market (Gwan-gi Traditional Market), located in Gwan-gi-ri, Maro-myeon, Boeun-gun, Chungcheongbuk-do, is a naturally formed 5-day periodic market. In its early days, it operated as a barter market for grains alongside a cattle market, thriving until the 1970s. However, with the opening of distribution industries and a sharp decline in the rural population, it gradually declined in the 1980s. Continuing its traditional heritage, it still operates as a 5-day market today, while administrative agencies and the market promotion association work to revitalize the traditional marketplace.

spot_mk_2755956.overview: Located in Mokhaeng-dong, Chungju-si, Chungcheongbuk-do, this wholesale market is bustling with various shops selling fruits like apples and pears, miscellaneous grains like corn, vegetables such as onions and green onions, and seafood like cutlassfish and clams. The market is located a short distance from Chungju IC and East Chungju IC. For smooth management, Chungju City operates the Chungju Agricultural and Fishery Wholesale Market Management Office. Nearby attractions include Hoamji Ecological Park, Jungangtap Historic Park, and Chungju.
